  • line 13: the test that failed, along with the name and contents of its dataset;
  • lines 14–24: the assertion that failed ([assertSame]) and the difference between the expected (-) and actual (+) arrays;
  • line 26: the file and line number of the assertion that failed;
  • lines 28–29: the summary.

When a test does not even run (for example, because a file loaded by [require_once] cannot be found), PHPUnit displays the corresponding PHP error, just as running a standard PHP script would.

docs.title: 11.7.5. [business] Layer Tests
docs.text:
The test class [BusinessTest] follows the same construction rules as the class [DaoTest]: [Tests/BusinessTest.php]:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace of the tests
namespace Application\Tests;

// the tested classes
use Application\DaoTaxWithTaxAdminDataInJsonFile;
use Application\InterfaceBusiness;
use Application\Business;
// the PHPUnit classes
use PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider;
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

// loading the classes of the [dao] and [business] layers
require_once __DIR__ . "/../TaxException.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../Utilities.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../TaxAdminData.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../TaxPayerData.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../InterfaceDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../TraitDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../DaoTaxWithTaxAdminDataInJsonFile.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../InterfaceBusiness.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../Business.php";

final class BusinessTest extends TestCase
{
    // the folder of version 4
    private const string ROOT = __DIR__ . "/..";
    // the tested [business] layer
    private InterfaceBusiness $business;

    // executed before each test
    #[\Override]
    protected function setUp(): void
    {
        // creation of the [dao] layer
        $dao = new DaoTaxWithTaxAdminDataInJsonFile(self::ROOT . "/taxadmindata.json");
        // creation of the [business] layer
        $this->business = new Business($dao);
    }

    // the taxpayers of the table of official figures
    public static function taxpayers(): array
    {
        // [married, children, salary, official tax, expected results of the algorithm]
        return [
            "couple, 2 children, 55555" => ["yes", 2, 55555, 2815,
                ["tax" => 2814, "surcharge" => 0, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.14]],
            "couple, 2 children, 50000" => ["yes", 2, 50000, 1385,
                ["tax" => 1384, "surcharge" => 0, "discount" => 384, "reduction" => 347, "rate" => 0.14]],
            "couple, 3 children, 50000" => ["yes", 3, 50000, 0,
                ["tax" => 0, "surcharge" => 0, "discount" => 720, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.14]],
            "single, 2 children, 100000" => ["no", 2, 100000, 19884,
                ["tax" => 19884, "surcharge" => 4480, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.41]],
            "single, 3 children, 100000" => ["no", 3, 100000, 16782,
                ["tax" => 16782, "surcharge" => 7176, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.41]],
            "couple, 3 children, 100000" => ["yes", 3, 100000, 9200,
                ["tax" => 9200, "surcharge" => 2180, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.3]],
            "couple, 5 children, 100000" => ["yes", 5, 100000, 4230,
                ["tax" => 4230, "surcharge" => 0, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.14]],
            "single, 0 children, 100000" => ["no", 0, 100000, 22986,
                ["tax" => 22986, "surcharge" => 0, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.41]],
            "couple, 2 children, 30000" => ["yes", 2, 30000, 0,
                ["tax" => 0, "surcharge" => 0, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.0]],
            "single, 0 children, 200000" => ["no", 0, 200000, 64211,
                ["tax" => 64210, "surcharge" => 7498, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.45]],
            "couple, 3 children, 200000" => ["yes", 3, 200000, 42843,
                ["tax" => 42842, "surcharge" => 17283, "discount" => 0, "reduction" => 0, "rate" => 0.41]],
        ];
    }

    // a test executed once for each of the taxpayers of the data provider
    #[DataProvider("taxpayers")]
    public function testCalculateTax(string $married, int $children, int $salary, int $officialTax, array $expected): void
    {
        // tax calculation
        $result = $this->business->calculateTax($married, $children, $salary);
        // the tax is the one of the official simulator to within 1 euro
        $this->assertEqualsWithDelta($officialTax, $result["tax"], 1);
        // the results are exactly the expected ones (same keys, same values, same types)
        $this->assertSame($expected, $result);
    }
}

Comments

  • lines 18–26: loading the files for layers [dao] and [business]. The test environment is the same as that of [main.php];
  • lines 37–43: instantiation of layers [dao] and [business], as in [main.php];
  • lines 46–73: the data provider: the eleven taxpayers from the table of official figures. Each dataset contains the taxpayer’s data, the tax amount generated by the tax authority’s official simulator [https://www3.impots.gouv.fr/simulateur/calcul_impot/2019/simplifie/index.htm], and the expected results of the algorithm described in the document;
  • line 76: the method [testCalculateTax] will be executed eleven times, once per taxpayer. The PHP 7 course originally included eleven nearly identical test methods, from [test1] to [test11]; the data provider eliminates this duplication;
  • line 80: the tax calculation is performed by the [business] layer;
  • line 82: We verify that the calculated tax matches the official simulator’s result to within 1 euro. We have seen that rounding issues caused the algorithm in the document to yield results that differed from the official ones by up to 1 euro;
  • line 84: We verify that the results table [tax, surcharge, discount, reduction, rate] is exactly as expected, including the data types: integers for the amounts, a real number for the rate. This is why the rate for the 9th taxpayer is written as 0.0 and not 0. This precise verification protects against any unintended changes to the algorithm in future versions.

The results of running these tests are those shown in the previous paragraph: all 11 tests in the [business] layer pass.

docs.title: 11.7.6. PHPUnit in VS Code
docs.text:
The easiest way to run the tests in [VS Code] is to use its built-in terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal): it opens in the project’s [php8-oct-2026] folder, and you type the command [php vendor/bin/phpunit scripts-console/tax/version-04/Tests] there. The up arrow on the keyboard recalls the last command: rerunning the tests after making a code change takes just one keystroke.

Some useful options for the [phpunit] command:

  • [--testdox]: displays tests as sentences;
  • [--filter testCalculateTax]: runs only those tests whose names contain the specified text;
  • [--stop-on-failure]: stops at the first failure.

There are also extensions for [VS Code] that integrate PHPUnit into the editor’s test explorer (for example, the “PHPUnit Test Explorer” extension): these allow you to run a test with a single click and display the results next to the code. They actually execute the same [phpunit] command that we type into the terminal.

docs.title: 11.7.7. Tests for Upcoming Versions
docs.text: Going forward, the tests for the [dao] and [business] layers will be identical to those in version 4. The only thing that will change is the test environment: the files loaded and the way the [dao] and [business] layers are built. We will therefore present only this one and the test results.

docs.title: 14. Application Exercise – Version 6
docs.text:
We have just implemented the following layered structure:

The DBMS used in the examples was MySQL. In the previous chapter, we noted that nothing in the classes implementing the [dao] layer suggested that a specific DBMS was being used. We will now verify this by using another DBMS, namely PostgreSQL. The layered architecture becomes as follows:

Version 6 does not contain any new classes: it uses the classes from version 5. It contains only data files and new main scripts:

version-06
├── Data
│   ├── database.json
│   ├── errors.json
│   ├── postgres-dbtaxes-2019.sql
│   ├── results.json
│   ├── taxadmindata.json
│   └── taxpayersdata.json
├── Main
│   ├── MainCalculateTaxWithTaxAdminDataInPostgresDatabase.php
│   └── MainTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2PostgresDatabase.php
└── Tests
    ├── data
    │   ├── database-incomplete.json
    │   └── database-nonexistent-user.json
    ├── BusinessTest.php
    └── DaoTest.php

docs.title: 14.1. Installation of the PostgreSQL DBMS
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course downloaded the PostgreSQL installer for Windows from the website https://www.postgresql.org/download/, ran it, and then changed the PostgreSQL Windows service—which launched automatically at system startup—to a manual-startup service. With [Laragon], it’s simpler. PostgreSQL isn’t installed by default, but [Laragon] can add it itself:

  • right-click in the [Laragon] window (or on its icon in the taskbar) to open its menu;
  • select [Tools > Quick add]. The list shows software that [Laragon] can download and install, including one or more versions of PostgreSQL, such as [postgresql-17];
  • Clicking on the desired version starts the download and installation. PostgreSQL is installed in the [<laragon>/bin/postgresql] folder, and its data in the [<laragon>/data/postgresql-NN] folder;
  • The [Start All] button now launches PostgreSQL with Apache and MySQL. The [Laragon] window indicates that it is listening on port 5432, its default port.

If the desired version of PostgreSQL is not listed, you can add it to the list: the [Tools > Quick add > Configuration] menu opens the [<laragon>/usr/packages.conf] file, which associates each program with the address of its archive. Add (or modify) a line in the form [postgresql-17=<address of the zip archive>], where the archive is the “binaries” archive for PostgreSQL for Windows provided by the company EDB (the “zip archive” link on the page https://www.enterprisedb.com/download-postgresql-binaries). Alternatively, without using this menu, you can extract this archive yourself into a subfolder of [<laragon>/bin/postgresql]: [Laragon] will find it the next time it starts up, and the version to use can be selected from the [PostgreSQL > Version] menu.

PostgreSQL is used only in this chapter and the next one. It works only when [Laragon] is running, and you can stop it from the [PostgreSQL] menu in [Laragon].

Like MySQL, PostgreSQL has an administrator, the superuser [postgres]. In the installation performed by [Laragon], it normally does not have a password. If a password was assigned to it, the tools will prompt for it.

The terminal for [Laragon] provides access to the command-line client for PostgreSQL, [psql], which is equivalent to the client [mysql]. The [PostgreSQL] menu in [Laragon] also offers the graphical tool [pgAdmin] when it is installed. The documentation for PostgreSQL is available at https://www.postgresql.org/docs/.

docs.title: 14.2. Enabling the PDO extension for the PostgreSQL DBMS
docs.text:
The PDO driver for PostgreSQL is the [pdo_pgsql] extension of PHP. You activate it the same way you did for the MySQL driver:

  • either in the [Laragon] menu: PHP / Extensions / pdo_pgsql;
  • or by verifying that the following line is not commented out (no semicolon at the beginning of the line) in the [php.ini] file (menu PHP / php.ini from [Laragon]):
extension=pdo_pgsql

After saving the change, restart the [Laragon] services ([Reload] button). Then verify that the driver is present using the [pdo-drivers.php] script from the section on MySQL, run in the [scripts-console/mysql] folder:

> php pdo-drivers.php
Available PDO drivers: mysql, pgsql, sqlite
extension [pdo_mysql]: loaded
extension [pdo_pgsql]: loaded
extension [pdo_sqlite]: loaded

The [pgsql] driver is one of the available drivers.

docs.title: 14.3. Creating the database [dbtaxes-2019]
docs.text:
Using PostgreSQL, we will create:

  • a user named [admtaxes] with the password [pwdtaxes];
  • a database named [dbtaxes-2019], of which this user will be the owner;
  • in this database, the tables [tbbrackets] and [tbconstants].

The PHP 7 course covered this task using the administration tool [pgAdmin], a web application that must be installed in addition to the DBMS. As with MySQL, we’ll write an SQL script instead: [Data/postgres-dbtaxes-2019.sql]:

-- database [dbtaxes-2019] of the tax calculation application - PostgreSQL DBMS
-- to be executed by the administrator [postgres] of the DBMS:
--   psql -U postgres -f postgres-dbtaxes-2019.sql
-- the database, its tables and its owner are recreated if they already exist

-- the database and its owner [admtaxes] with password [pwdtaxes]
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "dbtaxes-2019";
DROP ROLE IF EXISTS admtaxes;
CREATE ROLE admtaxes LOGIN PASSWORD 'pwdtaxes';
CREATE DATABASE "dbtaxes-2019" OWNER admtaxes ENCODING 'UTF8' TEMPLATE template0;

-- connection to the new database (psql client command)
\connect dbtaxes-2019

-- the tables are created by [admtaxes]: he will be their owner
SET ROLE admtaxes;

-- the table of the tax brackets
CREATE TABLE tbbrackets (
    id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
    limits NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    coeffr NUMERIC(6, 2) NOT NULL,
    coeffn NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);

-- the table of the tax calculation constants
CREATE TABLE tbconstants (
    id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
    half_share_qf_ceiling NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    single_income_ceiling_for_reduction NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    couple_income_ceiling_for_reduction NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    half_share_reduction_value NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    single_discount_ceiling NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    couple_discount_ceiling NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    single_tax_ceiling_for_discount NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    couple_tax_ceiling_for_discount NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    ten_percent_allowance_max NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    ten_percent_allowance_min NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);

Comments

  • Lines 7–8: We delete the database and user if they exist, so that the script can be rerun. With PostgreSQL, a name containing a hyphen is enclosed in quotation marks, not backticks as in MySQL: this is the first difference between the two DBMS scripts;
  • Line 9: PostgreSQL refers to its users as “roles.” The [LOGIN] attribute authorizes the role [admtaxes] to connect to the DBMS;
  • Line 10: Creation of the database [dbtaxes-2019]. Its owner is [admtaxes], which grants it full rights over the database. The character encoding is UTF-8. The database is built from the template database [template0], which supports any character encoding;
  • Line 13: This line is not a SQL command but a [psql] client command (it begins with a backslash). It connects the client to the database [dbtaxes-2019] that was just created. With PostgreSQL, there is no equivalent to the [USE] command from MySQL: a connection operates on a single database;
  • Line 16: The following commands are executed under the identity of [admtaxes], which will thus be the owner of the created tables;
  • Lines 19–25: the table [tbbrackets]. The primary key [id] is of type [INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY]: it is the DBMS that generates its values during inserts, just as the attribute [AUTO_INCREMENT] did for MySQL. This syntax conforms to the SQL standard; [AUTO_INCREMENT] is specific to MySQL. The [NUMERIC] type is equivalent to the [DECIMAL] type of MySQL;
  • Lines 28–41: the table [tbconstants]. Column names are written in lowercase, with words separated by underscores (half_share_qf_ceiling).

Why these column names? A distinctive feature of PostgreSQL is that column names may be case-sensitive (upper/lowercase), which is not usually the case with other DBMSs. For example, with MySQL, the query [select limits, coeffR, coeffN from tbbrackets] works even though the actual columns in the table [tbbrackets] are [LIMITS, COEFFR, COEFFN]. With PostgreSQL, it does not work, because PostgreSQL converts names that are not enclosed in quotation marks to lowercase: it actually executes the command [select limits, coeffr, coeffn from tbbrackets]. To prevent this from happening, you must use [select "LIMITS", "COEFFR", "COEFFN" from tbbrackets]—that is, enclose the column names in quotation marks. For these reasons, we give the columns lowercase names, and we cannot reuse the camelCase names (halfShareQfCeiling) of the MySQL database. Database object names can be a source of incompatibility between DBMSs, as certain names are reserved words in some DBMSs but not in others.

This script must be run by the superuser [postgres]. In the [Laragon] terminal opened in the [version-06/Data] folder, type the following command (the [-U] option specifies the user name, and the [-f] option specifies the file to run):

> psql -U postgres -f postgres-dbtaxes-2019.sql
psql:postgres-dbtaxes-2019.sql:7: NOTICE:  database "dbtaxes-2019" does not exist, skipping
DROP DATABASE
psql:postgres-dbtaxes-2019.sql:8: NOTICE:  role "admtaxes" does not exist, skipping
DROP ROLE
CREATE ROLE
CREATE DATABASE
You are now connected to database "dbtaxes-2019" as user "postgres".
SET
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
  • Lines 2 and 4: warnings (NOTICE) from the [DROP ... IF EXISTS] commands during the first execution: the database and role did not exist;
  • The other lines are the logs of the executed commands.

We verify the result by logging into the database as [admtaxes]. The [-h localhost] option requires a network connection to the local machine, as will PHP. [psql] then prompts for the password for [admtaxes], unless the server trusts local connections (see the section on testing, below). The [-c] option passes a command to be executed; the [psql] command [\dt] lists the database tables:

> psql -U admtaxes -h localhost -d dbtaxes-2019 -c "\dt"
            List of relations
 Schema |    Name     | Type  |  Owner
--------+-------------+-------+----------
 public | tbbrackets  | table | admtaxes
 public | tbconstants | table | admtaxes
(2 rows)

and the command [\d tbbrackets] displays the structure of the table [tbbrackets]:

> psql -U admtaxes -h localhost -d dbtaxes-2019 -c "\d tbbrackets"
                          Table "public.tbbrackets"
 Column |     Type      | Collation | Nullable |           Default
--------+---------------+-----------+----------+------------------------------
 id     | integer       |           | not null | generated always as identity
 limits | numeric(10,2) |           | not null |
 coeffr | numeric(6,2)  |           | not null |
 coeffn | numeric(10,2) |           | not null |
Indexes:
    "tbbrackets_pkey" PRIMARY KEY, btree (id)
  • Line 5: the primary key [id], generated by the DBMS (always generated as an identity);
  • Lines 9–10: the primary key index.

PostgreSQL can also be managed graphically. The [HeidiSQL] tool provided with [Laragon] can connect to a PostgreSQL server (network type “PostgreSQL (TCP/IP”), port 5432). The [pgAdmin] tool from the PHP 7 course can also be used ([https://www.pgadmin.org/]).

docs.title: 14.4. Populating the [dbtaxes-2019] database
docs.text:
We have already done this work with the MySQL DBMS in version 5. We simply need to modify the [database.json] file, which describes the database. The [version-06/Data/database.json] file is as follows:

{
    "dsn": "pgsql:host=localhost;dbname=dbtaxes-2019",
    "id": "admtaxes",
    "pwd": "pwdtaxes",
    "tableBrackets": "public.tbbrackets",
    "colId": "id",
    "colLimits": "limits",
    "colCoeffR": "coeffr",
    "colCoeffN": "coeffn",
    "tableConstants": "public.tbconstants",
    "colHalfShareQfCeiling": "half_share_qf_ceiling",
    "colSingleIncomeCeilingForReduction": "single_income_ceiling_for_reduction",
    "colCoupleIncomeCeilingForReduction": "couple_income_ceiling_for_reduction",
    "colHalfShareReductionValue": "half_share_reduction_value",
    "colSingleDiscountCeiling": "single_discount_ceiling",
    "colCoupleDiscountCeiling": "couple_discount_ceiling",
    "colSingleTaxCeilingForDiscount": "single_tax_ceiling_for_discount",
    "colCoupleTaxCeilingForDiscount": "couple_tax_ceiling_for_discount",
    "colTenPercentAllowanceMax": "ten_percent_allowance_max",
    "colTenPercentAllowanceMin": "ten_percent_allowance_min"
}
  • Line 2: The DSN has changed; the prefix [pgsql] indicates that we are dealing with the PostgreSQL DBMS. The port is not specified: it is the default port for PostgreSQL, 5432;
  • lines 5 and 10: the table names are prefixed with the name of the schema to which they belong, [public]. A PostgreSQL database can contain multiple schemas, which serve as namespaces for the tables. This was not strictly necessary since [public] is the default schema used when no schema is specified in the table name;
  • lines 11–20: the column names in the constants table have changed.

The [Main/MainTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2PostgresDatabase.php] script for populating the [dbtaxes-2019] database is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// inclusion of the interfaces and classes of version 5 needed for the transfer
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxException.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxAdminData.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/Database.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Utilities/Utilities.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/InterfaceDao4TransferAdminData2Database.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/DaoTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2Database.php";

// definition of the constants
const DATABASE_CONFIG_FILENAME = __DIR__ . "/../Data/database.json";
const TAXADMINDATA_FILENAME = __DIR__ . "/../Data/taxadmindata.json";

try {
    // creation of the [dao] layer
    $dao = new DaoTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2Database(DATABASE_CONFIG_FILENAME, TAXADMINDATA_FILENAME);
    // transfer of the data into the database
    $dao->transferAdminData2Database();
    print "The data of the tax administration have been transferred into the database\n";
} catch (TaxException $ex) {
    // we display the error
    print "Error no. {$ex->getCode()}: {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
}
// end
print "Done\n";

Comments

Only lines 10–15, which load the files required to run the application, have changed from the Version 5 script: the files are now located in the [version-05] folder, adjacent to the [version-06] folder. The constants on lines 18–19 refer to the files in the [version-06/Data] folder.

When this script is run, the following result is obtained:

> php MainTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2PostgresDatabase.php
The data of the tax administration have been transferred into the database
Done

and the following content in the [tbbrackets] table:

> psql -U admtaxes -h localhost -d dbtaxes-2019 -c "select * from tbbrackets"
 id |  limits   | coeffr |  coeffn
----+-----------+--------+----------
  1 |   9964.00 |   0.00 |     0.00
  2 |  27519.00 |   0.14 |  1394.96
  3 |  73779.00 |   0.30 |  5798.00
  4 | 156244.00 |   0.41 | 13913.69
  5 |      0.00 |   0.45 | 20163.45
(5 rows)

We repeat the same process for the constants table [tbconstants]. The [-x] option of [psql] displays each row vertically:

> psql -U admtaxes -h localhost -d dbtaxes-2019 -x -c "select * from tbconstants"
-[ RECORD 1 ]-----------------------+---------
id                                  | 1
half_share_qf_ceiling               | 1551.00
single_income_ceiling_for_reduction | 21037.00
couple_income_ceiling_for_reduction | 42074.00
half_share_reduction_value          | 3797.00
single_discount_ceiling             | 1196.00
couple_discount_ceiling             | 1970.00
single_tax_ceiling_for_discount     | 1595.00
couple_tax_ceiling_for_discount     | 2627.00
ten_percent_allowance_max           | 12502.00
ten_percent_allowance_min           | 437.00

This time, the [PDO::connect] method created an object of the [Pdo\Pgsql] class, and the PostgreSQL driver was used, without a single line of the [DaoTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2Database] class being modified. Note that to run the script, neither the Apache server nor the MySQL DBMS is required: only the PostgreSQL DBMS needs to be launched.

docs.title: 14.5. Tax Calculation
docs.text:
The [dao] [3] and [business] [2] layers have already been written. We have already written the main script for the MySQL DBMS in version 5. All we need to do is take the [MainCalculateTaxWithTaxAdminDataInMySQLDatabase.php] script and adapt it for the PostgreSQL DBMS. It is now called [MainCalculateTaxWithTaxAdminDataInPostgresDatabase.php]:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// inclusion of the interfaces and classes of version 5
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxException.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxAdminData.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxPayerData.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/Database.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Utilities/Utilities.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/InterfaceDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/TraitDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/DaoTaxWithTaxAdminDataInDatabase.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Business/InterfaceBusiness.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Business/Business.php";

// definition of the constants
const DATABASE_CONFIG_FILENAME = __DIR__ . "/../Data/database.json";
const TAXPAYERSDATA_FILENAME = __DIR__ . "/../Data/taxpayersdata.json";
const RESULTS_FILENAME = __DIR__ . "/../Data/results.json";
const ERRORS_FILENAME = __DIR__ . "/../Data/errors.json";

try {
    // creation of the [dao] layer
    $dao = new DaoTaxWithTaxAdminDataInDatabase(DATABASE_CONFIG_FILENAME);
    // creation of the [business] layer
    $business = new Business($dao);
    // tax calculation in batch mode
    $business->executeBatchTaxes(TAXPAYERSDATA_FILENAME, RESULTS_FILENAME, ERRORS_FILENAME);
    print "The results have been saved in the file [results.json]\n";
} catch (TaxException $ex) {
    // we display the error
    print "Error no. {$ex->getCode()}: {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
}
// end
print "Done\n";

Comments

Once again, only lines 10–19, which load the Version 5 files, have changed. The JSON files used are those from the [version-06/Data] folder, specifically the [database.json] file, which describes the PostgreSQL database.

Execution Results

> php MainCalculateTaxWithTaxAdminDataInPostgresDatabase.php
The results have been saved in the file [results.json]
Done

The files [errors.json] and [results.json] generated in the [version-06/Data] folder are identical to those obtained with the MySQL database in version 5.

docs.title: 14.6. [PHPUnit] Tests
docs.text: As with previous versions, we are validating this version using [PHPUnit] tests. The test classes [DaoTest] and [BusinessTest] from the [version-06/Tests] folder are the same as those in version 5. The only change is the test environment: the application files are loaded from the [version-05] folder, and the data comes from the [version-06/Data] folder.

docs.title: 14.6.1. Test of layer [dao]
docs.text:
The beginning of the [Tests/DaoTest.php] test is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace of the tests
namespace Application\Tests;

// the tested classes
use Application\DaoTaxWithTaxAdminDataInDatabase;
use Application\DaoTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2Database;
use Application\TaxException;
use Application\InterfaceDao;
use Application\TaxAdminData;
use Application\TaxPayerData;
// the PHPUnit classes
use PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider;
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

// loading the classes of the [dao] layer of version 5
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxException.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxAdminData.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/TaxPayerData.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Entities/Database.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Utilities/Utilities.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/InterfaceDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/TraitDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/DaoTaxWithTaxAdminDataInDatabase.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/InterfaceDao4TransferAdminData2Database.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../version-05/Dao/DaoTransferAdminDataFromJsonFile2Database.php";

final class DaoTest extends TestCase
{
    // the data folder of version 6
    private const string DATA = __DIR__ . "/../Data";
    // the tested [dao] layer
    private InterfaceDao $dao;
    // a temporary file for the errors
    private string $errorsFilename;

Comments

  • Lines 21–30: Test environment definition: the classes from layer [dao] of version 5 are loaded;
  • line 35: the test data is from version 6, specifically the file [database.json] from the PostgreSQL database.

The test methods are those from version 5, with one exception. The file [database-incomplete.json] in the folder [Tests/data] is the version 5 file adapted for the PostgreSQL database. However, the “incorrect password” test case from Version 5 has been replaced by a “user does not exist” test case:

    // incorrect descriptions of the database
    public static function invalidDatabases(): array
    {
        // [file name, expected error code]
        return [
            "non-existent file" => ["nonexistent.json", 15],
            "missing key" => ["database-incomplete.json", 21],
            // with PostgreSQL, we test a non-existent user rather than a wrong password:
            // if the server trusts the local connections ([trust] method), it does not check
            // the passwords, but it always refuses a user it does not know
            "non-existent user" => ["database-nonexistent-user.json", 30],
        ];
    }
  • Line 102: The file [database-nonexistent-user.json] describes the database with a user named [unknown], which PostgreSQL does not recognize. The connection fails, and the [dao] layer triggers a [TaxException] with code 30.

Why this change? For each connection type, a PostgreSQL server selects an authentication method specified in its configuration file [pg_hba.conf] (in the PostgreSQL data folder, [<laragon>/data/postgresql-NN] with [Laragon]). The [scram-sha-256] method verifies the password. The [trust] method, on the other hand, trusts the client: it accepts the connection without verifying the password, provided that the user exists. This is the method used by the PostgreSQL installation created by [Laragon] for connections originating from the local machine, which explains why the superuser [postgres] has no password. With this configuration, an incorrect password is accepted: the “incorrect password” test would fail, since the expected exception is not thrown. A nonexistent user, on the other hand, is denied access regardless of the authentication method: the test works on all installations. The [trust] method is convenient on a development machine; it should obviously not be used on a production server.

docs.title: 14.6.2. Testing the [business] layer
docs.text:
Similarly, the [Tests/BusinessTest.php] test is the one from version 5 with a modified environment:

docs.title: 4.1. The problem
docs.text:
The table above (a French page from lefigaro.fr) is used to calculate the tax in the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only their salary to report. As indicated in note (1), the tax calculated this way is the tax before three adjustments:

  • the family quotient cap, which applies to high incomes;
  • the discount and the reduction that apply to low-income earners.

Thus, the tax calculation involves the following steps [http://impotsurlerevenu.org/comprendre-le-calcul-de-l-impot/1217-calcul-de-l-impot-2019.php]:

We propose to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax in the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only a single salary to report. The rules used are those for the 2019 tax on 2018 income. They will serve as a guiding principle throughout this document: the algorithm will remain the same across different versions of the application; only its architecture will change.

docs.title: 4.1.1. Calculation of Gross Tax
docs.text:
The gross tax can be calculated as follows.

First, calculate the taxpayer’s number of shares:

  • each parent contributes 1 share;
  • the first two children each contribute 1/2 share;
  • subsequent children each contribute one share.

The number of shares is therefore:

  • nbShares = 1 + nbChildren * 0.5 + (nbChildren - 2) * 0.5 if the employee is unmarried;
  • nbShares = 2 + nbChildren * 0.5 + (nbChildren - 2) * 0.5 if they are married;

where nbChildren is the number of children, and the term (number of children - 2) * 0.5 applies only when there are three or more children. Next:

  • the taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.9 * S, where S is the annual salary;
  • the family quotient QF = R / nbShares is calculated;
  • calculate the gross tax I based on the following data (2019):
field1 (threshold for QF)field2 (coeffR)field3 (coeffN)99640027,5190.141,394.9673,7790.35,798156,2440.4113,913.6900.4520,163.45

Each row has 3 fields: field1, field2, field3. To calculate tax I, find the first row where QF <= field1 and use the values from that row. For example, for a married employee with two children and an annual salary S of 50,000 euros:

  • taxable income: R = 0.9 * S = 45,000;
  • number of shares: nbShares = 2 + 2 * 0.5 = 3;
  • family quotient: QF = 45,000 / 3 = 15,000.

The first row where QF <= field1 is as follows:

27519    0.14    1394.96

Tax I is then equal to 0.14*R – 1,394.96*nbShares=[0.14*45000-1394.96*3]=2,115. The tax is rounded down to the nearest euro.

If the condition QF <= field1 is satisfied starting from the first line, then the tax is zero.

If QF is such that the condition QF <= field1 is never satisfied, then the coefficients from the last line are used. In this case:

0    0.45    20163.45

which yields the gross tax I = 0.45*R – 20,163.45*nbShares.

docs.title: 4.1.2. Family Quotient Cap
docs.text:
To determine whether the family quotient cap QF applies, we recalculate the gross tax without including the children. Again, for the married employee with two children and an annual salary S of 50,000 euros:

  • taxable income: R = 0.9 * S = 45,000;
  • number of shares: nbShares = 2 (children are no longer counted);
  • family quotient: QF = 45,000 / 2 = 22,500.

The first line where QF <= field1 is as follows:

27519    0.14    1394.96

Tax I is then equal to 0.14*R – 1,394.96*nbShares=[0.14*45000-1394.96*2]=3,510.

  • Maximum child-related income: 1,551 * 2 = 3,102 euros;
  • minimum tax: 3,510 – 3,102 = 408 euros.

The gross tax with 3 shares, already calculated at 2,115 euros, is higher than the minimum tax of 408 euros, so the family cap does not apply here.

In general, the gross tax is max(tax1, tax2), where:

  • [tax1]: is the gross tax calculated with children;
  • [tax2]: is the gross tax calculated without children and reduced by the maximum deduction (here, 1,551 euros per half-share) related to children.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Calculation of the Discount
docs.text:
Again, for the married employee with two children and an annual salary S of 50,000 euros:

The gross tax (2,115) from the previous step is less than 2,627 euros for a married couple (1,595 euros for a single person): therefore, the discount applies. It is calculated as follows:

  • discount = threshold (couple=1,970 / single=1,196) - 0.75 * gross tax;
  • discount = 1,970 – 0.75 × 2,115 = 383.75, rounded to 384 euros;
  • new gross tax = 2,115 – 384 = 1,731 euros.

docs.title: 4.1.4. Calculation of the Reduction
docs.text:
Below a certain threshold, a 20% reduction is applied to the gross tax resulting from the previous calculations. In 2019, the thresholds are as follows:

  • single: 21,037 euros;
  • couple: 42,074 euros (the figure 37,968 used in the example above appears to be incorrect).

This threshold is increased by the value: 3,797 * (number of half-shares contributed by the children).

Again, for the married employee with two children and an annual salary S of 50,000 euros:

  • his taxable income (45,000 euros) is below the threshold (42,074 + 2 × 3,797) = 49,668 euros;
  • he is therefore entitled to a 20% reduction in his tax: 1,731 * 0.2 = 346.2 euros, rounded to 347 euros;
  • the taxpayer’s gross tax becomes: 1,731 – 347 = 1,384 euros.

docs.title: 4.1.5. Calculation of Net Tax
docs.text: Our calculation ends here: the net tax due will be 1,384 euros. In reality, the taxpayer may be eligible for other deductions, particularly for donations to public-interest or general-interest organizations.

docs.title: 4.1.6. High-Income Earners
docs.text: Our previous example applies to the majority of employees. However, the tax calculation differs for high-income earners.

docs.title: 4.1.6.1. Cap on the 10% reduction on annual income
docs.text:
In most cases, taxable income is calculated using the formula: R = 0.9 × S, where S is the annual salary. This is known as the 10% reduction. This reduction is capped. In 2019:

  • it cannot exceed 12,502 euros;
  • it cannot be less than 437 euros.

Consider the case of an unmarried employee with no children and an annual salary of 200,000 euros:

  • the 10% reduction is 200,000 euros > 12,502 euros. It is therefore capped at 12,502 euros.

docs.title: 4.1.6.2. Family Quotient Cap
docs.text:
Let’s consider a case where the family quotient cap described in the “Family Quotient Cap” section above applies: a couple with three children and an annual income of 100,000 euros. Let’s go through the calculation steps again:

  • the 10% deduction is 10,000 euros < 12,502 euros. The taxable income R is therefore 100,000 – 10,000 = 90,000 euros;
  • the couple has nbShares = 2 + 0.5 × 2 + 1 = 4 shares;
  • their family quotient is therefore QF = R / nbShares = 90,000 / 4 = 22,500 euros;
  • their gross tax I1 with children is I1 = 0.14 × 90,000 − 1,394.96 × 4 = 7,020 euros;
  • his gross tax I2 without children:
    • QF = 90,000 / 2 = 45,000 euros;
    • I2 = 0.3 × 90,000 − 5,798 × 2 = 15,404 euros;
    • The family quotient cap rule states that the benefit derived from children cannot exceed (1,551 × 4 half-shares) = 6,204 euros. However, in this case, it is I2-I1 = 15,404 – 7,020 = 8,384 euros, which is greater than 6,204 euros;
    • The gross tax is therefore recalculated as I3 = I2-6204 = 15,404 - 6,204 = 9,200 euros.

This couple will receive neither a discount nor a reduction, and their final tax will be 9,200 euros.

In the example above, the “surcharge” refers to the additional amount paid by high-income earners due to two factors:

  • the cap on the 10% deduction from annual income;
  • the cap on the family quotient.

This indicator could not be verified because the tax authority’s simulator does not provide it.

We can see that the document’s algorithm calculates the correct tax amount every time, though with a margin of error of 1 euro. This margin of error stems from rounding. All monetary amounts are rounded—sometimes up to the next euro, sometimes down to the nearest euro. Since the author is unaware of the official rounding rules, the monetary amounts in the document’s algorithm have been rounded:

  • up to the next euro for discounts and reductions;
  • down to the nearest euro for surcharges and the final tax.

In the following section, tests will be conducted to verify the validity of the results. These tests will be performed using the examples from the previous table with an accepted margin of error of 1 euro.

docs.title: 4.2. The script directory structure
docs.text:
The first two versions of the application are in the [scripts-console/tax] folder:

tax

For reference, the file [verified-results.txt] contains the results obtained using the official simulator for the taxpayers in the file [taxpayersdata.txt].

docs.title: 4.3.1. The Algorithm
docs.text:
We present an initial program in which:

  • the data needed to calculate the tax is hard-coded in the program as arrays and constants;
  • taxpayer data (marital status, children, salary) is stored in a first text file, [taxpayersdata.txt];
  • the results of the tax calculation (marital status, children, salary, tax, etc.) are stored in a second text file, [results.txt].

The data file [taxpayersdata.txt] (married, children, salary) is as follows:

yes,2,55555
yes,2,50000
yes,3,50000
no,2,100000
no,3,100000
yes,3,100000
yes,5,100000
no,0,100000
yes,2,30000
no,0,200000
yes,3,200000

The main program of the script [version-01/main.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict types for the parameters and results of functions
declare(strict_types=1);

// global constants
const HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING = 1551;
const SINGLE_INCOME_CEILING_FOR_REDUCTION = 21037;
const COUPLE_INCOME_CEILING_FOR_REDUCTION = 42074;
const HALF_SHARE_REDUCTION_VALUE = 3797;
const SINGLE_DISCOUNT_CEILING = 1196;
const COUPLE_DISCOUNT_CEILING = 1970;
const COUPLE_TAX_CEILING_FOR_DISCOUNT = 2627;
const SINGLE_TAX_CEILING_FOR_DISCOUNT = 1595;
const TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MAX = 12502;
const TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MIN = 437;

// definition of the local constants
$DATA = "taxpayersdata.txt";
$RESULTS = "results.txt";
$limits = [9964, 27519, 73779, 156244, 0];
$coeffR = [0, 0.14, 0.3, 0.41, 0.45];
$coeffN = [0, 1394.96, 5798, 13913.69, 20163.45];

// opening the data file
$data = is_readable($DATA) ? fopen($DATA, "r") : false;
if ($data === false) {
    print "Unable to open the data file [$DATA] for reading\n";
    exit;
}

// opening the results file
$results = fopen($RESULTS, "w");
if ($results === false) {
    print "Unable to create the results file [$RESULTS]\n";
    exit;
}

// we process the current line of the data file
while (($line = fgets($data, 100)) !== false) {
    // we remove the possible end-of-line mark
    $line = cutNewLineChar($line);
    // we retrieve the 3 fields married,children,salary that make up $line
    [$married, $children, $salary] = explode(",", $line);
    $married = strtolower($married);
    $children = (int) $children;
    $salary = (int) $salary;
    // we calculate the tax
    $result = calculateTax($married, $children, $salary, $limits, $coeffR, $coeffN);
    // we write the result into the results file
    $result = ["married" => $married, "children" => $children, "salary" => $salary] + $result;
    fputs($results, json_encode($result, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE) . "\n");
    // next data
}
// we close the files
fclose($data);
fclose($results);
print "The results have been saved in the file [$RESULTS]\n";

// end
exit;

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function cutNewLineChar(string $line): string
{
    // we remove the end-of-line mark of $line if it exists
    // (\r\n on Windows, \n on Unix)
    return rtrim($line, "\r\n");
}

Comments:

  • line 4: we enforce strict adherence to the types of parameters and function return values;
  • Lines 7–16: Definition of all constants needed to calculate the tax. The keyword [const] defines a global constant that is accessible throughout the script, including within functions. The PHP 7 course used the function [define("HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING", 1551)], which does the same thing and still exists. [const] is more readable and allows the editor to check the names of the constants. By convention, constant names are in uppercase;
  • line 19: the name of the text file containing taxpayer data (married status, children, salary);
  • line 20: the name of the text file containing the tax calculation results;
  • lines 21–23: the three data tables defining the different tax brackets used in the tax calculation. These are the three columns of the table in the “Calculation of Gross Tax” section;
  • lines 26–30: open the taxpayer data file for reading using [r]. The function [is_readable] first checks whether the file exists and can be read: if not, [$data] is set to [false]. This prevents the warning that [fopen] would issue if the file were missing. The function [fopen] also returns the value [false] if the file could not be opened;
  • lines 33–37: open the results file for writing using [w];
  • lines 40–54: loop to read the lines (married, children, salary) from the taxpayer data file;
  • line 40: the function [fgets] reads up to 100 characters and stops at the first end-of-line marker encountered. Here, all lines are less than 100 characters long. If an end-of-line character is encountered, it is included in the returned string. When the end of the file is reached, the function [fgets] returns the value [false];
  • line 42: the line-end character is removed. The file [taxpayersdata.txt] was created in Windows: its lines end with the two characters \r\n;
  • line 44: the components (married, children, salary) of the line are retrieved. These are three character strings;
  • lines 45–47: the marital status is converted to lowercase, and the number of children and the salary are converted to integers. These explicit conversions are necessary: in strict mode, the function [calculateTax] would not accept the string "2" for its parameter [int $children];
  • line 49: the tax is calculated. The result is returned as an associative array. Note that the salary, a [int], is passed to the [float $salary] parameter of the [calculateTax] function: this is the only conversion allowed in strict mode;
  • line 51: The keys [married, children, salary] are added to the beginning of the array retrieved previously. The + operator applied to two associative arrays returns an array containing the elements of both arrays;
  • line 52: the result is stored in the results file as a JSON string, with one line per taxpayer;
  • lines 56–57: Once the taxpayer data file has been fully processed, the files are closed;
  • line 64: the function that removes the line-end character from a line of the [$line] string. The line-end character is the string "\r\n" on Windows systems and "\n" on Unix systems. The result is the input string without its line-end character.

The function [calculateTax] is as follows:

// tax calculation
// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function calculateTax(string $married, int $children, float $salary, array $limits, array $coeffR, array $coeffN): array
{
    // $married: yes, no
    // $children: number of children
    // $salary: annual salary
    // $limits, $coeffR, $coeffN: the arrays of the data used to calculate the tax
    //
    // calculation of the tax with children
    $result1 = calculateTax2($married, $children, $salary, $limits, $coeffR, $coeffN);
    $tax1 = $result1["tax"];
    // calculation of the tax without the children
    if ($children !== 0) {
        $result2 = calculateTax2($married, 0, $salary, $limits, $coeffR, $coeffN);
        $tax2 = $result2["tax"];
        // application of the family quotient ceiling
        if ($children < 3) {
            // HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING euros for the first 2 children
            $tax2 = $tax2 - $children * HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING;
        } else {
            // HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING euros for the first 2 children, double for the following ones
            $tax2 = $tax2 - 2 * HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING - ($children - 2) * 2 * HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING;
        }
    } else {
        $tax2 = $tax1;
        $result2 = $result1;
    }
    // we take the highest tax with the rate and the surcharge that go with it
    if ($tax1 > $tax2) {
        $tax = $tax1;
        $rate = $result1["rate"];
        $surcharge = $result1["surcharge"];
    } else {
        $surcharge = $tax2 - $tax1 + $result2["surcharge"];
        $tax = $tax2;
        $rate = $result2["rate"];
    }
    // calculation of a possible discount
    $discount = getDiscount($married, $salary, $tax);
    $tax -= $discount;
    // calculation of a possible tax reduction
    $reduction = getReduction($married, $salary, $children, $tax);
    $tax -= $reduction;
    // result
    return [
        "tax" => (int) floor($tax),
        "surcharge" => (int) $surcharge,
        "discount" => (int) $discount,
        "reduction" => (int) $reduction,
        "rate" => $rate,
    ];
}

Comments:

  • Line 81: The gross tax is calculated including dependents. The result is in the form [["tax" => $tax, "surcharge" => $surcharge, "rate" => $coeffR[$i]]], where:
    • [tax]: the gross tax;
    • [surcharge]: the amount of the surcharge, if any. This applies when the 10% deduction exceeds the threshold of 12,502 euros;
    • [rate]: the taxpayer’s tax rate;
  • line 82: the gross tax [$tax1] due;
  • lines 84–85: if the taxpayer has at least one child, the tax calculation is redone using the same data but assuming 0 children. This second calculation is necessary to determine whether the tax reduction resulting from having children exceeds a certain threshold;
  • line 86: the gross tax [$tax2] due;
  • lines 88–94: For the gross tax [$tax2], the children are now factored in: each half-share contributed by the children results in a reduction of [HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING] euros. The first two children contribute one half-share each; subsequent children contribute one full share, for a total of two half-shares;
  • lines 96–97: case where the taxpayer has no children. In this case, calculating [$tax2] is unnecessary. It is equal to [$tax1];
  • lines 100–108: Two gross tax amounts have been calculated: [tax1, tax2]. The tax authority retains the higher of the two. This results in a gross tax amount of [$tax];
  • lines 110–111: the gross amount [$tax] may be subject to a discount;
  • lines 113–114: the gross amount [$tax] may be subject to a reduction;
  • Lines 116–122: [$tax] is now the net tax payable. The results are returned. The calculations were performed using real numbers ([float]): the functions [floor] (rounding down to the nearest integer) and [ceil] (rounding up to the nearest integer) also return real numbers. We convert the amounts to integers using [(int)] so that they appear without a decimal part. The rate remains a real number.

The function [calculateTax2] is as follows:

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function calculateTax2(string $married, int $children, float $salary, array $limits, array $coeffR, array $coeffN): array
{
    // $married: yes, no
    // $children: number of children
    // $salary: annual salary
    // $limits, $coeffR, $coeffN: the arrays of the data used to calculate the tax
    //
    // number of shares
    if ($married === "yes") {
        $nbShares = $children / 2 + 2;
    } else {
        $nbShares = $children / 2 + 1;
    }
    // 1 share per child from the 3rd one
    if ($children >= 3) {
        // one more half-share for each child from the 3rd one
        $nbShares += 0.5 * ($children - 2);
    }
    // taxable income
    $taxableIncome = getTaxableIncome($salary);
    // surcharge
    $surcharge = floor($taxableIncome - 0.9 * $salary);
    // for rounding problems
    if ($surcharge < 0) {
        $surcharge = 0;
    }
    // family quotient
    $quotient = $taxableIncome / $nbShares;
    // is put at the end of the limits array to stop the following loop
    $limits[count($limits) - 1] = $quotient;
    // calculation of the tax
    $i = 0;
    while ($quotient > $limits[$i]) {
        $i++;
    }
    // since we placed $quotient at the end of the $limits array, the previous loop
    // cannot go beyond the $limits array
    // now we can calculate the tax
    $tax = floor($taxableIncome * $coeffR[$i] - $nbShares * $coeffN[$i]);
    // result
    return ["tax" => $tax, "surcharge" => $surcharge, "rate" => $coeffR[$i]];
}

Comments:

  • Here, the tax is calculated using the so-called progressive tax scale;
  • lines 134–142: calculation of the taxpayer’s number of shares;
  • line 145: the taxable income is calculated using a function. As we have seen, it is not always 0.9*annualSalary. The 10% deduction is, in fact, capped at 12,502 euros;
  • line 147: calculation of any surcharge if the taxable income exceeds 0.9*annualSalary;
  • Lines 149–151: Corrects the fact that, due to rounding errors, the result is sometimes [$surcharge=-1];
  • line 153: the family quotient;
  • lines 155–160: this quotient is used to determine the taxpayer’s tax bracket. We search for the first element of [$limits] that is greater than or equal to the quotient. The quotient was stored in the last element of [$limits] (which was 0): the loop [while] therefore stops at this last element at the latest. Since the array [$limits] was passed by value, this modification affects only the local copy of the function;
  • line 164: Once the taxpayer’s tax bracket has been determined, their gross tax can be calculated. The function [floor($x)] returns the integer value immediately less than [$x];
  • line 166: the calculated information is returned.

The function [getTaxableIncome] is as follows:

// taxableIncome=annualSalary-allowance
// the allowance has a min and a max
function getTaxableIncome(float $salary): float
{
    // allowance of 10% of the salary
    $allowance = 0.1 * $salary;
    // this allowance cannot exceed TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MAX
    if ($allowance > TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MAX) {
        $allowance = TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MAX;
    }
    // the allowance cannot be lower than TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MIN
    if ($allowance < TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MIN) {
        $allowance = TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MIN;
    }
    // taxable income
    $taxableIncome = $salary - $allowance;
    // result
    return floor($taxableIncome);
}

Comments:

  • line 174: the standard deduction is 10% of annual salary;
  • Lines 176–178: The deduction cannot exceed the maximum deduction [TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MAX];
  • lines 180–182: the deduction cannot be less than the minimum deduction [TEN_PERCENT_ALLOWANCE_MIN];
  • lines 184–186: calculation of taxable income, rounded down to the nearest euro using function [floor].

The function [getDiscount] is as follows:

// calculates a possible discount
function getDiscount(string $married, float $salary, float $taxes): float
{
    // at the start, a zero discount
    $discount = 0;
    // maximum amount of tax to get the discount
    $taxCeilingForDiscount = $married === "yes" ? COUPLE_TAX_CEILING_FOR_DISCOUNT : SINGLE_TAX_CEILING_FOR_DISCOUNT;
    if ($taxes < $taxCeilingForDiscount) {
        // maximum amount of the discount
        $discountCeiling = $married === "yes" ? COUPLE_DISCOUNT_CEILING : SINGLE_DISCOUNT_CEILING;
        // theoretical discount
        $discount = $discountCeiling - 0.75 * $taxes;
        // the discount cannot exceed the amount of the tax
        if ($discount > $taxes) {
            $discount = $taxes;
        }
        // no discount < 0
        if ($discount < 0) {
            $discount = 0;
        }
    }
    // result
    return ceil($discount);
}

Comments:

  • line 195: maximum gross tax amount to qualify for a discount. This amount differs for single taxpayers and couples;
  • line 196: whether the taxpayer is eligible for the discount;
  • line 200: the discount formula. [$discountCeiling] is the maximum amount of the discount. This maximum amount is calculated on line 198. Again, it depends on the taxpayer’s status—married or single;
  • Lines 202–204: The discount cannot exceed the gross tax due. This is the case, for example, if [$taxes] equals 0;
  • lines 206–208: to avoid a negative discount;
  • Line 211: The discount is rounded up to the next euro.

The function [getReduction] is as follows:

// calculates a possible reduction
function getReduction(string $married, float $salary, int $children, float $taxes): float
{
    // the income ceiling to be entitled to the 20% reduction
    $incomeCeilingForReduction = $married === "yes" ? COUPLE_INCOME_CEILING_FOR_REDUCTION : SINGLE_INCOME_CEILING_FOR_REDUCTION;
    $incomeCeilingForReduction += $children * HALF_SHARE_REDUCTION_VALUE;
    if ($children > 2) {
        $incomeCeilingForReduction += ($children - 2) * HALF_SHARE_REDUCTION_VALUE;
    }
    // taxable income
    $taxableIncome = getTaxableIncome($salary);
    // reduction
    $reduction = 0;
    if ($taxableIncome < $incomeCeilingForReduction) {
        // 20% reduction
        $reduction = 0.2 * $taxes;
    }
    // result
    return ceil($reduction);
}

Comments:

  • lines 218–222: To be eligible for a tax reduction, the taxable income (line 224) must be less than a threshold calculated here. This threshold increases by [HALF_SHARE_REDUCTION_VALUE] for each half-share contributed by the children;
  • lines 227–230: If the taxpayer meets the conditions, they are entitled to a 20% tax reduction (line 229);
  • line 232: the reduction is rounded up to the next euro.

docs.title: 4.3.2. Results
docs.text:
Run the script in a terminal opened in the [version-01] folder:
