docs.title: 10.1. Introduction
docs.text:
The scripts for this chapter are in the [scripts-console/three-layers] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/three-layers
├── Business.php
├── Dao1.php
├── Dao2.php
├── IBusiness.php
├── IDao.php
├── main1.php
├── main2.php
└── Person.php

We will now explore how to structure a PHP application in layers:

In this diagram, the left layer initiates the use of the right layer. The roles of the layers are as follows:

  • [1]: The layer called [dao] (Data Access Objects) handles interactions with external data stores [4] (files, databases, web services, etc.). This layer is sometimes referred to as [DAL] (Data Access Layer), a term that better describes its role. This layer can read data from [3] or write data to [2]. It is called by the [business] [6] layer and returns results [7] to it;
  • [5]: a layer called [business] that brings together “business” procedures and is supplied with all the data they need. This is generally the most stable layer in a project because it does not depend on how the data is acquired. The data comes from two sources:
    • [9]: data provided by the PHP script;
    • [6, 7]: data requested from the [dao] layer;
  • [8]: the main script acts as the orchestrator. In a console application, it will:
    • create the layers [business] and [dao];
    • execute the application’s algorithm. This algorithm functions like an orchestrator: it contains no “business logic” or data access code. The main script simply calls the procedures of the [business] layer [9]. It completely ignores the [dao] layer and external data. It can provide the [business] layer with [9] data. In a console application, this data may come from configuration files or from the script user. It receives [10] results from the [business] layer. It may need to store certain results: to do so, it again uses the procedures of the [business] layer, which in turn will call upon the [dao] layer to perform the task;
    • Among the results, the main script may receive exceptions. It is the main script’s role to handle exceptions that are propagated up from all layers.

This layered architecture is designed to facilitate the application’s evolution. To achieve this, each layer implements an interface. Suppose that:

  • the [dao] layer is implemented by a class [Dao], which implements an interface [IDao];
  • the [business] layer is implemented by a class [Business], which implements an interface [IBusiness].

The procedures in layer [business] will then use interface [IDao] instead of class [Dao]. This allows the [dao] layer to be updated without affecting the [business] layer. Suppose that in version 1, the [Dao1] layer uses data from a database. Following an update, this data is now provided by a web service in version 2, [Dao2]. We will ensure that both classes, [Dao1] and [Dao2], implement the same interface, [IDao], and that they throw the same exceptions. If this is verified, the [Business] layer, which works with the [IDao] interface, will remain unchanged.

The same reasoning applies to the [business] layer.

The application will implement the following layered structure:

docs.title: 10.2. Objects Exchanged Between Layers
docs.text:
Normally, layers exchange various objects. Here, they will exchange objects of the following [Person] class: [Person.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// a person: an immutable object
final readonly class Person
{
    // constructor with promotion of the [id] attribute
    public function __construct(public int $id)
    {
    }

    // toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[Person($this->id)]";
    }
}

Comments

  • line 6: Objects exchanged between layers contain only data. They are made into immutable objects (class [readonly]): this prevents a layer from inadvertently modifying an object it received from another layer;
  • line 9: The person has only one attribute, their identifier [$id], initialized by the constructor through parameter promotion. We will assume that this identifier refers to a unique person in a data warehouse;
  • Lines 14–17: The method [__toString], which displays the person’s identifier.

docs.title: 10.3. [dao] Layer
docs.text:
The [IDao] interface implemented by the [dao] layer is as follows: [IDao.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// [dao] layer ------------------------
interface IDao
{
    // retrieving a person from an external repository
    // the identifier of the person is passed
    public function get(int $id): Person;

    // saving a person in an external repository
    public function save(Person $p): void;
}

This interface is implemented by the following [Dao1] class: [Dao1.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

final class Dao1 implements IDao
{
    // saving a person in an external repository
    #[\Override]
    public function save(Person $p): void
    {
        print "[Dao1]: Saving the person $p in the [local] database\n";
    }

    // retrieving a person from an external repository
    #[\Override]
    public function get(int $id): Person
    {
        print "[Dao1]: Retrieving the person with identity ($id) from the [local] database\n";
        return new Person($id);
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 5: The class [Dao1] implements the interface [IDao]. It is declared as [final]: it is not intended to be derived from;
  • the class does not interact with a data warehouse. It simply displays messages to track the code’s execution (line 11, line 18);
  • line 8: the attribute [#[\Override]] indicates that the method implements a method of the interface. If the method name is incorrect, PHP signals this;
  • line 19: We do indeed return a person with the ID passed as a parameter to the method.

We also implement the [IDao] interface with the following [Dao2] class, [Dao2.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

final class Dao2 implements IDao
{
    // saving a person in an external repository
    #[\Override]
    public function save(Person $p): void
    {
        print "[Dao2]: Saving the person $p in the [remote] database\n";
    }

    // retrieving a person from an external repository
    #[\Override]
    public function get(int $id): Person
    {
        print "[Dao2]: Retrieving the person with identity ($id) from the [remote] database\n";
        return new Person($id);
    }
}

The [Dao2] class is similar to the [Dao1] class, except that we have modified the messages displayed.

docs.title: 10.4. Layer [business]
docs.text:
Layer [business] provides the following [IBusiness] interface: [IBusiness.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// [business] layer ------------------------
interface IBusiness extends IDao
{
    // we process a person
    public function doSomething(Person $p): void;
}

Comments

  • Line 6: The [IBusiness] interface extends the [IDao] interface. This is not required at all. We’re doing this here because the example is simple: the [business] layer provides the main script with the [get] and [save] methods from the [dao] layer, which it hides from the main script;
  • Line 9: The method [doSomething] is specific to the [business] layer.

The PHP 7 course referred to the interface [IMétier] and the class [Métier], with an accent. PHP allows accented letters in identifiers, but a file named [Métier.php] causes problems with certain tools (ZIP archives, file systems, automatic class loading). We now stick to class and file names without accents: here, [IBusiness] and [Business].

The [IBusiness] interface is implemented by the following class: [Business] [Business.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

final class Business implements IBusiness
{
    // the [dao] layer is injected by the constructor
    public function __construct(private readonly IDao $dao)
    {
    }

    // we process a person
    #[\Override]
    public function doSomething(Person $p): void
    {
        // processing
        print "[Business]: Business processing of the person $p\n";
    }

    // saving the person
    #[\Override]
    public function save(Person $p): void
    {
        print "[Business]: Saving the person $p\n";
        // we ask the [dao] layer to do the saving
        $this->dao->save($p);
    }

    // retrieving a person
    #[\Override]
    public function get(int $id): Person
    {
        print "[Business]: Retrieving the person with identifier $id\n";
        // we ask the [dao] layer for the person
        return $this->dao->get($id);
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 8: The [business] layer must have a reference to the [dao] layer in order to use the latter’s methods. This reference is passed to it via its constructor and stored in the private, read-only attribute [$dao] (parameter promotion). Note that the parameter type is the [IDao] interface. Thus, the [business] layer will be able to work with any class that implements the [IDao] interface. If we switch from a [Dao1] layer to a [Dao2] layer, and both implement the [IDao] interface, the [business] layer does not need to be rewritten;
  • this technique is called constructor-based dependency injection: the class [Business] does not create the layer [dao] on which it depends; instead, it is provided to it. The PHP 7 course used a setter [setDao]. Constructor injection is now the norm: a [Business] object cannot exist without its [dao] layer, and this layer cannot be changed afterward ([readonly] attribute). This is also the approach taken by frameworks such as Symfony or Laravel;
  • lines 14–18: implementation of [IBusiness::doSomething];
  • lines 22–27: implementation of [IBusiness::save]. This method must save a person to a data warehouse. The [business] layer cannot do this. It calls upon the [dao] layer to perform this save (line 26);
  • lines 31–36: implementation of [IBusiness::get]. This method must retrieve from a data warehouse the person whose ID is passed to it as a parameter. The [business] layer cannot do this. It calls on the [dao] layer to perform the task (line 35).

Conclusion: Whenever the [business] layer needs to access data stored in the data warehouse, it must go through the [dao] layer, which was created specifically to access that data.

docs.title: 10.5. Main Script
docs.text:
We will write two orchestration scripts for this application. The first, [main1.php], will use the [Dao1] layer, while the second, [main2.php], will use the [Dao2] layer. We want to show that this has no impact on the code in the [Business] layer.

The [main1.php] script is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion of the classes and interfaces
require_once __DIR__ . "/Person.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IBusiness.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Dao1.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Business.php";

// creation of the layers: the [dao] layer is injected into the [business] layer
$business = new Business(new Dao1());
// use of the [business] layer
$person = $business->get(4);
$business->doSomething($person);
$business->save($person);

Comments

  • The [main1.php] script acts as the application's orchestrator. It loads the class and interface files (lines 7–11), creates the application’s layered structure (line 14), and then communicates with the [business] layer (lines 16–18);
  • line 14: it is here, and only here, that the implementation of the [dao] layer is selected;
  • According to the layered structure diagram, the [main1.php] script must communicate only with the [business] layer. It must not communicate with the [dao] layer, even though this is theoretically possible.

The results of the execution are as follows:

> php main1.php
[Business]: Retrieving the person with identifier 4
[Dao1]: Retrieving the person with identity (4) from the [local] database
[Business]: Business processing of the person [Person(4)]
[Business]: Saving the person [Person(4)]
[Dao1]: Saving the person [Person(4)] in the [local] database

Comments

  • Line 16 of the code caused lines 2 and 3 of the results to be written;
  • Line 17 of the code caused line 4 of the results to be written;
  • Line 18 of the code caused lines 5 and 6 of the results to be written.

The script [main2.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion of the classes and interfaces
require_once __DIR__ . "/Person.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IBusiness.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Dao2.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Business.php";

// creation of the layers: the [dao] layer is injected into the [business] layer
$business = new Business(new Dao2());
// use of the [business] layer
$person = $business->get(4);
$business->doSomething($person);
$business->save($person);

Comments

  • Lines 10 and 14: The layer structure now uses the [Dao2] layer. These are the only differences from [main1.php].

The results of the execution are as follows:

> php main2.php
[Business]: Retrieving the person with identifier 4
[Dao2]: Retrieving the person with identity (4) from the [remote] database
[Business]: Business processing of the person [Person(4)]
[Business]: Saving the person [Person(4)]
[Dao2]: Saving the person [Person(4)] in the [remote] database

The [Dao1] layer simulates access to a local database, while the [Dao2] layer simulates access to a remote database. As long as these two layers conform to the [IDao] interface, we can see that the code for the [Business] layer did not need to be changed.

We’ll apply what we’ve just learned to the tax calculation exercise that serves as our guiding example.

docs.title: 16. Network Functions
docs.text:
We will now discuss the network functions of PHP, which allow us to program using TCP / IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol). The scripts for this chapter are located in the [scripts-console/inet] folder of the course code:

php8-oct-2026
└── scripts-console
    └── inet
        ├── http
        ├── imap
        ├── ip
        ├── mailpit
        ├── smtp
        └── utilities

docs.title: 16.1.1. General Information
docs.text:
Consider communication between two remote machines, A and B:

When an application AppA on machine A wants to communicate with an application AppB on machine B on the Internet, it must know several things:

  • the IP (Internet Protocol) address or the name of machine B;
  • the port number used by the AppB application. This is because machine B may host many applications that operate on the Internet. When it receives information from the network, it must know which application the information is intended for. Applications on machine B access the network through interfaces also known as communication ports. This information is contained in the packet received by machine B so that it can be delivered to the correct application;
  • the communication protocols understood by machine B. In our study, we will use only the TCP / IP protocols;
  • the communication protocol supported by the AppB application. In fact, machines A and B will “communicate” with each other. What they say will be encapsulated in the TCP and IP protocols. However, when, at the other end of the chain, the AppB application receives the information sent by the AppA application, it must be able to interpret it. This is analogous to a situation where two people, A and B, communicate by phone: their conversation is carried by the phone. Speech is encoded as signals by phone A, transmitted over telephone lines, and arrives at phone B to be decoded. Person B then hears the speech. This is where the concept of a communication protocol comes into play: if A speaks French and B does not understand that language, A and B will not be able to communicate effectively.

Therefore, the two communicating applications must agree on the type of dialogue they will use. For example, the dialogue with a service named FTP is not the same as that with a service named POP: these two services do not accept the same commands. They have different dialogue protocols.

docs.title: 16.1.2. Characteristics of the TCP Protocol
docs.text:
Here, we will focus only on network communications using the TCP transport protocol, whose main characteristics are as follows:

  • The process that wishes to transmit data first establishes a connection with the process that will receive the information it is about to transmit. This connection is established between a port on the sending machine and a port on the receiving machine. A virtual path is thus created between the two ports, which will be reserved exclusively for the two processes that have established the connection;
  • All packets sent by the source process follow this virtual path and arrive in the order in which they were sent;
  • The transmitted data appears continuous. The sending process sends data at its own pace. This data is not necessarily sent immediately: the TCP protocol waits until it has enough data to send. It is stored in a structure called a TCP segment. Once this segment is filled, it will be transmitted to the IP layer, where it will be encapsulated in an IP packet;
  • Each segment sent by the TCP protocol is numbered. The receiving TCP protocol verifies that it is receiving the segments in sequence. For each segment received correctly, it sends an acknowledgment to the sender;
  • when the sender receives this acknowledgment, it notifies the sending process. The sending process can therefore confirm that a segment has been successfully delivered;
  • if, after a certain amount of time, the TCP protocol that sent a segment does not receive an acknowledgment, it retransmits the segment in question, thereby ensuring the quality of the information delivery service;
  • The virtual circuit established between the two communicating processes is full-duplex: this means that information can flow in both directions. Thus, the destination process can send acknowledgments even while the source process continues to send information. This allows, for example, the source TCP protocol to send multiple segments without waiting for an acknowledgment. If, after a certain amount of time, it realizes it has not received an acknowledgment for a specific segment No. n, it will resume sending segments from that point onward.

docs.title: 16.1.3. The Client-Server Relationship
docs.text: Communication over the Internet is often asymmetric: Machine A initiates a connection to request a service from Machine B. It specifies that it wants to establish a connection with Machine B’s SB1 service. Machine B either accepts or rejects the request. If it accepts, machine A can send its requests to service SB1. These requests must comply with the communication protocol understood by service SB1. A request-response dialogue is thus established between machine A, referred to as the client machine, and machine B, referred to as the server machine. One of the two partners will close the connection.

docs.title: 16.1.4. Client Architecture
docs.text:
The architecture of a network program requesting services from a server application will be as follows:

open the connection with the SB1 service of machine B
if successful then
    while not finished
        prepare a request
        send it to machine B
        wait for and retrieve the response
        process it
    end while
end if
close the connection

docs.title: 16.1.5. Server Architecture
docs.text:
The architecture of a program offering services will be as follows:

open the service on the local machine
while the service is open
    listen for connection requests on a port called the listening port
    when there is a request, have it handled by another task on another port called the service port
end while

The server program handles a client’s initial connection request differently from its subsequent requests for service. The program does not provide the service itself. If it did, it would no longer be listening for connection requests while the service was in progress, and clients would not be served. It therefore proceeds differently: as soon as a connection request is received on the listening port and then accepted, the server creates a task responsible for providing the service requested by the client. This service is provided on another port of the server machine called the service port. This allows multiple clients to be served at the same time.

A service task will have the following structure:

while the service has not been fully provided
    wait for a request on the service port
    when there is one, build the response
    send the response through the service port
end while
release the service port

Another way to serve multiple clients at once, without creating tasks, is to simultaneously monitor the listening port and the service ports using a function that waits for one of them to have something to send. This is what the TCP server we are going to write will do, using the [stream_select] function from PHP.

docs.title: 16.2.1. Introduction
docs.text:
When a client connects to a server, a dialogue is established between them. The nature of this dialogue constitutes what is known as the server’s communication protocol. Among the most common Internet protocols are the following:

  • HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol—the protocol for communicating with a web server (HTTP server);
  • SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol—the protocol for communicating with an email sending server (SMTP server);
  • POP: Post Office Protocol—the protocol for communicating with an email storage server (server POP). This is used to retrieve received emails, not to send them;
  • IMAP: Internet Message Access Protocol—the protocol for communicating with an email storage server (server IMAP). This protocol has gradually replaced the older POP protocol;
  • FTP: File Transfer Protocol—the protocol for communicating with a file storage server (server FTP).

All of these protocols are text-based: the client and server exchange lines of text. If you have a client capable of:

  • establish a connection with a TCP server;
  • display the text lines sent by the server on the console;
  • send to the server the text lines that a user would type on the keyboard;

then we can communicate with a TCP server that uses a text-based protocol, provided we know the rules of that protocol.

docs.title: 16.2.2. TCP Utilities
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course provided two Windows utilities, [RawTcpClient] and [RawTcpServer], written in C#. Here, we’re replacing them with two PHP scripts, which we’ll now examine: this is an opportunity to explore the network functions of PHP. They are located in the [inet/utilities] folder:

utilities
├── keyboard.php
├── tcp-client.php
└── tcp-server.php
  • [tcp-client.php] allows you to connect to port P on server S;
  • [tcp-server.php] creates a server that listens for clients on port P;
  • [keyboard.php] contains two functions used by the two previous scripts.

Note that there are also ready-made tools for this type of test. On Windows, the PowerShell command [Test-NetConnection localhost -Port 80] simply checks whether a service is responding on a port. The [curl] tool, which we’ll encounter with the HTTP protocol, can communicate with many servers, and its [-v] (verbose) option displays the client/server exchanges. Our two scripts, on the other hand, let us type the protocol commands ourselves.

docs.title: 16.2.2.1. The [tcp-server.php] server
docs.text:
The TCP [tcp-server.php] server is invoked using the syntax [php tcp-server.php port] to create a TCP service on port [port] of the local machine (the computer you are working on):

  • The server can serve multiple clients simultaneously;
  • the server executes the commands entered by the user via the keyboard. These commands are as follows:
    • list: lists the clients currently connected to the server. They are displayed in the format [id=x - name=y]. The [id] field is used to identify clients;
    • send x [text]: sends text to client #x (id=x). The square brackets [] are not sent. They are required in the command. They are used to visually delimit the text sent to the client;
    • close x: closes the connection with client #x;
    • quit: closes all connections and stops the service;
  • Lines sent by a client to the server are displayed on the console;
  • All communication with a client is logged in a text file named [logs/machine-port.txt], where [machine-port] identifies the client (its address IP and the port it uses).

The server code is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// generic TCP server
// syntax: php tcp-server.php port
// - waits for clients on the port [port] of the local machine and can serve several at a time;
// - displays the lines of text sent by the clients;
// - executes the commands typed on the keyboard:
//   list: lists the connected clients;
//   send id [text]: sends [text] (without the brackets) to the client no. id;
//   close id: closes the connection with the client no. id;
//   quit: closes all the connections and stops the server;
// - records the exchanges with each client in the file [logs/machine-port.txt]
//   where [machine-port] identifies the client

require_once __DIR__ . "/keyboard.php";

// analysis of the command-line arguments
if (count($argv) !== 2 || !ctype_digit($argv[1])) {
    print "Syntax: php tcp-server.php port\n";
    exit(1);
}
$port = $argv[1];

// opening the service on all the network interfaces of the local machine
$server = @stream_socket_server("tcp://0.0.0.0:$port", $errorNumber, $error);
if ($server === false) {
    print "Unable to open the service on the port [$port]: $error\n";
    exit(2);
}
print "Server listening on the port [$port]\n";
print "Commands: list, send id [text], close id, quit\n";
if (!is_dir(__DIR__ . "/logs")) {
    mkdir(__DIR__ . "/logs");
}

// the connected clients: id => [socket, name, log file, buffer]
$clients = [];
$nextId = 1;
// the keyboard is read by a child process
[$reader, $keyboard] = startKeyboardReader();
$echo = !stream_isatty(STDIN);
$keyboardBuffer = "";

// service loop
$done = false;
while (!$done) {
    // we watch: the listening port, the clients and the keyboard
    $reads = [$server, $keyboard, ...array_column($clients, "socket")];
    $writes = $exceptions = null;
    stream_select($reads, $writes, $exceptions, null);
    foreach ($reads as $stream) {
        if ($stream === $server) {
            // a new client connects
            $socket = stream_socket_accept($server, 0, $name);
            if ($socket !== false) {
                $id = $nextId++;
                $log = fopen(__DIR__ . "/logs/" . str_replace(":", "-", $name) . ".txt", "w");
                $clients[$id] = ["socket" => $socket, "name" => $name, "log" => $log, "buffer" => ""];
                print "Client no. $id [$name] connected\n";
            }
        } elseif ($stream === $keyboard) {
            // a command has been typed on the keyboard
            $data = fread($keyboard, 8192);
            if ($data === false || $data === "") {
                // end of the standard input: we stop the server
                $done = true;
                break;
            }
            foreach (extractLines($keyboardBuffer, $data) as $command) {
                if ($echo) {
                    print "$command\n";
                }
                if (execute($command, $clients)) {
                    $done = true;
                    break;
                }
            }
        } else {
            // a client has spoken
            $id = array_find_key($clients, fn(array $client): bool => $client["socket"] === $stream);
            if ($id === null) {
                // client closed in the meantime by the [close] command
                continue;
            }
            $data = fread($stream, 8192);
            if ($data === false || $data === "") {
                print "The client no. $id has closed the connection\n";
                close($clients, $id);
                continue;
            }
            foreach (extractLines($clients[$id]["buffer"], $data) as $line) {
                print "<-- client no. $id [$line]\n";
                fwrite($clients[$id]["log"], "<-- [$line]\n");
            }
        }
    }
}
// stopping the service
foreach (array_keys($clients) as $id) {
    close($clients, $id);
}
fclose($server);
proc_terminate($reader);
print "Server stopped\n";

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// executes a command typed on the keyboard - returns true if it is the [quit] command
function execute(string $command, array &$clients): bool
{
    // send id [text]
    if (preg_match('/^send\s+(\d+)\s+\[(.*)\]$/', $command, $fields)) {
        $id = (int) $fields[1];
        if (!isset($clients[$id])) {
            print "Unknown client no. $id\n";
        } else {
            fwrite($clients[$id]["socket"], "$fields[2]\r\n");
            fwrite($clients[$id]["log"], "--> [$fields[2]]\n");
        }
        return false;
    }
    // the other commands
    $words = preg_split('/\s+/', trim($command));
    switch ($words[0]) {
        case "list":
            foreach ($clients as $id => $client) {
                print "id=$id - name={$client["name"]}\n";
            }
            return false;
        case "close":
            $id = (int) ($words[1] ?? 0);
            if (!isset($clients[$id])) {
                print "Unknown client no. $id\n";
            } else {
                close($clients, $id);
                print "Connection with the client no. $id closed\n";
            }
            return false;
        case "quit":
            return true;
        default:
            print "Unknown command [$command]. Commands: list, send id [text], close id, quit\n";
            return false;
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// closes the connection with the client no. [$id]
function close(array &$clients, int $id): void
{
    fclose($clients[$id]["socket"]);
    fclose($clients[$id]["log"]);
    unset($clients[$id]);
}

Comments:

  • line 17: the file [keyboard.php] is loaded; we’ll discuss this later;
  • line 20: the array [$argv] contains the command-line arguments. [$argv[0]] is the name of the script, [$argv[1]] is the first argument, in this case the port number. The function [ctype_digit] verifies that the port number consists only of digits;
  • Line 27: The function [stream_socket_server] starts a TCP service. Its first parameter is an address in the form [tcp://interface:port]. The interface [0.0.0.0] refers to all of the machine’s network interfaces: the server can be reached via both [localhost] and the machine’s local network address IP. In the event of a failure (e.g., the port is already in use), the function returns [false] and stores an error number and an error message in the two variables passed as the second and third parameters. The operator [@] prevents PHP from displaying its own warning: we display our message;
  • line 39: the dictionary of connected clients. Each client is described by its socket (the connection linking it to the server), its name [address:port], its log file, and a buffer whose purpose we will discuss;
  • line 42: the keyboard is read by a child process. We’ll see why with the [keyboard.php] file. [$keyboard] is a stream into which lines typed on the keyboard are fed;
  • Line 43: The function [stream_isatty] determines whether standard input is the keyboard (a terminal) or not. If standard input has been redirected to a file ([php tcp-server.php 100 < commands.txt]), the commands read are not displayed on the screen. The server will then display them itself;
  • lines 48–52: the service loop. On each iteration, the server waits for one of the streams it is monitoring to have something to tell it: the listening port (a new client connects), the keyboard (a command has been typed), or one of the clients (it has sent text). The [...] operator breaks down the array of client sockets (obtained with [array_column]) into the [$reads] array;
  • Line 52: The [stream_select] function waits for one of the streams in the [$reads] array to be readable. The last parameter, [null], means: wait indefinitely. Upon return, the function has removed the streams with nothing to read from the array [$reads]. The second and third parameters concern the streams to which we want to write and exceptional events: we are not interested in them. Since they are passed by reference, we must pass variables to them—in this case, [$writes] and [$exceptions], which are equal to [null];
  • Lines 54–60: A new client connects. The function [stream_socket_accept] accepts the connection. It returns the service socket that connects the server to this client and stores the client’s identity in [$name] in the form [address:port]. A timeout of 0 means there is no wait: [stream_select] informed us that a client was waiting;
  • lines 63–75: A command was typed on the keyboard. The function [fread] reads whatever is available (up to 8,192 bytes). An empty string means the stream has been closed. The function [extractLines] splits what was read into complete lines;
  • lines 81–95: A client sent text. The function [array_find_key] (PHP 8.4) returns the key of the first array element that satisfies the condition expressed by the arrowed function [fn] passed as the second parameter: this retrieves the client’s ID from its socket. If [fread] returns an empty string, the client has closed the connection. Otherwise, each received line is displayed and recorded in the client’s log file;
  • Lines 110–141: The [execute] function executes a command entered via the keyboard. The [send id [text]] command is recognized by a regular expression. The text is sent to the client followed by the sequence \r\n: Internet protocols terminate text lines with the two characters CR (\r) and LF (\n);
  • line 150: the function [close] closes the connection with a client and removes it from the dictionary [$clients], passed by reference ([&]).

docs.title: 16.2.2.2. The file [keyboard.php]
docs.text:
The file [keyboard.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// tools shared by [tcp-client.php] and [tcp-server.php]

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// starts a child process that reads the keyboard and sends us back each typed line
// through a socket. Why? Our programs must watch both the network and the
// keyboard at the same time with the [stream_select] function. But on Windows, [stream_select]
// can only watch sockets, not the keyboard (STDIN).
// The ['socket'] descriptor of [proc_open] (PHP 8.0) connects the child process to the
// parent process through a socket, which [stream_select] can watch on every OS.
// returns the child process and the socket that delivers the lines typed on the keyboard
function startKeyboardReader(): array
{
    $process = proc_open(
        // the child process: a one-line PHP script that copies its input to its output
        [PHP_BINARY, "-r", 'while (($line = fgets(STDIN)) !== false) { echo $line; }'],
        // its input is our keyboard, its output is a socket
        [0 => STDIN, 1 => ["socket"], 2 => STDERR],
        $pipes
    );
    if ($process === false) {
        throw new RuntimeException("Unable to start the keyboard reader");
    }
    return [$process, $pipes[1]];
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// adds the bytes [$data] to the buffer [$buffer] and extracts the complete lines from it,
// returned without their end-of-line mark (\n or \r\n);
// the end of the buffer (an incomplete line) stays in the buffer
function extractLines(string &$buffer, string $data): array
{
    $buffer .= $data;
    $lines = explode("\n", $buffer);
    // the last element is the current line, not yet finished
    $buffer = array_pop($lines);
    return array_map(fn(string $line): string => rtrim($line, "\r"), $lines);
}

Comments:

  • Line 15: Our two scripts must monitor both the network and the keyboard at the same time. On Linux or macOS, we could pass the [STDIN] stream (the keyboard) to [stream_select]. On Windows, this isn’t possible: [stream_select] can only monitor sockets there. The workaround is to have a second process read the keyboard and send us the typed lines via a socket;
  • Lines 17–22: The function [proc_open] launches a child process. Its first parameter is the command to be executed, in the form of an array: the currently running PHP interpreter ([PHP_BINARY]) with the [-r] option, which executes the PHP code passed as an argument. This code copies each line read from its input to its output. The second parameter describes the child process’s streams: its input (0) is our standard input (the keyboard), its output (1) is a socket created by PHP (descriptor [['socket']], available since PHP 8.0), and its errors (2) are sent to our error output. The third parameter receives the created streams: [$pipes[1]] is our end of the socket;
  • line 34: when [stream_select] signals that a stream is ready to be read, [fread] returns what was received: this can be a line, multiple lines, or part of a line. The function [extractLines] adds these bytes to the buffer [$buffer] (passed by reference), extracts the complete lines from it, and keeps the unfinished line in the buffer. Note the arrow function [fn(string $line): string => rtrim($line, "\r")], which removes the trailing \r from lines ending with \r\n.

We could have read the lines using the function [fgets]. However, [fgets] reads the data in blocks and stores the lines it has not yet rendered in an internal buffer of PHP. [stream_select], which only monitors the network, would not see them. Reading with [fread] and splitting the lines ourselves avoids this pitfall.

docs.title: 16.2.2.3. The [tcp-client.php] client
docs.text:
The client TCP [tcp-client.php] is called using the syntax [php tcp-client.php [--quit command] [--tls] server port] to connect to port [port] on the server [server]:

  • Lines typed by the user on the keyboard are sent to the server;
  • the lines sent by the server are displayed on the console as soon as they arrive;
  • all communication is logged in a text file named [logs/server-port.txt];
  • the command [quit] stops the client. The option [--quit] allows you to choose a different command;
  • The option [--tls] encrypts the connection. We will need this to communicate with secure servers.

Its code is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// generic TCP client
// syntax: php tcp-client.php [--quit command] [--tls] server port
// - connects to the port [port] of the machine [server];
// - displays the lines of text sent by the server as soon as they arrive;
// - sends to the server the lines of text typed on the keyboard;
// - records all the exchanges in the file [logs/server-port.txt]
// options:
// --quit command: the command that stops the client ([quit] by default)
// --tls: the connection is encrypted (TLS) as soon as it is opened

require_once __DIR__ . "/keyboard.php";

// analysis of the command-line arguments
$quit = "quit";
$tls = false;
$arguments = [];
for ($i = 1; $i < count($argv); $i++) {
    match ($argv[$i]) {
        "--quit" => $quit = $argv[++$i] ?? $quit,
        "--tls" => $tls = true,
        default => $arguments[] = $argv[$i],
    };
}
if (count($arguments) !== 2 || !ctype_digit($arguments[1])) {
    print "Syntax: php tcp-client.php [--quit command] [--tls] server port\n";
    exit(1);
}
[$server, $port] = $arguments;

// opening the connection with the server
// with --tls, the server certificate is not checked: this is a discovery tool
$context = stream_context_create(["ssl" => ["verify_peer" => false, "verify_peer_name" => false]]);
$transport = $tls ? "tls" : "tcp";
$connection = @stream_socket_client("$transport://$server:$port", $errorNumber, $error, 10,
    STREAM_CLIENT_CONNECT, $context);
if ($connection === false) {
    print "Failed to connect to the server [$server:$port]: $error\n";
    exit(2);
}
$client = stream_socket_get_name($connection, false);
print "Client [$client] connected to the server [$server:$port]\n";
print "Type your commands ($quit to stop):\n";

// log file
if (!is_dir(__DIR__ . "/logs")) {
    mkdir(__DIR__ . "/logs");
}
$log = fopen(__DIR__ . "/logs/$server-$port.txt", "w");

// the keyboard is read by a child process
[$reader, $keyboard] = startKeyboardReader();
// if the standard input is a file (php tcp-client.php ... < commands.txt),
// the commands read are not displayed on the screen: we will display them ourselves
$echo = !stream_isatty(STDIN);
// buffers of the incomplete lines received from the server and the keyboard
$serverBuffer = "";
$keyboardBuffer = "";

// dialogue loop with the server
$done = false;
while (!$done) {
    // we wait until the server or the keyboard has something to tell us
    $reads = $keyboard !== null ? [$connection, $keyboard] : [$connection];
    $writes = $exceptions = null;
    // without a keyboard (end of the standard input), we do not wait for the server more than 2 seconds
    if (stream_select($reads, $writes, $exceptions, $keyboard !== null ? null : 2) === 0) {
        break;
    }
    // has the server spoken?
    if (in_array($connection, $reads, true)) {
        $data = fread($connection, 8192);
        if ($data === false || $data === "") {
            // the server has closed the connection
            if ($serverBuffer !== "") {
                display("<-- [$serverBuffer]", $log);
            }
            print "Connection with the server lost...\n";
            break;
        }
        foreach (extractLines($serverBuffer, $data) as $line) {
            display("<-- [$line]", $log);
        }
    }
    // has a line been typed on the keyboard?
    if ($keyboard !== null && in_array($keyboard, $reads, true)) {
        $data = fread($keyboard, 8192);
        if ($data === false || $data === "") {
            // end of the standard input
            $keyboard = null;
            continue;
        }
        foreach (extractLines($keyboardBuffer, $data) as $command) {
            if ($echo) {
                print "$command\n";
            }
            // end of the client?
            if ($command === $quit) {
                $done = true;
                break;
            }
            // we send the command to the server: the internet protocols
            // end the lines with the sequence \r\n
            fwrite($connection, "$command\r\n");
            fwrite($log, "--> [$command]\n");
        }
    }
}
// closing the connection, the log file and the keyboard reader
fclose($connection);
fclose($log);
proc_terminate($reader);
print "End of the client\n";

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// displays a received line and records it in the log file
function display(string $line, $log): void
{
    print "$line\n";
    fwrite($log, "$line\n");
}

Comments:

  • Lines 21–26: argument parsing. The expression [match] (PHP 8.0) compares its argument to the values of its branches using the operator [===] and evaluates the corresponding branch. Here, each branch is an assignment. [$argv[++$i] ?? $quit] returns the argument following [--quit] if it exists, and [$quit] otherwise;
  • line 32: array unpacking: [$server] receives [$arguments[0]], and [$port] receives [$arguments[1]];
  • Lines 36–39: The [stream_socket_client] function establishes a connection with the [tcp://server:port] service. With the [--tls] option, the address becomes [tls://server:port]: PHP then encrypts the connection using the TLS protocol (Transport Layer Security). The context created by [stream_context_create] specifies here that the server certificate should not be verified: for a discovery tool, this prevents issues with test servers that have self-signed certificates. The fourth parameter is the maximum time (in seconds) allowed to establish the connection;
  • line 44: the function [stream_socket_get_name] returns whether a connection is local (false) or remote (true), in the form [address:port];
  • Lines 65–70: the dialog loop. It has the same structure as the server’s: [stream_select] waits for the server or the keyboard to send something. When standard input is finished (as in the case of input redirected to a file), the client continues to display what the server sends, but does not wait for it for more than 2 seconds;
  • lines 73–85: The lines sent by the server are displayed, enclosed in square brackets, and written to the log file. If the server closes the connection, the loop stops;
  • lines 88–108: Each line typed on the keyboard is sent to the server, followed by the \r\n sequence, except for the client’s stop command;
  • line 115: Finally, the child process that reads from the keyboard is terminated.

docs.title: 16.2.2.4. An example
docs.text:
Let’s look at an example. Open two terminals (in VS Code, the [+] button in the [Terminal] view opens a new one) and navigate to the [inet/utilities] folder in each of them. In the first terminal, start the server on port 100. In the second, start the client and instruct it to connect to port 100 on the local machine [localhost], then type a line of text. Return to the server, respond to client #1, request the list of clients, close the connection with client #1, and stop the server.

Here is what the server displays (the commands typed on the keyboard are the lines [send 1 ...], [list], [close 1], and [quit]):

> php tcp-server.php 100
Server listening on the port [100]
Commands: list, send id [text], close id, quit
Client no. 1 [127.0.0.1:47966] connected
<-- client no. 1 [hello from client]
send 1 [hello from server]
list
id=1 - name=127.0.0.1:47966
close 1
Connection with the client no. 1 closed
quit
Server stopped
  • [Client no. 1 [127.0.0.1:47966] connected]: A client has been detected. The server assigned it number 1. The client is using port 47966 on the machine with address IP 127.0.0.1. This address belongs to [localhost], the local machine;
  • [<-- client no. 1 [hello from client]]: the line received from the client is enclosed in square brackets;
  • [send 1 [hello from server]]: the response sent to client #1. Only the text inside the square brackets is sent, not the brackets themselves;
  • [list]: the list of clients and its response;
  • [close 1] followed by [quit]: the connection with client #1 is closed, then the server is shut down.

And here is what the client displays:

> php tcp-client.php localhost 100
Client [127.0.0.1:47966] connected to the server [localhost:100]
Type your commands (quit to stop):
hello from client
<-- [hello from server]
Connection with the server lost...
End of the client
  • [hello from client]: the line typed on the keyboard;
  • [<-- [hello from server]]: the response received from the server. The text received is the one in square brackets;
  • [Connection with the server lost...]: the client detected that the server closed the connection.

Two log files were created in the [utilities/logs] folder, one by the server and one by the client. The server file is named after the client, [127.0.0.1-47966.txt]:

<-- [hello from client]
--> [hello from server]

The client file is named after the server, [localhost-100.txt]:

--> [hello from client]
<-- [hello from server]

docs.title: 16.3. Retrieve the name or address IP of a machine on the Internet
docs.text:
Computers on the Internet are identified by an address (IP, IPv4, or IPv6) and, most often, by a name. However, ultimately only the address is used. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary to know the address IP of a machine identified by its name. This is the role of the DNS service (Domain Name System).

The [inet/ip/ip-01.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// IP addresses and machine names of the internet

// the machines whose IP address and name we want
const HOSTS = ["istia.univ-angers.fr", "www.univ-angers.fr", "www.ibm.com", "www.php.net", "yahoo.com", "localhost", "xx"];

// we add the local machine, whose name is given by [gethostname]
foreach ([...HOSTS, gethostname()] as $host) {
    getIPandName($host);
}
// end
print "Done\n";

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function getIPandName(string $machineName): void
{
    // $machineName: name of the machine whose IP address we want
    print "---------------\n";
    // machineName --> IP address
    $ip = gethostbyname($machineName);
    if ($ip === $machineName) {
        print "Error, machine [$machineName] not found\n";
        return;
    }
    print "ip[$machineName]=$ip\n";
    // all the IPv4 addresses of the machine
    $ips = gethostbynamel($machineName);
    if ($ips !== false && count($ips) > 1) {
        print "all the IPv4 addresses of [$machineName]: " . implode(", ", $ips) . "\n";
    }
    // IP address --> machineName
    $name = gethostbyaddr($ip);
    if ($name === false || $name === $ip) {
        print "Error, no name for the address [$ip]\n";
    } else {
        print "name[$ip]=$name\n";
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 8: the list of machines for which we want the name and IP address;
  • line 11: the name of the local machine, returned by the function [gethostname], is added to this list. The operator [...] copies the elements of the array [HOSTS] into the new array;
  • line 18: the network functions of PHP are used in the function [getIPandName];
  • Line 23: The function [gethostbyname($machineName)] returns the address IPv4 "ip3.ip2.ip1.ip0" of the machine named $machineName. If the machine $machineName does not exist, the function returns $machineName as the result;
  • line 30: A machine may have multiple addresses, such as IPv4. The function [gethostbynamel] returns all of them in an array (or [false] if the operation fails);
  • line 35: the function [gethostbyaddr($ip)] retrieves the name of the machine with address $ip. If the address $ip has no name, the function returns $ip as the result, and [false] if the address is malformed.

The functions [gethostbyname] and [gethostbynamel] only recognize addresses of the form IPv4. To obtain the IPv6 addresses for a machine, you would use the [dns_get_record] function with the [DNS_AAAA] type.

Results:

> php ip-01.php
---------------
ip[istia.univ-angers.fr]=193.49.144.41
name[193.49.144.41]=ametys-fo-2.univ-angers.fr
---------------
ip[www.univ-angers.fr]=193.49.144.41
name[193.49.144.41]=ametys-fo-2.univ-angers.fr
---------------
ip[www.ibm.com]=23.217.77.36
name[23.217.77.36]=a23-217-77-36.deploy.static.akamaitechnologies.com
---------------
ip[www.php.net]=107.150.176.1
name[107.150.176.1]=107-150-176-1.bunnyinfra.net
---------------
ip[yahoo.com]=98.137.11.163
all the IPv4 addresses of [yahoo.com]: 98.137.11.164, 98.137.11.163, 74.6.231.21, 74.6.143.25, 74.6.231.20, 74.6.143.26
name[98.137.11.163]=media-router-fp74.prod.media.vip.gq1.yahoo.com

ip[localhost]=127.0.0.1
name[127.0.0.1]=localhost
---------------
Error, machine [xx] not found
