The Word documents, PDF, OpenOffice, and the image open normally: they have been decoded correctly.

The attached message [test-localhost.eml] was saved as an attachment. However, it is itself an email that, in turn, contains text and attachments. Note in the response [BODYSTRUCTURE] that the server was unable to parse this attached message because it is encoded in Base64: it returns an empty envelope ([(NIL NIL ...)]) and a structure reduced to empty text. To go further, we would need to download the attached message, decode it, and analyze its structure (MIME) ourselves. And this message could itself contain an attached email, and so on. Rather than writing this parser from scratch, we’ll use a library.

docs.title: 16.6.8. POP3 / IMAP client with the [zbateson/mail-mime-parser] library
docs.text:
Course PHP 7 used the [php-mime-mail-parser] library, which required the PHP and [mailparse] extensions, which had to be downloaded and installed separately. We will use the [zbateson/mail-mime-parser] library (https://github.com/zbateson/mail-mime-parser), written entirely in PHP: it was installed by the [composer install] command along with the other dependencies for the course, with no further action required. It parses the full text of a message, as rendered by the commands [RETR] from POP3 and [FETCH n BODY[]] from IMAP. The [imap-03.php] script will therefore work with both protocols.

To test it, we will send a message whose last attachment, [test-localhost-2.eml], itself contains an email attachment, [test-localhost.eml]:

  • [test-localhost-2.eml] contains 4 attachments (the Word documents PDF, OpenOffice, and the image) and the email [test-localhost.eml];
  • [test-localhost.eml] contains the same 4 attachments.

The configuration file [config-smtp-03.json] describes this email:

{
    "mail to localhost via localhost": {
        "smtp-server": "localhost",
        "smtp-port": 1025,
        "from": "guest@localhost",
        "to": "guest@localhost",
        "subject": "test-localhost-3",
        "message": "line 1\nline 2\nline 3",
        "tls": false,
        "attachments": [
            "/attachments/Hello from Symfony Mailer.docx",
            "/attachments/Hello from Symfony Mailer.pdf",
            "/attachments/Hello from Symfony Mailer.odt",
            "/attachments/Cours-Tutoriels-Serge-Tahé-1568x268.png",
            "/attachments/test-localhost-2.eml"
        ]
    }
}

It is used with the command [php smtp-02.php config-smtp-03.json].

The script [imap-03.php] uses the same configuration file, [config-imap-01.json], as the previous scripts. It is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// IMAP / POP3 client used to read mails
// the analysis of the messages is entrusted to the [zbateson/mail-mime-parser] library
// available at the URL [https://github.com/zbateson/mail-mime-parser]

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . "/../../../vendor/autoload.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/ImapClient.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Pop3Client.php";

use ZBateson\MailMimeParser\IMessage;
use ZBateson\MailMimeParser\Message;

// the parameters for reading the mail
const CONFIG_FILE_NAME = "config-imap-01.json";

// we retrieve the configuration
if (!file_exists(CONFIG_FILE_NAME)) {
    print "The configuration file " . CONFIG_FILE_NAME . " does not exist\n";
    exit(1);
}
$mailboxes = json_decode(file_get_contents(CONFIG_FILE_NAME), true);

// reading the mailboxes
foreach ($mailboxes as $name => $info) {
    if (($info["enabled"] ?? true) === false) {
        continue;
    }
    print "------------Reading the mailbox [$name]\n";
    readmailbox($name, $info);
}
// end
print "Done\n";

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function readmailbox(string $name, array $info): void
{
    // an IMAP or POP3 client depending on the configuration
    $client = match ($info["protocol"]) {
        "imap" => new ImapClient($info),
        "pop3" => new Pop3Client($info),
    };
    try {
        // connection
        $nbmsg = $client->connect();
        print "Connection established with the server [$name].\n";
        print "There are [$nbmsg] messages in the mailbox [$name]\n";
        // unread messages
        print "Retrieving the list of the unread messages of the mailbox [$name]\n";
        $msgNumbers = $client->unread();
        if (count($msgNumbers) === 0) {
            print "There are no new messages in the mailbox [$name]\n";
        }
        // we go through the list of the unread messages
        foreach ($msgNumbers as $msgNumber) {
            print "---message no. [$msgNumber]\n";
            // we retrieve the full text of the message and analyze it
            getMailBody($client->message($msgNumber), "{$info["output-dir"]}/message-$msgNumber");
            // if the protocol is POP3, we delete the message after retrieving it
            if ($info["protocol"] === "pop3") {
                $client->delete($msgNumber);
            }
        }
    } catch (RuntimeException $ex) {
        print "Error: " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
    } finally {
        try {
            $client->close();
            print "Connection closed successfully.\n";
        } catch (RuntimeException $ex) {
            print "Closing the connection failed: " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
        }
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// analysis of the full text of a message
function getMailBody(string $text, string $outputDir): void
{
    // the library analyzes the text of the message and turns it into an [IMessage] object
    // (false: the text is no longer used once the object is built)
    $message = Message::from($text, false);
    // we save the different parts of the message in the folder [$outputDir]
    getParts($message, $outputDir);
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// saving the different parts of a message
function getParts(IMessage $message, string $outputDir): void
{
    // we create the folder where the message is saved if need be
    if (!is_dir($outputDir) && !mkdir($outputDir, recursive: true)) {
        print "The folder [$outputDir] could not be created\n";
        return;
    }
    // the headers of the message (from, to, subject...), decoded
    $headers = [];
    foreach ($message->getAllHeaders() as $header) {
        $headers[] = "{$header->getName()}: {$header->getValue()}";
    }
    // we save the text messages
    for ($i = 1; $i <= $message->getTextPartCount(); $i++) {
        print "-- Saving a message of type [text/plain]\n";
        saveMessage($message->getTextContent($i - 1), false, $headers, "$outputDir/message_$i.txt");
    }
    // we save the html messages
    for ($i = 1; $i <= $message->getHtmlPartCount(); $i++) {
        print "-- Saving a message of type [text/html]\n";
        saveMessage($message->getHtmlContent($i - 1), true, $headers, "$outputDir/message_$i.html");
    }
    // we go through the list of the attachments
    $iAttachment = 0;
    foreach ($message->getAllAttachmentParts() as $attachment) {
        // type and name of the attachment
        $fileType = $attachment->getContentType();
        $fileName = freeName($outputDir, $attachment->getFilename() ?? "attachment");
        print "-- Saving an attachment of type [$fileType] in the file [$fileName]\n";
        // we save the attachment, decoded
        $attachment->saveContent($fileName);
        // special case of the message/rfc822 type
        if ($fileType === "message/rfc822") {
            // the attachment is itself a message - we analyze it recursively
            // in a subfolder [rfc822-1], [rfc822-2]...
            $iAttachment++;
            $attachedMessage = Message::from($attachment->getBinaryContentStream()->getContents(), false);
            getParts($attachedMessage, "$outputDir/rfc822-$iAttachment");
        }
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// a free file name in the folder [$dir]: x.pdf, otherwise x_1.pdf, x_2.pdf...
function freeName(string $dir, string $name): string
{
    $info = pathinfo($name);
    $extension = isset($info["extension"]) ? ".{$info["extension"]}" : "";
    $candidate = "$dir/$name";
    for ($i = 1; file_exists($candidate); $i++) {
        $candidate = "$dir/{$info["filename"]}_$i$extension";
    }
    return $candidate;
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// saving a text message preceded by the headers of the message
function saveMessage(string $text, bool $html, array $headers, string $filename): void
{
    // in HTML, each header is ended by <br/> to be alone on its line
    $endOfLine = $html ? "<br/>\n" : "\n";
    $contents = implode($endOfLine, $headers) . $endOfLine . $endOfLine . $text;
    if (file_put_contents($filename, $contents) === false) {
        print "The message could not be saved in the file [$filename]\n";
    } else {
        print "The message has been saved in the file [$filename]\n";
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 10: the Composer class loader for the [zbateson/mail-mime-parser] library;
  • Lines 14–15: The two types from the library that we are using: the [IMessage] interface and the [Message] class that implements it;
  • line 21: we check that the configuration file exists;
  • line 39: the [readmailbox] function has the same structure as in [imap-01.php]. The client IMAP or POP3 is this time created directly by an expression [match];
  • line 61: the complete message text is requested from the function [getMailBody];
  • Lines 81–87: The static method [Message::from] parses the message text and returns a [IMessage] object. The function [getParts] then saves its various parts;
  • line 92: the function [getParts] takes two parameters:
    • the message [$message] to be analyzed;
    • [$outputDir]: the folder in which the message’s text and attachments are to be saved;
  • lines 101–102: the headers of the message being analyzed (from, to, subject, etc.) are retrieved. The method [getValue] returns the decoded value of a header;
  • lines 105–107: A message may have multiple parts ([text/plain]). The [getTextContent($i - 1)] method returns the text of the i-th part (parts are numbered starting from 0), decoded and converted using UTF-8. We save them all, giving each one a different filename;
  • lines 110–112: same procedure for the [text/html] parts;
  • line 116: iterate through the list of attachments in the message;
  • lines 118–119: the attachment type (Content-Type header) and its name, decoded by the library regardless of how it is encoded. The [freeName] function returns a filename that does not yet exist in the folder;
  • line 122: the [saveContent] method saves the decoded content of the attachment to a file;
  • lines 124–129: if the attachment is an email, it is in turn parsed via a recursive call to the function [getParts]. Its decoded content is obtained by the [getBinaryContentStream] method, which returns a stream; the entire content of this stream is then read using the [getContents] method. If the analyzed message has two email attachments, the first will be saved in the [$outputDir/rfc822-1] folder and the second in the [$outputDir/rfc822-2] folder;
  • Line 136: If the file [x.pdf] already exists, the function [freeName] tries the names [x_1.pdf], [x_2.pdf]... until it finds a filename that does not exist. The function [pathinfo] splits a filename into a filename and an extension;
  • line 149: the function [saveMessage] saves the message text preceded by the message headers. In the case of a HTML text, each header ends with the tag [<br/>].

docs.title: 22. Practical Exercise – Version 11
docs.text:
It is still common for web services to send their response in the form of a XML document rather than a JSON document:

  • the JSON document is smaller, but you need instructions to understand it;
  • the XML document is more verbose but is self-documenting. It is immediately understandable.

We are modifying the client/server application from version 10 so that the server now sends a XML document in response to its clients. In doing so, we are putting the previous chapter into practice.

docs.title: 22.1. The server
docs.text:
This architecture will be implemented by the following files:

scripts-web/tax/version-11
├── Data
│   ├── .htaccess
│   ├── config-server.json
│   └── logs.txt
├── Utilities
│   ├── XmlUtilities.php
│   └── testXml.php
└── tax-server.php

docs.title: 22.1.1. The [XmlUtilities] class
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course added a method, [getXmlForArrayOfAttributes], to the [Utilities] class that rendered the XML document from an array. Our server already uses the [Utilities] class from version 5 (for the [Database] class): we create a new [XmlUtilities] class:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// utility functions for the XML format: the class can be neither instantiated nor derived
final class XmlUtilities
{
    // private constructor: the class cannot be instantiated
    private function __construct()
    {
    }

    // returns the XML document of an array [$data]: the root element is named [$root]
    // the keys of the array become element names, the values their content
    public static function arrayToXml(array $data, string $root): string
    {
        // an empty XML document (new DOM API of PHP 8.4)
        $document = \Dom\XMLDocument::createEmpty();
        // the document will be indented
        $document->formatOutput = true;
        // the root element and its descendants
        $document->append(self::element($document, $root, $data));
        // the XML text of the document
        return $document->saveXml();
    }

    // returns the XML element [<$name>$value</$name>]
    private static function element(\Dom\XMLDocument $document, string $name, mixed $value): \Dom\Element
    {
        $element = $document->createElement($name);
        if (is_array($value)) {
            // an array: each element of the array becomes a child element (recursive call)
            foreach ($value as $key => $subValue) {
                // the elements of a list (keys 0, 1, 2...) are named [item]
                $element->append(self::element($document, is_int($key) ? "item" : $key, $subValue));
            }
        } else {
            // a simple value becomes the text of the element (the characters <, >, & are encoded by DOM)
            $element->textContent = match (true) {
                is_bool($value) => $value ? "true" : "false",
                default => (string) $value,
            };
        }
        return $element;
    }
}

Comments

  • line 9: Like the [Utilities] class in version 5, this class has only static methods. It is [final], and its constructor is private: it cannot be derived from or instantiated;
  • line 18: The static method [arrayToXml] returns the document XML from the array [$data] passed as a parameter. The second parameter is the name of the document’s root element;
  • line 21: We use the new API DOM from PHP 8.4, introduced in the previous chapter. The static method [createEmpty] creates an empty XML document. Script PHP 7 used [SimpleXML], which can also generate a document, but not as well: you had to code the special characters in the text yourself using the [htmlspecialchars] function;
  • line 23: the resulting document will be indented, making it more readable;
  • line 25: the document’s root element, created by the [element] method, is added to the document;
  • line 27: the method [saveXml] renders the text XML in the document;
  • line 31: the private method [element] returns the element XML with the name [$name], representing the value [$value];
  • line 33: the [createElement] method of the document creates the element;
  • Lines 34–38: If the value is an array, each of its elements becomes a child element, created by a recursive call to the [element] method. The keys of the array become the names of the child elements. The keys of a list are the integers 0, 1, 2..., which cannot be XML element names: these elements are therefore named [item]. The script PHP 7 referred to them as [i0], [i1], [i2]...;
  • lines 40–45: otherwise, the value becomes the element’s text, assigned to its [textContent] property. The characters [<], [>], and [&] in the text are encoded as DOM ([<], [>], [&]). Booleans are written as [true] and [false]; other values are converted to strings. The expression [match (true)] selects the first branch whose condition is true.

We write the following test script, [testXml.php]:

<?php

// strict compliance with the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// dependency
require_once __DIR__ . "/XmlUtilities.php";

use Application\XmlUtilities;

// an associative array
$array = [
    "lastName" => "amédée",
    "firstName" => "sylvain",
    "age" => 40,
    "children" => [
        ["lastName" => "amédée", "firstName" => "béatrice", "age" => 6],
        ["lastName" => "amédée", "firstName" => "bertrand", "age" => 4],
    ],
    "remark" => "<married> & happy",
];
// the response is an XML document
header("Content-Type: application/xml; charset=utf-8");
print XmlUtilities::arrayToXml($array, "person");
  • lines 12–21: an associative array containing a list and text with special characters from XML;
  • line 23: the function [header] sets the header HTTP [Content-Type] of the response: it is a XML document;
  • line 24: the XML document in the table, with root element [person], is sent to the client.

  • line 19: the characters [<], [>], and [&] have been encoded.

The changes to the server script are as follows:

}

// sending the HTTP response to the client
// $result: the array to send, in the form of the XML document <response>...</response>
// $statusCode: the HTTP status of the response
// $headers: HTTP headers to add to the response
// $logger: the application's log (null if it could not be created)
// $redis: the Redis client (null if it has not been created yet)
function sendResponse(
    array $result,
    int $statusCode,
    array $headers = [],
    ?Logger $logger = null,
    ?RedisClient $redis = null
): void {
    // the XML response
    $response = new Response(XmlUtilities::arrayToXml($result, "response"), $statusCode, $headers);
    $response->headers->set("Content-Type", "application/xml; charset=utf-8");
    // sending
    $response->send();
    // log in JSON, more concise than XML
    $logger?->write(json_encode(
        ["response" => $result],
        JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION
    ));
    // closing the connection to the Redis server
    $redis?->disconnect();
}

docs.title: 22.2.1. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [ClientDao] class from version 9 is modified to account for the new response format. [SimpleXML] is used to process this response:

        try {
            // we make the request to the server
            $response = $this->httpClient->request("GET", $this->urlServer, $options);
            // the status, the headers and the XML document of the response, even in case of error (parameter false)
            $statusCode = $response->getStatusCode();
            $headers = $response->getHeaders(false);
            $content = $response->getContent(false);
        } catch (ExceptionInterface $ex) {
            // the server could not be reached
            throw new TaxException("Error communicating with the server ({$ex->getMessage()})", 40, $ex);
        }
        // logs
        // print "$content\n";
        // the server sends the XML document <response>...</response>
        // the LIBXML_NOERROR and LIBXML_NOWARNING options avoid PHP warnings if the XML is invalid
        $xml = simplexml_load_string($content, options: LIBXML_NOERROR | LIBXML_NOWARNING);
        if ($xml === false || $xml->getName() !== "response") {
            throw new TaxException("Invalid server response [$content]", 41);
        }
        // error?
        if ($statusCode !== 200) {
            // we throw an exception whose message is the server's response, converted to JSON (more concise),
            // completed by its HTTP status
            $serverResponse = json_decode(json_encode($xml, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
            $message = json_encode(
                ["HTTP status" => $statusCode] + $serverResponse,
                JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR
            );
            throw new TaxException($message, 42);
        }
        // we retrieve the session cookie if it is not known yet
        if ($this->sessionCookie === null) {
            foreach ($headers["set-cookie"] ?? [] as $cookie) {
                if (preg_match('/^PHPSESSID=(.+?);/', $cookie, $fields) === 1) {
                    $this->sessionCookie = "PHPSESSID=$fields[1]";
                }
            }
        }
        // we return the response: the array [tax, surcharge, discount, reduction, rate]
        // in the XML document, all the values are texts: we convert them into their type
        return [
            "tax" => (int) $xml->tax,
            "surcharge" => (int) $xml->surcharge,
            "discount" => (int) $xml->discount,
            "reduction" => (int) $xml->reduction,
            "rate" => (float) $xml->rate,
        ];
    }
}

Comments

  • line 63: The server’s response is read. It is a XML [<response>…</response>] document;
  • line 72: the [simplexml_load_string] function parses the received XML document and returns a [SimpleXMLElement] object representing its root element, or [false] if the document is not a valid XML document. By default, the [libxml] library used by [SimpleXML] also reports document errors as PHP warnings: the options [LIBXML_NOERROR] and [LIBXML_NOWARNING] suppress them. They are passed via the argument named [options], which avoids having to write the parameter [class_name] that precedes it in the function signature;
  • line 73: the method [getName] returns the name of the root element, which must be [response];
  • Lines 77–85: In the event of an error, the exception message will be the string JSON from the server’s response rather than the received string XML, because the string JSON is more concise. To obtain the associative array for the response XML, we use a classic trick: the function [json_encode] can convert an object [SimpleXMLElement] into JSON, and [json_decode] then converts this JSON into an array. The exception message thus has the same format as in previous versions;
  • lines 97–103: the results array is returned. The child elements of the [response] element are accessed as properties of the [$xml] object ([$xml->tax]). In a XML document, all values are text: unlike JSON, XML does not distinguish between integers, real numbers, and character strings. Each value is therefore converted to the type expected by the [business] layer using the [(int)] and [(float)] operators. The PHP 7 client returned the values as strings.

Test

docs.title: 23. Practical Exercise – Version 12
docs.text: In this chapter, we will write a web application that follows the MVC architecture (Model-View-Controller). The application will be able to return responses in three formats: JSON, XML, and HTML. There is a significant increase in complexity between what we are about to do and what we have done previously. We will reuse most of the concepts covered so far and will detail all the steps leading to the final application.

docs.title: 23.1. MVC Architecture
docs.text:
We will implement the architecture model known as MVC (Model–View–Controller) as follows:

The processing of a client request will proceed as follows:

  • 1 - Request: The requested URL parameters will be in the form [http://machine:port/context/main.php?action=anAction&param1=v1&param2=v2&…]. The [Main controller] will use the [action] parameter from the URL to “route” the request to the secondary controller responsible for processing this action. The remainder of the URL and [param1=v1&param2=v2&…] consists of optional parameters that will be passed to the action. The C in MVC is the string [Main controller, Controller / Action]. If no controller can process the requested action, the server will respond that the requested action is invalid;
  • 2 - Processing:
    • The selected action [2a] can use the parameters passed to it by [Main controller]. These parameters may come from several sources: the [/param1/param2/…] path from URL, the [param1=v1&param2=v2] parameters from URL, or parameters submitted by the browser with its request;
    • When processing the user’s request, the action may require the [business] and [2b] layers. Once the client’s request has been processed, it may trigger various responses. A classic example is: an error response if the request could not be processed correctly, or a confirmation response otherwise;
    • [Controller / Action] will return its response, [2c], to the main controller along with a status code. These status codes will uniquely represent the current state of the application. They will be either success codes or error codes;
  • 3 - Response:
    • Depending on whether the client requested a response of JSON, XML, or HTML, the [Main controller] will instantiate the appropriate response type ([3a]) and instruct it to send the response to the client. The [Main controller] will pass it the response and status code provided by the [Controller / Action] that was executed;
    • if the desired response is of type JSON or XML, the selected response will format the response from [Controller / Action] that was provided to it and send it via [3c]. The client capable of processing this response can be a PHP console script or a JavaScript script embedded in a HTML page;
    • if the desired response is of type HTML, the selected response will choose one of the HTML views [3b] ([View1], [View2]…) using the status code provided to it. This is the V for MVC. Each status code corresponds to a single view. This view V will display the response from the executed [Controller / Action]. It formats the data from this response using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. This data is called the view model. It is the “M” in MVC. The client is most often a web browser.

Now, let’s clarify the relationship between web architecture MVC and layered architecture. Depending on how the model is defined, these two concepts may or may not be related. Let’s consider a single-layer web application MVC:

In the example above, each [Controller / Action] component incorporates parts of the [business] and [dao] layers. The [web] layer does indeed have a MVC architecture, but the application as a whole does not have a layered architecture. Here, there is only one layer that does everything.

Now, let’s consider a multi-layer web architecture:

The [web] layer can be implemented without following the MVC model. We then have a multi-layer architecture, but the web layer does not implement the MVC model.

For example, in the .NET world, the [web] layer can be implemented using ASP.NET Core MVC, resulting in a layered architecture with a [web] layer of type MVC. Once this is done, we can replace this ASP.NET Core MVC layer with a ASP.NET Core [Razor Pages] layer while keeping the rest (business logic, DAO, driver) unchanged. We then have a layered architecture with a [web] layer that is no longer of type MVC.

In MVC, we stated that model M is that of view V, i.e.,the set of data displayed by view V. Another definition of model M for MVC is given:

Many authors consider that what is to the right of layer [web] forms the M model of MVC. To avoid ambiguity, we can refer to:

  • the domain model when referring to everything to the right of the layer [web];
  • the view model when referring to the data displayed by a view V.

docs.title: 23.2. Project Structure
docs.text:
For this project, we are using a directory structure that mirrors the MVC model. In [VS Code], the [scripts-web/tax/version-12] folder contains the following elements:

scripts-web/tax/version-12
├── Controllers
│   ├── AuthenticateUserController.php
│   ├── CalculateTaxController.php
│   ├── DeleteSimulationController.php
│   ├── DisplayTaxCalculationController.php
│   ├── EndSessionController.php
│   ├── InitSessionController.php
│   ├── InterfaceController.php
│   └── ListSimulationsController.php
├── Data
│   ├── .htaccess
│   ├── config.json
│   └── logs.txt
├── Entities
│   ├── Action.php
│   ├── ControllerResult.php
│   ├── ResponseType.php
│   └── Simulation.php
├── Responses
│   ├── HtmlResponse.php
│   ├── InterfaceResponse.php
│   ├── JsonResponse.php
│   ├── ParentResponse.php
│   └── XmlResponse.php
├── Tests
│   ├── view-authentication.php
│   ├── view-errors.php
│   ├── view-simulations-list.php
│   └── view-tax-calculation.php
├── Views
│   ├── logo.jpg
│   ├── v-authentication.php
│   ├── v-banner.php
│   ├── v-errors.php
│   ├── v-menu.php
│   ├── v-simulations-list.php
│   ├── v-tax-calculation.php
│   ├── view-authentication.php
│   ├── view-errors.php
│   ├── view-simulations-list.php
│   └── view-tax-calculation.php
├── index.php
└── main.php
  • [main.php] is the main controller for our MVC model. It is the C in MVC;
  • the [Controllers] folder contains the secondary controllers. Each one handles a specific action. This action is specified in the URL, for example, […/main.php?action=authenticate-user]. Based on this action, the main controller [main.php] will select a secondary controller—in this case, [AuthenticateUserController]—to handle the requested action. These controllers are also part of the C in MVC;
  • the [Responses] folder contains the classes responsible for sending the response to the client. There is one class for each type of desired response:
    • [JsonResponse]: for a JSON response;
    • [XmlResponse]: for a response of type XML;
    • [HtmlResponse]: for a HTML response;
  • The [Views] file contains the HTML views when a HTML response is desired. This is the V of MVC. They are activated by the class [HtmlResponse], which passes them the data to be displayed. This data is the view model. According to the terminology adopted for the M, this data can be the M of MVC;
  • the [Tests] folder contains test versions of the views, which allow you to adjust their visual appearance;
  • the folder [Entities] contains classes and enumerations used by the various controllers;
  • the [Data] folder contains the configuration file [config.json] and the log file [logs.txt]. As in previous versions, the [.htaccess] file in version 8 prevents [Apache] from serving its files: the configuration contains passwords.

The PHP 7 course copied the classes for layers [business] and [dao] (folder [Model]) and the utilities (folder [Utilities]). We do not copy them: as in previous versions, these classes are loaded from the folders of versions 5, 8, 9, and 11, where they were originally written.

Using this directory structure, we can describe the flow of processing for an action requested by a client:

  • [main.php] receives the request;
  • after performing some preliminary checks (is the action one of the accepted actions?), it forwards the request to the secondary controller responsible for processing that action;
  • the secondary controller performs its tasks. In carrying out this task, it may need the layers [business] and [dao], as well as the entities in the folder [Entities]. It returns its response to the primary controller [main.php], which activated it;
  • depending on the type of response [JSON, XML, HTML] requested by the client, the main controller [main.php] activates one of the responses from the folder [Responses];
  • The responses [JsonResponse, XmlResponse] send the response JSON or XML to the client, respectively;
  • The response [HtmlResponse] uses one of the views from the folder [Views] to send a response HTML to the client;
  • the various components access the [Logger] class in version 9 to write logs to the [Data/logs.txt] file. The following are logged:
    • the requested action;
    • the response from its controller. This is recorded in the JSON format regardless of the requested [JSON, XML, HTML] type;
  • in the event of a fatal error (status HTTP 500 Internal Server Error), the main controller [main.php] sends an email to the administrator using the [SendAdminMail] class from version 9.

docs.title: 23.3. Application Actions
docs.text:
The client sends the action to be executed to the web server as a [action] parameter in the URL [/main.php?action=xxx]. The PHP 7 course listed the actions allowed in the configuration file, each associated with the name of its controller class. We use an enumeration (PHP 8.1), the [Action] enumeration from the [Entities] folder:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// the actions accepted by the application: the value of a case is the name of the action in the URL
enum Action: string
{
    case InitSession = "init-session";
    case AuthenticateUser = "authenticate-user";
    case CalculateTax = "calculate-tax";
    case ListSimulations = "list-simulations";
    case DeleteSimulation = "delete-simulation";
    case EndSession = "end-session";
    case DisplayTaxCalculation = "display-tax-calculation";

    // does the action require the session type (json, xml, html) to be known?
    public function requiresSessionType(): bool
    {
        return $this !== self::InitSession;
    }

    // does the action require the user to be authenticated?
    public function requiresAuthentication(): bool
    {
        return match ($this) {
            self::InitSession, self::AuthenticateUser => false,
            default => true,
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • line 9: The enumeration [Action] is a “backed” enumeration: each of its cases has a value, in this case of type [string]. We encountered enumerations in the chapter on classes;
  • Line 11: [init-session] starts a session of tax calculation simulations. This action specifies the type of responses desired: [JSON, XML, HTML];
  • line 12: Once the session type is set, the client must authenticate using the action [authenticate-user]. Until the client is authenticated, all other actions are prohibited except for [init-session];
  • line 13: Once authenticated, the client can perform a series of tax calculations using action [calculate-tax];
  • line 14: At any time, the customer can request to view the list of simulations they have performed using action [list-simulations];
  • line 15: They can delete some of them using action [delete-simulation];
  • line 16: The customer ends their simulation session using action [end-session]. From that point on, they will need to log in again if they want to use the application;
  • line 17: In the HTML application, the action [display-tax-calculation] displays the form used to calculate the tax;
  • lines 20–23: An enumeration can have methods. Within a method, [$this] refers to the enumeration item for which the method is being called. The method [requiresSessionType] specifies whether the action can be executed only when the session type is known: this is the case for all actions except [init-session]. The cases of an enumeration are unique objects: they are compared using the [===] operator;
  • Lines 26–32: The method [requiresAuthentication] determines whether the action can only be performed by an authenticated user: this is the case for all actions except [init-session] and [authenticate-user]. The expression [match] allows multiple values, separated by commas, within the same branch.

These rules, which were previously written in the main controller for the PHP 7 course, are now grouped together with the action definitions.

Comments

  • line 2: the file JSON describing the database MySQL [dbtaxes-2019], which is for version 8. The path is relative to the folder [version-12];
  • Lines 3–33: the PHP files for the application. These first contain the classes that have already been written:
    • the [TaxException, TaxAdminData, Database] entities and the [Utilities] class from version 5;
    • layers [dao] and [business] from versions 8 and 9;
    • the utilities [Logger] and [SendAdminMail] from version 9 and [XmlUtilities] from version 11;
    • and the classes from version 12, which we will now present. The file PHP 7 also contained the absolute paths to third-party libraries ([C:/myprograms/laragon-lite/www/vendor/autoload.php]): the class loader from [Composer] is now loaded directly by [main.php], using a relative path;
  • lines 34–39: the user authorized to use the application;
  • lines 40–48: the email contact information for the application administrator. The email is sent to the [Mailpit] server, which listens on port 1025 (see version 9);
  • line 49: the path to the log file;
  • lines 50–54: the details of the [Redis] server, which serves as the scope memory for [application] (see version 10);
  • lines 55–59: [HTML view => array of the status codes leading to this view] associations. These are described a little further on;
  • line 60: the [view-errors.php] view is displayed in a HTML session whenever an abnormal error occurs:
    • An application such as JSON or XML is typically queried using a programmed client. The client passes parameters to the server, which may be missing or incorrect. The controllers handle these cases and return error codes to the client. All possible error cases must be handled;
    • with a HTML application, it’s a little different. Under normal use, the web application utilizes only a subset of the possible use cases for the JSON and XML clients. Let’s take an example: the [calculate-tax] action expects three posted parameters (sent by a POST): [married, children, salary]. With a JSON client that allows you to enter URL manually, you can request the action [calculate-tax] with a GET instead of a POST, or with a POST without any posted parameters when three are required, and so on. The JSON server must handle all these cases. With a web application, the [calculate-tax] action will be requested from a web form where neither of the two previous cases is possible: the [calculate-tax] action will be called with a POST and all three [married, children, salary] parameters. However, the user can reproduce certain errors by manually entering URL values into the browser. For security reasons, this scenario must be handled;
    • the view [view-errors.php] will be displayed whenever a secondary controller returns a status code that is incompatible with the web application, i.e.,a status code not present in the [views] key of the configuration file. We are opting for this solution for educational purposes. Another possible option would be to re-display the view currently shown in the client’s browser so that the user gets the impression that the server is not responding to their hand-crafted URL requests.

Compared to the configuration file for the PHP 7 course, the keys [rootDirectory] (the root directory is now known as [main.php]), [actions] (replaced by the enumeration [Action]), and [types] (replaced by the enumeration [ResponseType] presented below) have been removed.

docs.title: 23.5.1. The [curl] tool
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course used the graphical tool [Postman] to query the various URL components of the web application. We use the command-line tool [curl], introduced in the chapter on web services. It allows us to:

  • use any URL: these are created manually;
  • to query the web server using a GET, POST, PUT, OPTIONS… (options [-X] and [-d]);
  • specify the parameters for GET (in URL) or POST (options [-d] and [--data-urlencode]);
  • set the HTTP headers for the request (option [-H]);
  • to receive a response in the JSON, XML, or HTML format;
  • to have access to the HTTP headers of the response (option [-i]);
  • to handle the session cookie like a browser: the [-c cookies.txt] option saves the cookies sent by the server to the [cookies.txt] file, while the [-b cookies.txt] option sends them back to the server.

Since we manually generate the requested URL files, we’ll be able to test all possible error scenarios and see how the server responds. Remember that in a [PowerShell] terminal, you must type [curl.exe] instead of [curl]. All commands in this chapter are entered in a terminal opened in any working directory, where [curl] creates the file [cookies.txt].

To post the parameter [married], we’ll use the option [--data-urlencode "married=yes"], which URL-encodes the parameter’s name and value if necessary. The parameter names ([married], [number]...) contain no accented characters, so in URL we can write them as they are.

docs.title: 23.5.2. The Symfony / Serializer Library
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course used the [Symfony / Serializer] library to serialize server responses into JSON and XML, which may contain [Simulation] objects. It had two advantages: the same API for both JSON and XML; the serialization of objects with private attributes, exposed via getters.

We do not use it in this version, although it is installed in the [vendor] folder for the course:

  • our class [Simulation] is a [readonly] class with public attributes (see the following paragraph). The function [json_encode] directly serializes an object’s public attributes: the JSON serialization no longer requires a library;
  • for XML, we have the [XmlUtilities] class from version 11, which produces XML documents in the same format as those from version 11, which XML clients already know how to process. All you need to do is provide it with an array, after converting the [Simulation] objects into associative arrays;
  • the server never has to deserialize JSON or XML into objects, which was the other advantage highlighted by the PHP 7 course.

The [Symfony / Serializer] library would therefore only add one more dependency here. It remains a good choice when you need to deserialize documents into typed objects or handle many different formats.

docs.title: 23.6. Application Entities
docs.text:
The [Entities] folder contains two enumerations, [Action] (already presented) and [ResponseType] (presented along with the server responses), and two classes. The [Simulation] class encapsulates the elements of a tax calculation simulation:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// a tax calculation simulation: an immutable object
final readonly class Simulation
{
    // the attributes are public: they cannot be modified (readonly) but
    // they are read directly, without getters, and serialized by [json_encode]
    public function __construct(
        // the calculation parameters
        public string $married,
        public int $children,
        public int $salary,
        // the calculation result
        public int $tax,
        public int $surcharge,
        public int $discount,
        public int $reduction,
        public float $rate,
    ) {
    }
}

Comments

  • line 9: the class is [readonly] (PHP 8.2): all its attributes are read-only. A simulation is an immutable object: once constructed, it does not change;
  • Lines 13–24: The attributes are declared and initialized by passing in the constructor’s parameters (PHP 8.0). They are typed: [string] for marital status, [int] for other parameters and amounts, and [float] for the tax rate;
  • the attributes are public: since they are read-only, it is no longer necessary to protect them with getters. The class PHP 7 [Simulation] derived from the class [BaseEntity], had eight untyped attributes [protected], and eight getters.

The second class, [ControllerResult], represents the result that a secondary controller returns to the main controller:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// the result returned by a secondary controller to the main controller
final readonly class ControllerResult
{
    public function __construct(
        // the HTTP status code of the response
        public int $statusCode,
        // the status of the application after the action has been executed
        public int $status,
        // the response itself: a message, a list of messages, a simulation...
        public mixed $response,
        // HTTP headers to add to the response
        public array $headers = [],
    ) {
    }
}
  • line 13: the status code HTTP of the response to be sent to the client;
  • line 15: the state of the application after the action has been executed;
  • line 17: the response itself. Its type depends on the action: a message, a list of error messages, a simulation, or a list of simulations. The type [mixed] (PHP 8.0) accepts any value;
  • line 19: the HTTP headers to be added to the response. This is an optional parameter.

In the PHP 7 course, the controllers returned the array [[$statusCode, $status, $content, $headers]]. An object with named and typed attributes is safer: you cannot make a mistake in the order of the elements.

docs.title: 23.7. The app's utilities
docs.text:
The application uses three utilities that have already been described:

  • the [Logger] class from version 9 allows you to log events to a text file;
  • the [SendAdminMail] class from version 9 allows you to send an email to the application administrator;
  • the [XmlUtilities] class from version 11 retrieves the XML document from a table.

docs.title: 23.8. The [business] and [dao] layers
docs.text:
The classes and interfaces of the layers [business] and [dao] have all been defined and used in previous versions:

ClassRoleTaxExceptionThe class of exceptions thrown by the [dao] layer. Version 5, folder [Entities]InterfaceServerDaoInterface implemented by the [dao] layer of the server. Version 8, folder [Dao]ServerDaoImplementation of the [InterfaceServerDao] interface: tax data is read from the database. Version 8ServerDaoWithSessionClass derived from [ServerDao]: Tax data can be provided to the constructor. Version 9, folder [Dao]InterfaceServerBusinessInterface implemented by the [business] layer of the server. Version 8, folder [Business]ServerBusinessImplementation of the [InterfaceServerBusiness] interface: tax calculation. Version 8

The application currently under development therefore makes extensive use of elements that have already been presented and used:

  • the [business] and [dao] layers;
  • the utilities [Logger], [SendAdminMail], and [XmlUtilities];
  • the entities [TaxException, TaxAdminData, Database].

We will focus on the [web] layer of the application:

docs.title: 23.9.1. Introduction
docs.text:
The main controller [main.php] is configured by the file [Data/config.json]. Let’s review its position in our MVC architecture:

The main controller [main.php] is the first element in the MVC architecture to process the client’s request. It has several roles:

  • First, it performs basic checks:
    • Does its configuration file exist and is it valid?
    • it loads all the project dependencies. This involves loading all components of the MVC architecture;
    • Has the requested action been specified? If so, is it valid?
  • If the requested action is valid, it selects [2a]—the secondary controller that will process it—and passes it the information it needs: the application configuration, the request HTTP, and the session;
  • it retrieves [2c] the response from the secondary controller. Depending on the type (JSON, XML, HTML) of response requested by the client, it selects [3a] the response (JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse) responsible for sending the response to the client and passes it all the information it needs (the request HTTP, the session, the application configuration, and the response from the secondary controller).

docs.title: 23.9.2. [main.php] - 1
docs.text:
The beginning of the primary controller [main.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict compliance with the declared types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// PHP errors are not sent to the client (they go to the web server's log)
ini_set("display_errors", "0");

// the application's root folder: the paths of the configuration file are relative to this folder
const ROOT_DIRECTORY = __DIR__;
// path of the configuration file
const CONFIG_FILENAME = ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/Data/config.json";

// Composer's autoloader (Symfony, Predis)
require_once ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/../../../vendor/autoload.php";

// we retrieve the configuration
$fileContents = is_readable(CONFIG_FILENAME) ? file_get_contents(CONFIG_FILENAME) : false;
if ($fileContents === false) {
    sendConfigError(131, "The configuration file [config.json] does not exist");
}
try {
    $config = json_decode($fileContents, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (\JsonException) {
    sendConfigError(132, "The configuration file [config.json] could not be processed correctly");
}

Comments

  • Lines 10–12: The main controller uses the following classes from the Symfony library [HttpFoundation]:
    • [Request]: the HTTP request currently being processed;
    • [Response]: the HTTP response to the client;
    • [Session]: the web application session;
  • Line 15: Errors detected by PHP are not included in the document sent to the client: they would corrupt the responses JSON or XML. They remain logged in the web server’s error log (Apache’s [error.log] file). During development, this line can be commented out: the PHP errors will then appear in the responses received by [curl] or the browser. This aids in debugging. The PHP 7 script also modified the error reporting level using [error_reporting(E_ALL && !E_WARNING && !E_NOTICE)], an expression that was, incidentally, incorrect (it required the bitwise operators [&] and [~]): on the contrary, we want to ignore no errors;
  • line 18: the application’s root directory, which is that of the [main.php] script. The paths in the configuration file are relative to this directory. The constant is defined in the [Application] namespace: it is therefore visible to classes in that namespace, particularly the controller that will calculate the tax;
  • line 20: the path to the configuration file;
  • line 23: the class loader from [Composer] is loaded, making the Symfony and Predis classes available. It is loaded before the configuration is read: the error response sent if the configuration fails uses the Symfony class [Response]. The PHP 7 script used an absolute path here;
  • lines 26–29: the configuration file is read. If it does not exist or cannot be read, an error response with status [131] is sent to the client via the [sendConfigError] function;
  • lines 30–34: The JSON from the configuration file is decoded. With the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option, the [json_decode] function throws a [JsonException] exception if the JSON is invalid. An error response is then sent with status [132]. Starting with PHP 8.0, the [catch] clause can omit the exception variable when it is not used: [catch (\JsonException)];

Here we have an existing and syntactically correct configuration file. It would also be necessary to verify that the expected keys are actually present in this file. We will consider this to be part of the developer’s normal debugging work.

The function [sendConfigError] is defined at the end of the script:

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// error on the configuration file: JSON 500 response then end of the script
// the application's classes are not loaded yet: we use [Response] directly
function sendConfigError(int $status, string $message): never
{
    $json = json_encode(["action" => "", "status" => $status, "response" => $message], JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    $response = new Response($json, Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
    $response->headers->set("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8");
    $response->send();
    exit;
}
  • Line 124: The return type [never] (PHP 8.1) indicates that the function never returns control to the caller; it always terminates with [exit] or an exception. A code analyzer such as the [PHP Intelephense] extension of [VS Code] then knows that the code following a call to [sendConfigError] is executed only if the configuration could be read;
  • line 126: all responses generated by the web application will have three keys:
    • [action]: the action requested by the client (unknown here);
    • [status]: the state of the application after executing this action;
    • [response]: the web server’s response;
  • line 127: Since the application’s classes have not yet been loaded, a Symfony response is constructed directly, with the status [500 Internal Server Error];
  • line 128: the response is a JSON document encoded in UTF-8;
  • line 129: the response is sent to the client.

docs.title: 23.9.3. [curl] Tests - 1
docs.text:
We will verify the server’s behavior when the configuration file is missing or incorrect. Let’s rename [Data/config.json] to [Data/config2.json], then request the URL from the main controller:

> curl -i "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/tax/version-12/main.php"
HTTP/1.0 500 Internal Server Error
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:51:52 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"action":"","status":131,"response":"The configuration file [config.json] does not exist"}
  • Line 1: The option [-i] instructs [curl] to display the HTTP headers from the response;
  • Line 2: The server returned status code [500 Internal Server Error];
  • line 8: The response is a JSON document;
  • line 10: the JSON document from the response. This is indeed the one we were expecting.

Let's rename the file back to [config.json], then make it syntactically incorrect—for example, by deleting everything after its second line. We no longer display the headers HTTP:

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/tax/version-12/main.php"
{"action":"","status":132,"response":"The configuration file [config.json] could not be processed correctly"}

This initial test showed us that we can send any type of request to the server under test and that we receive the complete response: the HTTP headers and the document that follows them. Let’s not forget to restore the contents of the [config.json] file.

docs.title: 23.9.4. [main.php] – 2
docs.text:
We’ll now resume our analysis of the main controller, [main.php]:

// we include the application's dependencies
foreach ($config["dependencies"] as $dependency) {
    require_once ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/$dependency";
}

// the current request
$request = Request::createFromGlobals();
// the session - started after loading the classes: it contains [Simulation] objects
$session = new Session();
$session->start();

// creating the log file
try {
    $logger = new Logger(ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/" . $config["logsFilename"]);
} catch (TaxException) {
    // error 500 - JSON response without logs
    $content = [
        "action" => "",
        "status" => 133,
        "response" => "The log file [{$config["logsFilename"]}] could not be created",
    ];
    (new JsonResponse())->send($request, $session, $config, Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, $content);
    exit;
}

Comments

  • lines 37–39: We include all the application’s dependencies. We’ve already encountered this code several times;
  • line 42: All information from the client’s request is encapsulated in the Symfony object [Request];
  • lines 44–45: a new session is started, or the existing session is retrieved if the client has sent a session cookie. The session is started after the application classes have been loaded: it will contain [Simulation] objects, and the [Simulation] class must be defined by the time PHP reconstructs the session objects;
  • Lines 48–59: We attempt to create the [Logger] object, which will allow us to log events to the [Data/logs.txt] file. This creation may fail: the constructor for [Logger] then throws a [TaxException] exception;
  • lines 52–56: the error response, with status [133]. The message uses the log file name specified in the configuration rather than the full path: the full path would reveal the server’s folder structure to the client;
  • line 57: the response is sent via a [JsonResponse] object, without a log since one could not be created. The application classes are now loaded: they can be used;
  • Line 58: The script is terminated.

All responses sent to the client implement the following [InterfaceResponse] interface, from the [Responses] folder:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// the interface implemented by the three response types [JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse]
interface InterfaceResponse
{
    // sending the response to the client
    // Request $request: the request being processed
    // Session $session: the web application's session
    // array $config: the application's configuration
    // int $statusCode: the HTTP status code of the response
    // array $content: the server's response, the array [action, status, response]
    // array $headers: the HTTP headers to add to the response
    // ?Logger $logger: the application's log (null if it could not be created)
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void;
}
  • Lines 23–31: The [InterfaceResponse] interface has a single method, [send], for sending the response to the client;
  • lines 16–22: the meaning of the various parameters of the [send] method;
  • lines 27–29: The parameters [$statusCode], [$content], and [$headers] contain the result from the secondary controller and the keys [action, status] added by the primary controller. However, the response may require additional information. Therefore, it is provided with the first three parameters, which give it access to all information regarding the request, the session, and the configuration;
  • Line 30: The response requires [Logger] because it will log the response sent to the client. The type [?Logger] indicates that the parameter may be [null]: this is the case when the log could not be created. In the PHP 7 signature, the parameters [Request $request = NULL] and [Logger $logger = NULL] were implicitly nullable: this syntax has been deprecated since PHP 8.4. Additionally, declaring an optional parameter before required parameters has been deprecated since PHP 8.0.

The class [JsonResponse] implements the interface [InterfaceResponse] as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// a JSON response
final class JsonResponse extends ParentResponse
{
    #[\Override]
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void {
        // JSON serialization: [json_encode] also serializes the public attributes of the [Simulation] objects
        $json = json_encode($content, self::JSON_OPTIONS);
        // sending the response by the parent class
        $this->sendResponse($statusCode, $json, "application/json", $headers);
        // log
        $logger?->write("response=$json");
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 13: The class extends the abstract class [ParentResponse], which implements the interface [InterfaceResponse]. All response types extend this class. It is this parent class that sends the response to the client. Because this code is common to all response types, it has been factored into a parent class. Our [JsonResponse] class is not Symfony’s [JsonResponse] class: it is in the [Application] namespace, and we do not import the Symfony class;
  • Line 15: The attribute [Override] (PHP 8.3) indicates that the method [send] implements a method from a parent class or an interface. If this were not the case (due to a typo in the name, for example), PHP would report an error;
  • Line 26: The response [$content] is serialized to JSON. The options for [json_encode] are defined once and for all in the parent class. The function [json_encode] serializes a [Simulation] object as a JSON object whose keys are the names of its public attributes;
  • line 28: the parent class is asked to send the response to the client, specifying the document type as [application/json];
  • line 30: the response JSON is logged. The null-safe operator [?->] calls the method [write] only if [$logger] is not [null].

The code for the parent class [ParentResponse] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// the parent class of the three response types: it factors out what they have in common
// it is abstract: the [send] method of the interface is implemented by the child classes
abstract class ParentResponse implements InterfaceResponse
{
    // the [json_encode] options used by all the responses
    protected const int JSON_OPTIONS = JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES
        | JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR;

    // actual sending of the response to the client
    // $statusCode: the HTTP status code of the response
    // $body: the body of the response, depending on the case a JSON, XML or HTML string
    // $contentType: the type of the document sent (application/json, application/xml, text/html)
    // $headers: the HTTP headers to add to the response
    protected function sendResponse(int $statusCode, string $body, string $contentType, array $headers): void
    {
        // the Symfony response
        $response = new Response($body, $statusCode, $headers);
        // the type of the document sent, UTF-8 encoded
        $response->headers->set("Content-Type", "$contentType; charset=utf-8");
        // sending the HTTP headers then the body of the response
        $response->send();
    }

    // log of the response in JSON, whatever the type of the response sent
    protected function log(?Logger $logger, array $content): void
    {
        $logger?->write("response=" . json_encode($content, self::JSON_OPTIONS));
    }

    // returns the data [$data] in which the objects (simulations) have been replaced
    // by the associative array of their public attributes
    protected static function toArray(mixed $data): mixed
    {
        return match (true) {
            is_object($data) => self::toArray(get_object_vars($data)),
            is_array($data) => array_map(self::toArray(...), $data),
            default => $data,
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 13: The class is abstract; it cannot be instantiated. It implements the [InterfaceResponse] interface without defining the [send] method, which will be defined by the child classes. In the PHP 7 course, [ParentResponse] was a regular class that the child classes extended while implementing the interface;
  • Line 16: the options of [json_encode] common to all responses. Since PHP 8.3, a class constant can be typed:
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE]: accented characters are written as-is and not in the form [\u00e9];
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES]: The character [/] is not encoded as [\/];
    • [JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION]: A real number is always written with a decimal point (a zero rate is written as [0.0]);
    • [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR]: A serialization error throws a [JsonException] exception;
  • line 24: the [sendResponse] method sends the response to the client. Note that the response body [$body] is of type [string] and is therefore ready to be sent;
  • line 27: the Symfony class constructor [Response] receives the response body, status, and headers;
  • line 29: the type of the sent document, encoded as UTF-8;
  • line 31: the response is sent to the client;
  • line 35: the method [log] logs the response as JSON. It will be used by the responses XML and HTML;
  • lines 42–49: the static method [toArray] returns the data [$data], in which the objects have been replaced by the associative array of their public attributes. It will be used by the response XML:
    • the expression [match (true)] selects the first branch whose condition is true;
    • line 45: an object is replaced by the array of its attributes, returned by the function [get_object_vars]. When called from outside the object’s class, it returns only its public attributes. The attributes themselves may be objects; therefore, [toArray] is called;
    • line 46: Each element of an array is transformed by [toArray]. The syntax [self::toArray(...)] (PHP 8.1) creates an anonymous function (a [Closure]) from the method [toArray]: this is the syntax for first-class callables. With a single array, the function [array_map] preserves the array keys;
    • line 47: the other values (strings, numbers) are returned as-is.

docs.title: 23.9.5. [curl] Tests – 2
docs.text:
Let’s modify the file [config.json] as follows: ["logsFilename": "Data"]. The log file is now [Data], which is a folder. Creating the file [Data] should therefore fail:

> curl -i "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/tax/version-12/main.php"
HTTP/1.0 500 Internal Server Error
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:51:52 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: max-age=0, private, must-revalidate
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=5c2f09b4ca8ff3ceb0601052072f6256; path=/
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"action":"","status":133,"response":"The log file [Data] could not be created"}
  • Line 2: Status [500 Internal Server Error];
  • Line 7: the session cookie: the session was started before the log was created;
  • line 12: the expected response JSON.

Let’s restore the value [Data/logs.txt] to the key [logsFilename].

docs.title: 23.9.6. [main.php] – 3
docs.text:
Let’s continue examining the main controller [main.php]:

// 1st log
$logger->write("---new request");

// the requested action
$actionName = strtolower(trim($request->query->getString("action")));
$logger->write("action [$actionName] requested");
// is the action one of the cases of the [Action] enumeration? (null otherwise)
$action = Action::tryFrom($actionName);
// preliminary checks: an error result, or null if the action can be executed
$error = match (true) {
    !$request->query->has("action") => [101, "missing parameter [action]"],
    $action === null => [102, "invalid action [$actionName]"],
    $action->requiresSessionType() && !$session->has("type")
        => [103, "no session in progress. Start with action [init-session]"],
    $action->requiresAuthentication() && !$session->has("user")
        => [104, "action requested by unauthenticated user"],
    default => null,
};
if ($error !== null) {
    // we prepare the error response without sending it
    [$status, $message] = $error;
    $result = new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, $status, [$message]);
} else {
    // we execute the action with its secondary controller
    $controller = match ($action) {
        Action::InitSession => new InitSessionController(),
        Action::AuthenticateUser => new AuthenticateUserController(),
        Action::CalculateTax => new CalculateTaxController(),
        Action::ListSimulations => new ListSimulationsController(),
        Action::DeleteSimulation => new DeleteSimulationController(),
        Action::EndSession => new EndSessionController(),
        Action::DisplayTaxCalculation => new DisplayTaxCalculationController(),
    };
    $logger->write("controller : " . $controller::class);
    $result = $controller->execute($config, $request, $session);
}

// the response to the client: [action, status] then the controller's response
$content = ["action" => $actionName, "status" => $result->status, "response" => $result->response];
// fatal error: we send an email to the administrator
if ($result->statusCode === Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) {
    // [SendAdminMail] catches all the exceptions and logs them itself
    (new SendAdminMail($config["adminMail"], $logger))
        ->send(json_encode($content, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR));
}
// the type of the response is in the session - JSON by default if it has not been set yet
$type = ResponseType::tryFrom($session->get("type", "")) ?? ResponseType::Json;
// the [InterfaceResponse] object of the requested type sends the response to the client
$type->response()->send(
    $request,
    $session,
    $config,
    $result->statusCode,
    $content,
    $result->headers,
    $logger
);
// end
exit;

Comments

  • line 62: We log the fact that we have a new request. We couldn’t do this before because we weren’t sure we had a valid log file;
  • line 65: the parameter [action] must be part of URL in the form [main.php?action=anAction]. It is therefore part of the [$request->query] parameters of URL. Symfony’s [getString] method returns the parameter’s value as a string, or an empty string if the parameter is missing;
  • line 66: the requested action is logged;
  • line 68: the static method [tryFrom] of a backed enumeration returns the enumeration case whose value is [$actionName], or [null] if no case has that value. The method [from] would do the same thing but would throw a [ValueError] exception in the second case;
  • lines 70–78: preliminary checks. Their result, [$error], is either an array [status, message] describing the first error encountered, or [null] if the action can be executed. The conditions are evaluated in the following order:
    • line 71: the parameter [action] is missing from URL: status [101];
    • line 72: the action is unknown: status [102];
    • line 73: the application provides three response types (JSON, XML, HTML). This type is set by action [init-session], which places it in the session, associated with key [type]. Except for action [init-session], all actions must be performed with a key [type] in the session; otherwise, the status is [103];
    • Line 75: Except for actions [init-session] and [authenticate-user], all actions must be performed after authentication. Authentication is performed using the [authenticate-user] action, which, if authentication is successful, sets a [user] key in the session; otherwise, the status is [104];
    • line 77: no error;
  • lines 79–82: if the requested action or its execution context is incorrect, the error response is prepared but not sent: status [400 Bad Request], status, error list (with a single error in this case). The [[$status, $message] = $error] destructuring assigns the two elements of the [$error] array in a single statement;
  • lines 85–93: this is a valid operation. We instantiate the secondary controller that will process it. The PHP 7 course constructed the controller class name from the configuration ([__NAMESPACE__ . $config["actions"][$action]]) and then instantiated it with [new $controller()]. The expression [match] on the cases of the enumeration [Action] is safer: the code analyzer for [VS Code] checks the class names, and if a case is added to the enumeration without adding it here, [match] will throw a [UnhandledMatchError] exception instead of instantiating a random class;
  • line 94: the name of the secondary controller is logged for verification during development. Starting with PHP 8.0, [$object::class] returns the full class name of an object;
  • line 95: the secondary controller is executed. It returns a [ControllerResult] object. We’ll come back to secondary controllers a little later;
  • We then reach line 99 either because an error occurred or after a controller was executed. In either case, the object [$result] contains everything needed to generate the response to the client;
  • Line 99: The response to the client is a three-key array named [action, status, response]. The key [action] will facilitate better tracking of the logs in the file [logs.txt]. The key [status] will serve two purposes:
    • it will allow clients JSON and XML to determine the state into which the executed action has placed the web application;
    • in the case of a HTML response, it will allow the system to select the HTML view to be sent to the client browser;
  • Lines 101–104: Special case of status code [500 Internal Server Error]. If a controller has set this status code, it means the application cannot function. This is the case, for example, with tax calculations if the DBMS or the [Redis] server has not been started or is no longer responding. An email is then sent to the application administrator to notify them, using class [SendAdminMail] from version 9;
  • Line 107: The response type [JSON, XML, HTML] is determined. If the action [init-session] was executed successfully, this type is present in the session, associated with the key [type]. If this is not the case, the [get] method of the session returns the default value [""], [tryFrom] returns [null], and the operator [??] selects the type JSON;
  • Lines 109–117: The method [response] of the enumeration [ResponseType], described later, returns the object [JsonResponse], [XmlResponse] or [HtmlResponse], which is appropriate for the session type. Its method [send] sends the response to the client. Since the three classes implement the same [InterfaceResponse] interface, their [send] methods all have the same signature;
  • Line 119: The main controller has completed its work. The script PHP 7 used to close the log file here; our class [Logger] no longer has a method [close].

We will test various error scenarios for the [action] parameter of URL:

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/tax/version-12/main.php"
{"action":"","status":101,"response":["missing parameter [action]"]}

{"action":"x","status":102,"response":["invalid action [x]"]}
