We can see that the tax administration data is always retrieved from the database and never from the session. Let’s return to the code of the test that was run:

    // executed before each test
    #[\Override]
    protected function setUp(): void
    {
        // creation of the [dao] and [business] layers as in the main script
        $clientDao = new ClientDao(self::$config["urlServer"], self::$config["user"], self::$config["httpClientOptions"]);
        $this->business = new ClientBusiness($clientDao);
    }
  • Line 41: The [setUp] method is executed before each test. A new [ClientDao] is therefore created for each test, with a session cookie [null]. This explains why this client does not benefit from any session: it’s as if the 11 tests were performed by 11 different users.

This example shows that the session is not the right place to store tax administration data. Indeed, this data is shared by all users of the application. However, in this case, it is duplicated in each of their sessions.

In web programming, there are three types of visibility for shared data:

  • data shared by all users of the web application. This is generally read-only data. PHP does not natively support this type of storage: each request is executed by a script that starts with an empty memory;
  • data shared among requests from the same client. This data is stored in the session. We refer to this as the client session to denote the client’s memory. All requests from a client have access to this session. They can store and read information there. In the previous scripts, this session is implemented by the Symfony object [HttpFoundation\Session\Session];
  • the request context. A user's request can be processed through several successive actions. The request context allows action 1 to pass information to action 2. With [HttpFoundation], the request is implemented by the object [Request], and its context is implemented by its attribute [attributes].

Tools are available to assign application memory to PHP. The new version of the application exercise demonstrates the use of one such tool.

docs.title: 21. Processing XML Documents
docs.text:
The web services we have written so far exchange JSON data. The XML (eXtensible Markup Language) has long been the most widely used exchange format, and it is still commonly encountered: SOAP web services, RSS feeds, configuration files, office documents (a [.odt] or [.docx] file is an archive of XML files). PHP provides two APIs for working with it:

  • [SimpleXML]: a very simple API, where the document elements become object properties;
  • [DOM] (Document Object Model): the standard API of W3C, which is more comprehensive and also allows you to modify a document. PHP 8.4 introduced a new version, in the [Dom] namespace, compliant with the current web standard.

The scripts in this chapter are located in the [scripts-console/xml] folder:

scripts-console/xml
├── data.xml
├── dom-01.php
└── simplexml-01.php

docs.title: 21.1. The document under consideration
docs.text:
We are considering the following file: XML [data.xml]:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

<tribe>
    <teacher>
        <person gender="M">
            <lastName>dupont</lastName>
            <firstName>jean</firstName>
            <age>28</age>
            this is a comment
        </person>
        <section>27</section>
    </teacher>
    <student>
        <person gender="F">
            <lastName>martin</lastName>
            <firstName>charline</firstName>
            <age>22</age>
        </person>
        <course>dess IAIE</course>
    </student>
</tribe>

A XML document is a tree of elements:

  • line 1: the prolog, which specifies the version of XML and the document’s character encoding;
  • lines 3–21: the root element [tribe]. A XML document has exactly one root;
  • lines 4–12: the [teacher] element, a child of [tribe]. It has two children, [person] and [section];
  • line 5: the element [person] has an attribute [gender] with a value of [M];
  • line 9: an element can contain both other elements and text;
  • lines 13–20: the element [student], which has the same structure as [teacher].

docs.title: 21.2. Processing with SimpleXML
docs.text:
We analyze this document using the following [simplexml-01.php] script:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// the XML file to be used
const FILE_NAME = "data.xml";

// loading the XML document
$xml = simplexml_load_file(FILE_NAME);
if ($xml === false) {
    print "The file [" . FILE_NAME . "] could not be used\n";
    exit(1);
}
// display of the document
print_r($xml);
// the [gender] attribute of the teaching person
print_r($xml->teacher->person['gender']);
// values of elements and attributes, converted to strings
$lastName = (string) $xml->teacher->person->lastName;
print "lastName=$lastName\n";
$gender = (string) $xml->teacher->person['gender'];
print "gender=$gender\n";
$course = (string) $xml->student->course;
print "course=$course\n";
// existence of an element
print "isset(lastName)=" . var_export(isset($xml->teacher->person->lastName), true) . "\n";
print "isset(xx)=" . var_export(isset($xml->teacher->person->xx), true) . "\n";
// a conversion to an integer
$age = (int) $xml->student->person->age;
print "age of the student=$age\n";
// iterating over all the <person> elements of the document with XPath
foreach ($xml->xpath('//person') as $person) {
    print "person: {$person->firstName} {$person->lastName} ({$person['gender']})\n";
}

Comments

  • line 6: The filename XML is a constant. The script is executed in its own folder, that of [data.xml];
  • Line 9: The [simplexml_load_file] function loads the document and returns an object of type [SimpleXMLElement], which represents the root element [tribe]. In the event of an error (missing file, malformed XML), it returns [false], which we test on line 10;
  • line 15: display of the document. [print_r] shows how [SimpleXML] views the tree XML;
  • line 17: child elements are accessed as properties ([$xml->teacher->person]), and attributes as array keys ([['gender']]). Note that the root [tribe] does not appear in the code: [$xml] is already that element;
  • line 19: [$xml->teacher->person->lastName] is not a string but an object [SimpleXMLElement]. Converting [(string)] yields its text. With [declare(strict_types=1)], it is best to perform this conversion explicitly before passing the value to a function that expects a string;
  • Line 21: the value of the [gender] attribute;
  • Lines 26–27: [isset] determines whether an element exists. The script PHP 7 displayed the Boolean result using [print], which returns [1] for [true] and an empty string for [false]. We use [var_export], which displays [true] or [false];
  • line 29: the conversion [(int)] returns the integer value of the element’s text;
  • line 32: the method [xpath] evaluates an expression XPath. The expression [//person] refers to all [person] elements in the document, regardless of their level. This returns an array of [SimpleXMLElement].

Console output

> php simplexml-01.php
SimpleXMLElement Object
(
    [teacher] => SimpleXMLElement Object
        (
            [person] => SimpleXMLElement Object
                (
                    [@attributes] => Array
                        (
                            [gender] => M
                        )

                    [lastName] => dupont
                    [firstName] => jean
                    [age] => 28
                )

            [section] => 27
        )

    [student] => SimpleXMLElement Object
        (
            [person] => SimpleXMLElement Object
                (
                    [@attributes] => Array
                        (
                            [gender] => F
                        )

                    [lastName] => martin
                    [firstName] => charline
                    [age] => 22
                )

            [course] => dess IAIE
        )

)
SimpleXMLElement Object
(
    [0] => M
)
lastName=dupont
gender=M
course=dess IAIE
isset(lastName)=true
isset(xx)=false
age of the student=22
person: jean dupont (M)
person: charline martin (F)
  • Lines 2–38: the document XML in the form of a [SimpleXMLElement] object. Note that the text [this is a comment] does not appear: [print_r] shows only the elements and attributes;
  • lines 39–42: an attribute is also a [SimpleXMLElement] object;
  • lines 43–48: the values read from the document;
  • lines 49–50: the XPath traversal of the two people.

docs.title: 21.3. Processing with the new DOM API from PHP 8.4
docs.text:
Starting with PHP 8.4, the [Dom] namespace offers a new DOM API: the [Dom\XMLDocument] class for XML documents and the [Dom\HTMLDocument] class for HTML5 documents. It is a better replacement for the old [DOMDocument] class (which is still available): it complies with the current DOM standard and provides the [querySelector] and [querySelectorAll] methods familiar to JavaScript developers. These methods allow you to search for elements using CSS selectors.

The [dom-01.php] script uses the same document:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// the same document used with the new DOM API of PHP 8.4

use Dom\XMLDocument;

// the XML file to be used
const FILE_NAME = "data.xml";

try {
    // loading the XML document
    $document = XMLDocument::createFromFile(FILE_NAME);
} catch (Throwable $ex) {
    print "The file [" . FILE_NAME . "] could not be used: {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}
// the root element
print "root=" . $document->documentElement->tagName . "\n";
// the 1st teaching person, found with a CSS selector
$person = $document->querySelector('teacher > person');
print "lastName=" . $person->querySelector('lastName')->textContent . "\n";
print "gender=" . $person->getAttribute('gender') . "\n";
print "course=" . $document->querySelector('student > course')->textContent . "\n";
// a missing element: querySelector returns null
print "xx exists=" . var_export($person->querySelector('xx') !== null, true) . "\n";
// all the persons of the document
foreach ($document->querySelectorAll('person') as $person) {
    // the nullsafe operator ?-> protects against a missing element
    $firstName = $person->querySelector('firstName')?->textContent ?? '?';
    $lastName = $person->querySelector('lastName')?->textContent ?? '?';
    print "person: $firstName $lastName ({$person->getAttribute('gender')})\n";
}
// modifying the document: we change the content of the teacher's <section> element
$section = $document->querySelector('teacher > section');
$section->textContent = "26";
// the modified document, as XML text
print $document->saveXml($document->querySelector('teacher')) . "\n";

Comments

  • line 7: the [XMLDocument] class in the [Dom] namespace;
  • Line 14: The static method [createFromFile] loads the document. Unlike [simplexml_load_file], it throws an exception if an error occurs;
  • line 20: the property [documentElement] is the root element; [tagName] is its name;
  • line 22: the selector CSS [teacher > person] refers to an element [person] that is a direct child of an element [teacher]. [querySelector] returns the first matching element, or [null] if there are none;
  • line 23: the [textContent] property is the text contained in the element;
  • line 24: the value of an attribute;
  • line 27: a missing element returns [null];
  • line 29: all [person] elements in the document;
  • Line 31: If the element [firstName] were missing, [querySelector('firstName')] would result in [null]. The null-safe operator [?->] (PHP 8.0) then returns [null] instead of causing an error, and the operator [??] replaces this [null] with ['?'];
  • line 37: the API DOM also allows the document to be modified: here, the text of the [section] element is changed;
  • line 39: [saveXml] returns the text XML from the document, or from one of its elements if it is passed as a parameter.

Console output

> php dom-01.php
root=tribe
lastName=dupont
gender=M
course=dess IAIE
xx exists=false
person: jean dupont (M)
person: charline martin (F)
<teacher>
        <person gender="M">
            <lastName>dupont</lastName>
            <firstName>jean</firstName>
            <age>28</age>
            this is a comment
        </person>
        <section>26</section>
    </teacher>
  • line 16: the modification made by the script.

These two examples do not show all the capabilities of [SimpleXML] and [DOM], but they are sufficient for us to write a new version of the application exercise. The documentation for PHP describes them in detail: SimpleXML and DOM.

docs.title: 2. Setting Up a Development Environment
docs.text:
The scripts were written and tested in the following environment:

  • an [Apache] / [MySQL] DBMS / [PHP] 8.5 web server environment called [Laragon];
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor and its extension [PHP Intelephense];
  • the dependency manager [Composer], provided with [Laragon], which installs the PHP libraries used by the course.

Other tools (the mail server [Mailpit], the [PostgreSQL] DBMS and the server [Redis]) are only relevant to certain chapters: their installation is described in the relevant chapters.

docs.title: 2.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] is a package for [Windows] that combines several software components:

  • a web server ([Apache]). We will use it to write web scripts in PHP;
  • the [MySQL] DBMS ([PostgreSQL] can be added to this, see the chapter on version 6);
  • the PHP scripting language, in several versions, including version 8.5;
  • a [Redis] server that implements a cache for web applications;
  • the [Composer] tool;
  • a command-line terminal in which all these tools can be used directly.

[Laragon] can be downloaded from https://laragon.org/download/. It is free to use with all its features; a prompt occasionally appears asking you to purchase a license to support its development, which is optional. Installation is straightforward: simply accept the default settings. [Laragon] is then installed in the [C:\laragon] folder, which we will refer to as <laragon> from here on:

C:\laragon
├── bin\        the software: apache, mysql, php, redis, composer…
├── data\       the DBMS data
├── etc\        configuration files
├── tmp\
└── www\        the root of the Apache web server: http://localhost

Launching [Laragon] displays its main window:

  • The [Démarrer tout] (Start All) button starts the [Apache] web server, as well as the [MySQL] DBMS. The window then indicates, for each of them, that it is active and on which port it is listening: 80 for [Apache], 3306 for [MySQL];
  • the [Web] button displays the [http://localhost] page, which corresponds to the [<laragon>/www] folder;
  • the [Base de données] (Database) button launches a database administration tool ([HeidiSQL], included with [Laragon]);
  • The [Terminal] button opens a command terminal in which [php], [composer], [mysql]… can be used directly;
  • The [Racine] (Root) button opens the [Windows] file explorer to the [<laragon>/www] folder. This is where you should place all web applications managed by the [Apache] server from [Laragon];
  • Right-clicking in the window (or on the [Laragon] icon in the taskbar) opens the [Laragon] menu, which provides access to the configuration settings for each application.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Select PHP 8.5
docs.text:
[Laragon] may contain multiple versions of PHP. The version to use is selected from its menu under the [PHP > Version] section. Select version 8.5 (the most recent in the 8.5 series). It will then be used by both the [Apache] server and the [php] terminal command.

In order for the [php] command to also be usable in [VS Code] terminals, the PHP folder must be located within the PATH folder of [Windows]. [Laragon] handles this: [Tools > Path > Add Laragon to Path] menu. Then open a new terminal (terminals that are already open will not see the change) and type:

> php -v

The command should display the version of PHP, 8.5.x.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Configure PHP for training
docs.text:
PHP is configured via a text file named [php.ini], accessible through the [Laragon] menu under the [PHP > php.ini] section. During training, PHP must report all errors, warnings, and deprecations. Verify that the file contains the following lines (or modify them):

error_reporting = E_ALL
display_errors = On
display_startup_errors = On
log_errors = On
error_log = C:/laragon/tmp/php_errors.log
date.timezone = Europe/Paris
  • [error_reporting = E_ALL]: PHP reports everything, including the [Deprecated] messages that announce deprecated features. A production configuration often uses [E_ALL & ~E_DEPRECATED], which hides them: that’s not what we want here;
  • [display_errors = On]: Messages are displayed in the script’s output (the terminal or the web page);
  • [log_errors = On]: Messages are also written to the error log;
  • [error_log]: the log file. Without this line, a console script writes its log to the terminal itself, and each message would appear there twice (once preceded by [PHP], once without it);
  • [date.timezone]: the time zone used by date functions.

The course also uses several extensions of PHP. They are enabled in the [Laragon] menu, under the [PHP > Extensions] section, or in the [php.ini] file using lines of the form [extension=name]. The extensions used are: [curl], [mbstring], [openssl], [pdo_mysql], [pdo_pgsql], [fileinfo], and [zip] (the latter is used by [Composer] to decompress the libraries it downloads). After modifying the [php.ini] file, you must restart [Apache] (the [Reload] button in [Laragon]); the console scripts, on the other hand, re-read the [php.ini] file each time they run.

You can verify the configuration in a terminal using the command [php --ini] (the [php.ini] file used) and [php -m] (the list of loaded extensions). The first script in the next chapter, [phpinfo.php], displays the entire configuration.

docs.title: 2.2. Installing VS Code
docs.text:
[Visual Studio Code] is a free editor from Microsoft, available for download at https://code.visualstudio.com/. Here, it replaces the [NetBeans] IDE used in the PHP 7 course.

Once [VS Code] is installed, add support for the PHP language: in the [Extensions] panel (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for and install the [PHP Intelephense] extension. It provides:

  • code completion: PHP functions, classes, their methods, and their attributes are suggested as you type;
  • display of documentation for a function or method when you hover over its name;
  • error detection as you type (undefined variables, incorrect types, nonexistent methods, etc.), which are underlined in the code and listed in the [Problems] panel;
  • code navigation: pressing Ctrl+click on a class or function name opens its definition, including those in the libraries within the [vendor] folder.

[Intelephense] must know the version of PHP being used to identify its new features: in the [VS Code] settings (Ctrl+comma), search for “intelephense php version” and enter 8.5.

Next, open the course code folder in [VS Code] ([File > Open Folder] menu). A terminal opens via the [Terminal > New Terminal] menu: it is set to the open folder, and you type the commands [php], [composer], [curl]… To run a console script, navigate to its folder (command [cd]) and type [php script-name.php].

docs.title: 2.3. Installing the Course Code
docs.text:
The course code files are contained in a folder named [php8-oct-2026], which can be downloaded at the beginning of this document. Place it in the [<laragon>/www] folder:

C:\laragon\www
└── php8-oct-2026
    ├── composer.json
    ├── phpunit.xml
    ├── scripts-console
    └── scripts-web

Its web scripts are then accessible at URLs [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/...]. For example, once [Apache] is launched, the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/composer.json] should display the file [composer.json].

docs.title: 2.4. Installing Libraries with Composer
docs.text:
Like most programming languages, PHP has a dependency manager, [Composer], which downloads the libraries a project needs from the [packagist.org] repository. The libraries used by the course are declared in the [composer.json] file in the [php8-oct-2026] folder:

{
    "name": "stahe/php8-oct-2026",
    "description": "Code of the course \"Introduction to the PHP 8 language by example\" (October 2026)",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": ">=8.5",
        "symfony/http-foundation": "^8.0",
        "symfony/http-client": "^8.0",
        "symfony/mailer": "^8.0",
        "symfony/mime": "^8.0",
        "predis/predis": "^3.0",
        "zbateson/mail-mime-parser": "^3.0"
    },
    "require-dev": {
        "phpunit/phpunit": "^12.0"
    },
    "config": {
        "sort-packages": true
    }
}
  • Line 6: the libraries required to run the scripts. Each is identified by a name in the form [vendor/library] and a version constraint: [^8.0] means “any version of 8.x starting with 8.0.” Their roles are described in the chapters that use them;
  • line 7: the project requires PHP 8.5 or later;
  • line 15: libraries used solely for development, in this case the [PHPUnit] testing framework.

To install these libraries, open a terminal in the [php8-oct-2026] folder (the [Laragon] terminal, or the [VS Code] terminal) and type:

> composer install

[Composer] then creates a folder named [vendor] containing the libraries and their dependencies, as well as a file named [vendor/autoload.php]. A script that wants to use these libraries simply needs to include this file, which automatically loads their classes the first time they are used. The scripts in this course do this using a path relative to their own folder, for example:

require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

The constant [__DIR__] refers to the folder of the script that uses it: therefore, the path does not depend on the folder in which the script is run, nor on where the [php8-oct-2026] folder is located.

Verify the installation by displaying the version of [PHPUnit]:

> php vendor/bin/phpunit --version
PHPUnit 12.5.37 by Sebastian Bergmann and contributors.

Now that the working environment has been installed, we can cover the basics of PHP.

docs.title: 3.1. The Script Directory Structure
docs.text:
The scripts for this chapter are located in two folders within the [scripts-console] folder of the course code:

php8-oct-2026
└── scripts-console
    ├── basics
    │   ├── phpinfo.php
    │   ├── basics-01.php
    │   ├── basics-02.php
    │   ├── ...
    │   ├── basics-17.php
    │   └── info.txt
    └── json
        ├── family.json
        ├── json-01.php
        ├── json-02.php
        └── json-03.php

These are “console” scripts: they run in a terminal using the [php script-name.php] command and output their results to that same terminal. Web scripts, which are executed by the [Apache] server running on [Laragon] and displayed by a browser, will be covered later.

docs.title: 3.2. Configuring PHP
docs.text:
PHP comes preconfigured via a text file named [php.ini]. All of these settings can be changed programmatically. The configuration of PHP greatly influences script execution. It is therefore important to understand it. The following script, [phpinfo.php], allows you to do this:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// displays the PHP configuration
phpinfo();

Comments:

  • line 3: This line will appear at the beginning of all scripts in this course. We will explain it in the section on type conversions;
  • Line 6: The function [phpinfo] displays the configuration of PHP.

Let’s open a terminal in the [scripts-console/basics] folder and run the script. Here is an excerpt:

> php phpinfo.php
phpinfo()
PHP Version => 8.5.11
…
Server API => Command Line Interface
…
PHP API => 20250925
PHP Extension => 20250925
Zend Extension => 420250925
PHP Integer Size => 64 bits
Debug Build => no
Zend Memory Manager => enabled
IPv6 Support => enabled
…
display_errors => STDOUT => STDOUT
error_reporting => 30719 => 30719
memory_limit => 512M => 512M
max_execution_time => 0 => 0
…

The [phpinfo] function displays nearly 1,500 configuration lines here. We won’t comment on them because most pertain to advanced usage of PHP. Let’s highlight a few:

  • [PHP Version]: the version of PHP being used—in this case, 8.5;
  • [Server API]: how PHP was launched. [Command Line Interface] (CLI) refers to the interpreter running in a terminal. When PHP is executed by the [Apache] server, this line changes, and the configuration may be different;
  • [display_errors] and [error_reporting]: PHP displays all errors, warnings, and deprecation notices. The value 30719 corresponds to the constant [E_ALL] as of PHP 8.4. This is the configuration required during training: a warning almost always indicates a programming error.

An important line in the full output is line [Loaded Configuration File]: it indicates which [php.ini] file was used to configure the PHP that runs your scripts. With [Laragon], this is a file like [C:\laragon\bin\php\php-8.5.x-Win32-vs17-x64\php.ini]. You can also obtain it directly using the command [php --ini]. If you want to modify the execution configuration of PHP, this is the file you need to edit ([Laragon] provides access to it via its menu, under the [PHP > php.ini] section). There are numerous comments in this file explaining the purpose of the various configurations.

docs.title: 3.3.1. The code
docs.text:
Below is a [basics-01.php] program that demonstrates the basic features of PHP:

<?php

// strict checking of the types of function parameters and results
declare(strict_types=1);

// this is a comment
// variable used without having been declared
$name = "dupont";
// a screen display
print "name=$name\n";
// an array with elements of different types
$array = ["one", "two", 3, 4];
// its number of elements
$n = count($array);
// a loop
for ($i = 0; $i < $n; $i++) {
    print "array[$i]=$array[$i]\n";
}
// initialization of 2 variables with the contents of an array
[$string1, $string2] = ["string1", "string2"];
// concatenation of the 2 strings
$string3 = $string1 . $string2;
// display result
print "[$string1,$string2,$string3]\n";
// using a function
display($string1);
// the type of a variable can be known
displayType("n", $n);
displayType("string1", $string1);
displayType("array", $array);
// the type of a variable can change during execution
$n = "has changed";
displayType("n", $n);
// a function can return a result
$res1 = f1(4);
print "res1=$res1\n";
// a function can return an array of values
[$res1, $res2, $res3] = f2();
print "(res1,res2,res3)=[$res1,$res2,$res3]\n";
// we could have retrieved these values in an array
$t = f2();
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
    print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
}
// some tests
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
    // only displays the strings
    if (gettype($t[$i]) === "string") {
        print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    }
}
// comparison operators == and ===
if ("2" == 2) {
    print "with the == operator, the string 2 is equal to the integer 2\n";
} else {
    print "with the == operator, the string 2 is not equal to the integer 2\n";
}
if ("2" === 2) {
    print "with the === operator, the string 2 is equal to the integer 2\n";
} else {
    print "with the === operator, the string 2 is not equal to the integer 2\n";
}
// a comparison whose result changed with PHP 8
if (0 == "abc") {
    print "with the == operator, the integer 0 is equal to the string abc\n";
} else {
    print "with the == operator, the integer 0 is not equal to the string abc\n";
}
// other tests
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
    // only displays the integers > 10
    if (is_int($t[$i]) && $t[$i] > 10) {
        print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    }
}
// a while loop
$t = [8, 5, 0, -2, 3, 4];
$i = 0;
$sum = 0;
while ($i < count($t) && $t[$i] > 0) {
    print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    $sum += $t[$i];   // $sum = $sum + $t[$i]
    $i++;             // $i = $i + 1
}
print "sum=$sum\n";

// end of program
exit;

//----------------------------------
function display(string $string): void
{
    // displays $string
    print "string=$string\n";
}

//----------------------------------
function displayType(string $name, mixed $variable): void
{
    // displays the type of $variable
    print "type[variable $" . $name . "]=" . gettype($variable) . "\n";
}

//----------------------------------
function f1(int $param): int
{
    // adds 10 to $param
    return $param + 10;
}

//----------------------------------
function f2(): array
{
    // returns 3 values
    return ["one", 0, 100];
}

The results:

> php basics-01.php
name=dupont
array[0]=one
array[1]=two
array[2]=3
array[3]=4
[string1,string2,string1string2]
string=string1
type[variable $n]=integer
type[variable $string1]=string
type[variable $array]=array
type[variable $n]=string
res1=14
(res1,res2,res3)=[one,0,100]
t[0]=one
t[1]=0
t[2]=100
t[0]=one
with the == operator, the string 2 is equal to the integer 2
with the === operator, the string 2 is not equal to the integer 2
with the == operator, the integer 0 is not equal to the string abc
t[2]=100
t[0]=8
t[1]=5
sum=13

Comments:

  • line 4: instructs PHP to strictly check the declared types of the parameters and function returns. We’ll return to this in the section on type changes. For now, note that all the scripts in this course begin this way;
  • line 8: In PHP, variables are not declared. They have a dynamic type that can change over time. [$name] represents the variable with identifier [name];
  • line 10: To write to the screen, you can use the statement [print] or the statement [echo];
  • Line 12: The notation [[...]] is used to define an array. The notation [$array[$i]] represents element No. [$i] of the array [$array], where the first element is numbered 0. The older notation [array("one", "two", 3, 4)] is still accepted, but we will not use it;
  • line 14: the function [count($array)] returns the number of elements in the array [$array];
  • lines 16–18: a loop. Since this loop contains only one statement, curly braces are optional. In the rest of this document, we will always use curly braces regardless of the number of statements;
  • line 17: strings are enclosed in double quotes " or single quotes '. Inside double quotes, the variables [$variable] are evaluated (also called “interpolated”), but not inside single quotes;
  • line 20: You can assign the elements of an array to multiple variables in a single operation. Here, [$string1="string1"] and [$string2="string2"]. This syntax, called destructuring, replaces the [list] function from older versions of PHP: [list($string1, $string2) = ...] is still accepted;
  • line 22: the . (period) operator is the string concatenation operator;
  • Lines 91–95: The keyword [function] defines a function. A function can be defined anywhere in the script, even after it has been used. Here, [string $string] indicates that the parameter [$string] must be a string, and [: void] indicates that the function returns no result. These type declarations are optional in PHP, but we will use them consistently: they document the code and allow PHP (and the editor) to detect errors;
  • line 98: the type [mixed] (PHP 8.0) means “any type.” The parameter [$variable] can accept an integer, a string, an array, etc.;
  • line 101: the predefined function [gettype($variable)] returns a string representing the type of [$variable]. The results show that this type can change over time: [$n] is first an integer and then a string;
  • line 105: a function returns a result using the statement [return]. The type of this result is declared after the parentheses: [: int]. The calling code can ignore or retrieve the results of a function;
  • line 112: a function can return multiple values by grouping them into an array;
  • lines 53–62: The [===] operator performs a strict comparison of two elements: they must have the same type and the same value to be equal. The [] operator is less strict: two elements can be equal without being of the same type. In this case, the comparison is performed after both elements have been converted to the same type. It is quite easy to “overlook” these implicit conversions and thus end up with unexpected results, such as discovering that a condition is true when you expected it to be false. To avoid this pitfall, we will consistently use the comparison operator [=] (and its negation, [!==]);
  • lines 64–68: an example of these implicit conversions. In PHP 7, the string “abc” was converted to the number 0, and the expression [0 == "abc"] was true! Since PHP 8.0, when comparing a number to a string that does not represent a number, the number is converted to a string, and the expression is false. The behavior of [] has therefore changed from one version to the next: all the more reason to prefer [=];
  • Line 72: The function [is_int] returns [true] if its parameter is an integer. Similarly, there are [is_string], [is_float], [is_bool], [is_array]… The operator [&&] is the logical AND. You can also use the logical operators [||] (OR) and [!] (NOT). PHP also supports the keywords [and] and [or], but their lower priority compared to assignment can lead to unexpected results: we will not use them;
  • line 80: a loop [while]. It stops as soon as the condition is false—in this case, as soon as the array is traversed or a negative or zero element is encountered;
  • Line 88: The [exit] statement stops the script from executing. The functions that follow are not executed at this point, but they are recognized by the entire script.

Note that the script does not end with the [?>] closing tag for the PHP code. It is not essential. Furthermore, in a web context, it can cause problems if it is followed by spaces or line breaks, which are difficult to detect because they are not visible in a text editor. The [PSR-12] recommendation, in fact, specifies that it should be omitted in files containing only PHP. Therefore, in the remainder of this document, we will systematically omit it.

Note: In this document, we will use the keyword [print] to display text on the console. Another way to do the same thing is to use the keyword [echo]. There are subtle differences between these two keywords, but in the context of this document, there will be none. So if you prefer to use [echo], then go ahead.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Using VS Code
docs.text:
To work on the course scripts, open the [php8-oct-2026] folder within [VS Code] ([File > Open Folder] menu). The file tree appears in the explorer on the left side of the window. To run a script:

  • open an integrated terminal ([Terminal > New Terminal] menu). It opens in the [php8-oct-2026] folder;
  • navigate to the script’s folder: [cd scripts-console/basics];
  • run the script: [php basics-01.php]. The results are displayed in the terminal. Alternatively, in the file explorer, you can right-click the [basics] folder and select [Open in Integrated Terminal].

If the command [php] is not recognized, it means that the PHP folder is not located in the Windows PATH directory: [Laragon] adds it there when you check the corresponding option in its [Tools > Path] menu. The [php -v] command should display version 8.5.

The [PHP Intelephense] extension analyzes the code as you type and flags problems with a wavy line under the incorrect code. Hovering the mouse over this line displays the message. All issues in the file are listed in the [Problems] panel ([View > Problems] menu). Among the useful warnings:

  • [Undefined variable]: a variable is being used without having been initialized. This is often a typo in the variable name;
  • [Undefined function]: A function that does not exist is being called; again, this is often a typo;
  • [Expected type 'int'. Found 'string'.]: An actual parameter does not have the type declared by the function. This is one of the major benefits of type declarations: the error is reported even before execution;
  • [Expected 2 arguments. Found 1.]: The number of actual parameters does not match the function’s definition.

Hovering over a function name displays its signature (parameters, types, return value) and its documentation, including for the predefined functions of PHP. To ensure that [Intelephense] is aware of recent language updates, check the settings for [VS Code] ([File > Preferences > Settings] menu, search for “intelephense php version”) to ensure that the specified version of PHP is 8.5. While learning the language, it is advisable to correct all reported warnings. This is a great way to learn.

[Intelephense] can also format a file (right-click, [Format Document]) according to the coding recommendations in [PSR-12]. The PSR (PHP Standard Recommendations) are guidelines for producing standard code, thereby facilitating interoperability and the maintenance of code written by different people. They are published by the [PHP-FIG] on the www.php-fig.org website. The [PSR-1] and [PSR-12] recommendations establish the rules for writing code. Here are the rules from [PSR-1]:

ElementRuleClass constantsClass constants MUST be written in uppercase letters with the _ character as a separator.Ex: [const VAT_RATE]MethodsMethod names MUST be written in camelCase.Example: [public function executeBatchTaxes()]PropertiesProperty names SHOULD be written consistently within a single codebase, as StudlyCaps, camelCase, or under_score.Examples: [$AnnualSalary], [$annualSalary], [$annual_salary]Side EffectsA file SHOULD either declare new symbols (classes, functions, constants, etc.) without any side effects, or execute code with side effects, but SHOULD NOT do both.TypesType names (classes, interfaces, etc.) MUST be written in StudlyCaps. Each type is in its own file and in a namespace with at least one level.Example: [class ScholarshipStudent]

The side-effects rule states that a file must contain:

  • either declarations of types (classes, interfaces), functions, or constants;
  • or executable code without declarations of new types.

For simplicity, the examples in this chapter do not follow this rule: each script is a single file that defines its functions and uses them. Splitting the code across multiple files would be too cumbersome for basic examples. For the application presented as the central theme of this document, we will strive to follow these recommendations as closely as possible once it is written using classes.

docs.title: 3.4.1. Example 1
docs.text:
The script [basics-02.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// scope of variables

function f1(): void
{
    // we use the global variable $i
    global $i;
    $i++;
    $j = 10;
    print "f1[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function f2(): void
{
    // we use the global variable $i
    global $i;
    $i++;
    $j = 20;
    print "f2[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function f3(): void
{
    // we use a local variable $i
    $i = 4;
    $j = 30;
    print "f3[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

// tests
$i = 0;
$j = 0;  // these two variables are known to a function f
// only if it explicitly declares with the global statement
// that it wants to use them
f1();
f2();
f3();
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";

The results:

> php basics-02.php
f1[i,j]=[1,10]
f2[i,j]=[2,20]
f3[i,j]=[4,30]
test[i,j]=[2,0]

Comments:

  • Lines 34–35: Define two variables, [$i] and [$j], in the main program. These variables are not recognized within the functions. Thus, on line 12, the variable [$j] in the function [f1] is a local variable of the function [f1] and is different from the variable [$j] in the main program;
  • line 10: a function can access a variable named [$variable] from the main program via the keyword [global]. Here, the statement refers to the global variable [$i] in the main program;
  • line 28: the function [f3] has not declared [$i] as global; its variable [$i] is a local variable, unrelated to the one in the main program.

The use of [global] is not recommended: a function that modifies global variables is difficult to understand and test. It is preferable for a function to receive its data via its parameters and return its results via [return]. This is what we will do in the following example.

docs.title: 3.4.2. Example 2
docs.text:
The [basics-03.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// the scope of a variable is global to code blocks
$i = 0;
{
    $i = 4;
    $i++;
}
print "i=$i\n";

The results:

> php basics-03.php
i=5

Comments:

In some languages, a variable defined within curly braces has a scope limited to those braces: it is not accessible outside of them. The results above show that this is not the case in PHP. The variable [$i] used on line 8 inside the curly braces is the same as the one used on lines 6 and 11 outside of them.

docs.title: 3.5. Type Changes
docs.text:
Variables in PHP do not have a fixed type. The type may change at runtime depending on the value assigned to the variable. In operations involving data of various types, the PHP interpreter performs implicit conversions to bring the operands into a common type. These implicit conversions, if unknown to the developer, can be a source of errors that are difficult to detect. Below is a [basics-04.php] script demonstrating implicit and explicit conversions. Let’s start with the first part:

<?php

// strict types when passing parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// implicit type changes
// type --> bool
print "Conversion to a boolean------------------------------\n";
showBool("abcd", "abcd");
showBool("", "");
showBool("[1, 2, 3]", [1, 2, 3]);
showBool("[]", []);
showBool("null", null);
showBool("0.0", 0.0);
showBool("0", 0);
showBool("4.6", 4.6);
showBool("\"0\"", "0");

function showBool(string $prefix, mixed $var): void
{
    print "(bool) $prefix : ";
    // the conversion of $var to a boolean is done automatically in the following test
    if ($var) {
        print "true";
    } else {
        print "false";
    }
    print "\n";
}

Comments:

  • line 4: Requests strict type checking of a function’s parameters when the type is specified (and of the type of its return value). We’ll explain this instruction a bit later;
  • line 19: The purpose of the function [showBool] is to demonstrate the implicit (automatic) conversion performed by the PHP interpreter when a value of any type must be converted to a Boolean (line 23);
  • line 19: the parameter [$prefix] must be of type [string]. The parameter [$var] is of type [mixed]: the actual parameter can therefore be of any type. The function [showBool] returns no value ([void]);
  • Line 23: In the [if ($var)] statement, the value of [$var] must be converted to a Boolean so that [if] can be evaluated. Surprisingly, the PHP interpreter returns a result for any type of value provided to it;
  • lines 9–17: the value of the function parameter for [showBool] will be, in succession:
    • line 9: a non-empty string: result [true] (case is not significant, TRUE=true);
    • line 10: an empty string: result [false];
    • line 11: a non-empty array: result [true];
    • line 12: an empty array: result [false];
    • line 13: the value [null] (no value): result [false];
    • line 14: the real number 0: result [false];
    • line 15: the integer 0: result [false];
    • line 16: a real number (or integer) other than 0: result [true];
    • line 17: a trap: the string "0" is converted to [false], while any other non-empty string is converted to [true].

This is shown by the resulting screen outputs:

Conversion to a boolean------------------------------
(bool) abcd : true
(bool)  : false
(bool) [1, 2, 3] : true
(bool) [] : false
(bool) null : false
(bool) 0.0 : false
(bool) 0 : false
(bool) 4.6 : true
(bool) "0" : false

Let’s continue with the script code:

// implicit type changes from string to a numeric type
// string --> number
print "Conversion string to number------------------------------\n";
showNumber("12");
showNumber("45.67");
showNumber("12abcd");
try {
    showNumber("abcd");
} catch (TypeError $error) {
    print "(abcd): error [" . $error->getMessage() . "]\n";
}

function showNumber(string $var): void
{
    $number = $var + 1;
    var_dump($number);
    print "($var): $number\n";
}

Comments:

  • line 43: the function [showNumber] accepts a parameter of type [string] and does not return a result ([void]);
  • line 45: this parameter is used in an arithmetic operation, which will force the PHP interpreter to attempt to convert [$var] into a number:
    • line 34: will convert the string "12" to the integer 12;
    • line 35: will convert the string "45.67" to the real number 45.67;
    • line 36: the string "12abcd" begins with a number. PHP uses this number, 12, but issues a warning;
    • line 38: the string "abcd" contains no numbers. In PHP 7, it was converted to 0 with a simple warning. Since PHP 8.0, this operation is no longer possible: PHP throws a [TypeError]-type error, which, if not intercepted, would terminate the script;
  • lines 37–41: the [try { ... } catch (TypeError $error) { ... }] structure allows this error to be caught and execution to continue. [$error->getMessage()] is the error message. Exceptions will be covered in a later chapter; for now, it is sufficient to know that the code in the [catch] block is executed when the code in the [try] block causes a [TypeError] error.

Here are the results of the execution:

Conversion string to number------------------------------
int(13)
(12): 13
float(46.67)
(45.67): 46.67

Warning: A non-numeric value encountered in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/basics/basics-04.php on line 45
int(13)
(12abcd): 13
(abcd): error [Unsupported operand types: string + int]

The function [var_dump] displays the type and value of its parameter: int(13) is the integer 13, and float(46.67) is the floating-point number 46.67.

Note that the [declare(strict_types=1)] statement did not prevent the string "12" from being converted to a number. This is an important point: strict mode applies only to the passing of parameters to functions and the results they return. It does not affect conversions performed by operators (+, ., ==…) or by the [if]. Here’s what it does change:

  • without [declare(strict_types=1)] (so-called “coercive” mode), if a function expects a [int] and is passed the string “12,” PHP converts the string to the integer 12;
  • with [declare(strict_types=1)] (strict mode), the same call results in a [TypeError] error. The actual parameter must be exactly of the expected type. There is one exception: a [int] is accepted where a [float] is expected.

This statement must be the first in the file and applies only to function calls made within that file. We will use it in all scripts: it transforms silent conversions—which are sources of errors—into reported errors. We will see an example in the section on passing parameters.

Let’s continue the script code with explicit type conversions:

// explicit type changes
// to int
print "Explicit conversion to int------------------------------\n";
showInt("12.45");
showInt(67.8);
showInt(true);
showInt(null);

function showInt(mixed $var): void
{
    print "parameter: ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "result of the conversion: ";
    var_dump((int) $var);
}

Comments:

  • Line 58: The function [showInt] accepts a parameter of any type ([mixed]) and does not return a result. It converts the parameter [$var] to an integer (line 63). In general, to convert a variable of type [$var] to type T, write [(T) $var], where T can be: int, bool, float, string, array, or object. The notations (integer), (boolean), (double), and (binary) from older versions of PHP are obsolete: PHP 8.5 flags them as deprecated. The (real) syntax, on the other hand, was removed as of PHP 8.0;
  • line 53: converts the string "12.45" to the integer 12;
  • line 54: converts the floating-point number 67.8 to the integer 67 (the decimal part is lost);
  • line 55: converts the Boolean [true] to the integer 1 (the Boolean [false] to the integer 0);
  • line 56: converts the value [null] to the integer 0.

This is what the screen displays show:

Explicit conversion to int------------------------------
parameter: string(5) "12.45"
result of the conversion: int(12)
parameter: float(67.8)
result of the conversion: int(67)
parameter: bool(true)
result of the conversion: int(1)
parameter: NULL
result of the conversion: int(0)

We continue our analysis of the script with the explicit conversion of values to the [float] type:

// to float
print "Explicit conversion to float------------------------------\n";
showFloat("12.45");
showFloat(67);
showFloat(true);
showFloat(null);

function showFloat(mixed $var): void
{
    print "parameter: ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "result of the conversion: ";
    var_dump((float) $var);
}

Comments:

  • line 73: the function [showFloat] takes a parameter of any type and does not return a result;
  • line 78: the value of this parameter is explicitly converted to [float];
  • line 68: the string "12.45" is converted to the real number 12.45;
  • line 69: the integer 67 is converted to the real number 67;
  • line 70: the Boolean value [true] is converted to the real number 1 (the value [false] is converted to the number 0);
  • line 71: the value [null] is converted to the real number 0.

This is shown by the screen output:

Explicit conversion to float------------------------------
parameter: string(5) "12.45"
result of the conversion: float(12.45)
parameter: int(67)
result of the conversion: float(67)
parameter: bool(true)
result of the conversion: float(1)
parameter: NULL
result of the conversion: float(0)

We conclude the presentation of the script by examining conversions to the type [string]:

// to string
print "Explicit conversion to string------------------------------\n";
showString(5);
showString(6.7);
showString(false);
showString(null);

function showString(mixed $var): void
{
    print "parameter: ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "result of the conversion: ";
    var_dump((string) $var);
}

Comments:

  • line 88: the function [showString] takes a parameter of any type and does not return a result;
  • line 93: the parameter value is converted to type [string];
  • line 83: the integer 5 will be converted to the string "5";
  • line 84: the floating-point number 6.7 will be converted to the string "6.7";
  • line 85: the boolean [false] will be converted to an empty string;
  • line 86: the value [null] will be converted to an empty string.

Here are the screen results:

Explicit conversion to string------------------------------
parameter: int(5)
result of the conversion: string(1) "5"
parameter: float(6.7)
result of the conversion: string(3) "6.7"
parameter: bool(false)
result of the conversion: string(0) ""
parameter: NULL
result of the conversion: string(0) ""

docs.title: 3.6.1. Standard one-dimensional arrays
docs.text:
There are two notations for arrays in PHP:

$array = ["one", 2, "three"];
$opposites = ["small" => "big", "beautiful" => "ugly", "expensive" => "cheap"];

Array 1 is called an array (or list), and array 2 is called a dictionary or associative array, where elements are denoted as key => value. The notation [$opposites["beautiful"]] refers to the value associated with the key "beautiful." In this case, it is the string "ugly." Array 1 is simply a variant of the dictionary and could be written as:

$array = [0 => "one", 1 => 2, 2 => "three"];

This gives us [$array[2]="three"]. Ultimately, there are only dictionaries. In the case of a classic array of n elements, the keys are the integers in the range [0,n-1].

The script [basics-05.php] demonstrates operations for manipulating an array of values:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// classic arrays
// initialization
$tab1 = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
// traversal - 1
print "tab1 has " . count($tab1) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// traversal - 2
print "tab1 has " . count($tab1) . " elements\n";
foreach ($tab1 as $key => $value) {
    print "tab1[$key]=$value\n";
}
// adding elements
$tab1[] = $i++;
$tab1[] = $i++;
// traversal - 3
print "tab1 has " . count($tab1) . " elements\n";
$i = 0;
foreach ($tab1 as $element) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$element\n";
    $i++;
}
// removing the last element
array_pop($tab1);
// traversal - 4
print "tab1 has " . count($tab1) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// removing the first element
array_shift($tab1);
// traversal - 5
print "tab1 has " . count($tab1) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// adding at the end of the array
array_push($tab1, -2);
// traversal - 6
print "tab1 has " . count($tab1) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// adding at the beginning of the array
array_unshift($tab1, -1);
// traversal - 7
print "tab1 has " . count($tab1) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// first and last elements (PHP 8.5)
print "first element: " . array_first($tab1) . ", last element: " . array_last($tab1) . "\n";

> php basics-05.php

tab1[1]=1

Comments:

  • Line 15: The array is iterated over using a [foreach]. This syntax element allows you to iterate over a dictionary—and therefore an array—using two different syntaxes: [foreach ($dictionary as $key => $value)] and [foreach ($array as $value)]. The first syntax returns a (key, value) pair on each iteration, while the second returns only the value. The PHP 7 course used the function [each] here, which was already obsolete at the time: it was removed in PHP 8.0. [foreach] is the standard way to iterate through an array;
  • Line 19: The notation [$array[] = value] adds the element [value] as the last element of [$array]. Here, [$i] is equal to 6 after the first loop for [for]: 6 is added, then 7;
  • line 24: an iteration using the second syntax of [foreach];
  • line 29: the function [array_pop($array)] removes the last element from [$array];
  • line 36: the function [array_shift($array)] removes the first element from [$array]. The remaining elements are renumbered starting from 0;
  • line 43: The function [array_push($array, value)] adds [value] as the last element of [$array];
  • line 50: The function [array_unshift($array, value)] adds [value] as the first element of [$array];
  • line 57: the functions [array_first] and [array_last], introduced with PHP 8.5, return the first and last elements of an array (or [null] if the array is empty).

docs.title: 3.6.2. The dictionary or associative array
docs.text:
The script [basics-06.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dictionaries
$spouses = ["Pierre" => "Gisèle", "Paul" => "Virginie", "Jacques" => "Lucette", "Jean" => ""];
// traversal - 1
print "Number of elements in the dictionary: " . count($spouses) . "\n";
foreach ($spouses as $key => $value) {
    print "spouses[$key]=$value\n";
}
// sorting the dictionary by key
ksort($spouses);
// traversal - 2
foreach ($spouses as $key => $value) {
    print "spouses[$key]=$value\n";
}
// list of the dictionary keys
$keys = array_keys($spouses);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($keys); $i++) {
    print "keys[$i]=$keys[$i]\n";
}
// list of the dictionary values
$values = array_values($spouses);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($values); $i++) {
    print "values[$i]=$values[$i]\n";
}
// is a classic array a list? and a dictionary?
print "values is a list: " . var_export(array_is_list($values), true) . "\n";
print "spouses is a list: " . var_export(array_is_list($spouses), true) . "\n";
// searching for a key
exists($spouses, "Jacques");
exists($spouses, "Lucette");
exists($spouses, "Jean");
// default value if the key does not exist: operator ??
print "spouse of Lucette: " . ($spouses["Lucette"] ?? "unknown") . "\n";
// removing a key-value pair
unset($spouses["Jean"]);
print "Number of elements in the dictionary: " . count($spouses) . "\n";
foreach ($spouses as $key => $value) {
    print "spouses[$key]=$value\n";
}
// end
exit;

function exists(array $spouses, string $husband): void
{
    // checks whether the key $husband exists in the dictionary $spouses
    if (isset($spouses[$husband])) {
        print "The key [$husband] exists, associated with the value [$spouses[$husband]]\n";
    } else {
        print "The key [$husband] does not exist\n";
    }
}

The results:

> php basics-06.php
Number of elements in the dictionary: 4
spouses[Pierre]=Gisèle
spouses[Paul]=Virginie
spouses[Jacques]=Lucette
spouses[Jean]=
spouses[Jacques]=Lucette
spouses[Jean]=
spouses[Paul]=Virginie
spouses[Pierre]=Gisèle
keys[0]=Jacques
keys[1]=Jean
keys[2]=Paul
keys[3]=Pierre
values[0]=Lucette
values[1]=
values[2]=Virginie
values[3]=Gisèle
values is a list: true
spouses is a list: false
The key [Jacques] exists, associated with the value [Lucette]
The key [Lucette] does not exist
The key [Jean] exists, associated with the value []
spouse of Lucette: unknown
Number of elements in the dictionary: 3
spouses[Jacques]=Lucette
spouses[Paul]=Virginie
spouses[Pierre]=Gisèle

Comments:

The code above applies to a dictionary what we previously saw for a simple array. We’ll only comment on the new features:

  • line 13: the function [ksort] (key sort) sorts a dictionary in natural key order;
  • line 19: the function [array_keys($dictionary)] returns the list of dictionary keys as an array;
  • line 24: the [array_values($dictionary)] function returns the list of dictionary values as an array;
  • line 29: the function [array_is_list] (PHP 8.1) returns [true] if the array keys are 0, 1, 2… in that order, that is, if the array is a list. The function [var_export] returns the PHP representation of a value (“true” or “false”);
  • line 46: the function [exists] takes an array ([array]) and a string ([string]);
  • line 49: the function [isset($variable)] returns [true] if the variable [$variable] exists and does not have the value [null]; otherwise, it returns [false]. When applied to an array element, it determines whether a key exists. The function [array_key_exists($key, $array)] does the same thing, but returns [true] even if the value associated with the key is [null];
  • line 36: the [??] operator (“null coalescing”) returns its left operand if it exists and is not [null], and its right operand otherwise. This is a concise way to obtain a default value for a missing key, without a warning;
  • line 38: the function [unset($variable)] deletes the variable [$variable], which is an element of the dictionary here.

docs.title: 3.6.3. Multidimensional Arrays
docs.text:
The script [basics-07.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// classic multidimensional arrays
// initialization
$multi = [[0, 1, 2], [10, 11, 12, 13], [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]];
// traversal
for ($i1 = 0; $i1 < count($multi); $i1++) {
    for ($i2 = 0; $i2 < count($multi[$i1]); $i2++) {
        print "multi[$i1][$i2]=" . $multi[$i1][$i2] . "\n";
    }
}
// multidimensional dictionaries
// initialization
$multi = ["zero" => [0, 1, 2], "one" => [10, 11, 12, 13], "two" => [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]];
// traversal
foreach ($multi as $key => $value) {
    for ($i2 = 0; $i2 < count($value); $i2++) {
        print "multi[$key][$i2]={$multi[$key][$i2]}\n";
    }
}

Results:

> php basics-07.php
multi[0][0]=0
multi[0][1]=1
multi[0][2]=2
multi[1][0]=10
multi[1][1]=11
multi[1][2]=12
multi[1][3]=13
multi[2][0]=20
multi[2][1]=21
multi[2][2]=22
multi[2][3]=23
multi[2][4]=24
multi[zero][0]=0
multi[zero][1]=1
multi[zero][2]=2
multi[one][0]=10
multi[one][1]=11
multi[one][2]=12
multi[one][3]=13
multi[two][0]=20
multi[two][1]=21
multi[two][2]=22
multi[two][3]=23
multi[two][4]=24

Comments:

  • Line 7: The elements of the array [$multi] are themselves arrays;
  • line 11: Inside a string enclosed in quotation marks, simple interpolation of [$multi[$i1][$i2]] does not work: PHP would evaluate to only [$multi[$i1]]. So we remove the expression from the string and use concatenation;
  • line 16: the array [$multi] becomes a dictionary (key, value) where each value is an array;
  • line 20: another solution: within a string enclosed in quotes, the notation [{$expression}] allows a complex expression to be evaluated. We’ll revisit this in the next section.

docs.title: 3.7.1. Notation
docs.text:
The script [basics-08.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// string notation
$string1 = "one";
$string2 = 'one';
print "[$string1,$string2]\n";
// between single quotes, variables are not evaluated
print '[$string1,$string2]' . "\n";
// the {$...} notation delimits the expression to evaluate
$person = ["name" => "dupont", "age" => 34];
print "{$person['name']} is {$person['age']} years old\n";
// a string over several lines (heredoc)
$text = <<<END
    name: $string1
    age: {$person['age']}
    END;
print "$text\n";

Results:

> php basics-08.php
[one,one]
[$string1,$string2]
dupont is 34 years old
name: one
age: 34

Comments:

  • Lines 6–7: A string can be enclosed in quotation marks or single quotes;
  • line 8: when enclosed in quotation marks, variables are evaluated;
  • line 10: within single quotes, they are not evaluated: the string is displayed as-is. Similarly, [\n] does not denote a line break here, hence the concatenation of ["\n"];
  • line 13: the notation [{$...}] allows for the evaluation of expressions more complex than a simple variable within a string—in this case, elements of a dictionary. The [${variable}] notation from older versions of PHP has been deprecated since PHP 8.2: it should not be used;
  • Lines 15–18: The [heredoc] syntax allows a string to span multiple lines. The string begins after [<<<END] and ends with the marker [END] (the name is arbitrary). Variables within it are evaluated as if they were enclosed in quotes. Starting with PHP 7.3, the end marker can be indented: this indentation is then removed from all lines of the string.

docs.title: 3.7.2. Comparison
docs.text:
The script [basics-09.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the type of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// comparison function
function compareStrings(string $string1, string $string2): void
{
    // compares string1 and string2
    if ($string1 === $string2) {
        print "[$string1] is equal to [$string2]\n";
    } else {
        print "[$string1] is different from [$string2]\n";
    }
}

// string comparison tests
compareStrings("abcd", "abcd");
compareStrings("", "");
compareStrings("1", "");

// searching for a substring (PHP 8)
$file = "taxpayersdata.txt";
print "[$file] contains [data]: " . var_export(str_contains($file, "data"), true) . "\n";
print "[$file] starts with [tax]: " . var_export(str_starts_with($file, "tax"), true) . "\n";
print "[$file] ends with [.json]: " . var_export(str_ends_with($file, ".json"), true) . "\n";
// position of a substring
print "position of [data] in [$file]: " . strpos($file, "data") . "\n";
// length, uppercase
print "length of [$file]: " . strlen($file) . ", in uppercase: " . strtoupper($file) . "\n";
// beware: strlen counts bytes, mb_strlen counts characters
print "strlen(\"café\")=" . strlen("café") . ", mb_strlen(\"café\")=" . mb_strlen("café") . "\n";

Results:

> php basics-09.php
[abcd] is equal to [abcd]
[] is equal to []
[1] is different from []
[taxpayersdata.txt] contains [data]: true
[taxpayersdata.txt] starts with [tax]: true
[taxpayersdata.txt] ends with [.json]: false
position of [data] in [taxpayersdata.txt]: 9
length of [taxpayersdata.txt]: 17, in uppercase: TAXPAYERSDATA.TXT
strlen("café")=5, mb_strlen("café")=4

Comments:

  • Line 10: We could have used the comparator [] instead of [=]. The latter operator is more restrictive in that it requires both operands to be of the same type. Note that here, it could have been replaced by the operator [] since the type of both parameters is set to [string]* in the function signature. However, we will continue to use *[=];
  • line 24: the function [str_contains($string, $substring)] (PHP 8.0) returns [true] if [$substring] is present in [$string];
  • line 25: the function [str_starts_with] (PHP 8.0) checks for the start of a string;
  • line 26: the function [str_ends_with] (PHP 8.0) checks for the end of a string;
  • line 28: the function [strpos($string, $substring)] returns the position of [$substring] in [$string], where the first character has position 0, and [false] if the substring is absent. Before PHP 8, the presence of a substring was checked using [strpos(...) !== false], which was a misleading notation since position 0 is converted to [false]: [str_contains] is much more readable;
  • line 30: the function [strlen] returns the length of a string, and [strtoupper] converts it to uppercase;
  • line 32: [strlen] counts bytes, not characters. The course files are encoded in UTF-8, where an accented character takes up two bytes: “café” has 4 characters but 5 bytes. The functions of the [mbstring] extension (mb_strlen, mb_substr, mb_strtoupper…) operate on characters.

docs.title: 3.7.3. Relationships Between Strings and Arrays
docs.text:
The script [basics-10.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// string to array
$string = "1:2:3:4";
$tab = explode(":", $string);
// array traversal
print "tab has " . count($tab) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
}
// array to string
$string2 = implode(":", $tab);
print "string2=$string2\n";
// let's add an empty field
$string .= ":";
print "string=$string\n";
$tab = explode(":", $string);
// array traversal
print "tab has " . count($tab) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
} // we now have 5 elements, the last one being empty
// let's add an empty field again
$string .= ":";
print "string=$string\n";
$tab = explode(":", $string);
// array traversal
print "tab has " . count($tab) . " elements\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
} // we now have 6 elements, the last two being empty

Results:

> php basics-10.php
tab has 4 elements
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
string2=1:2:3:4
string=1:2:3:4:
tab has 5 elements
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
tab[4]=
string=1:2:3:4::
tab has 6 elements
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
tab[4]=
tab[5]=

Comments:

  • Line 7: The [explode($separator, $string)] function retrieves the fields from [$string] separated by [$separator]. Thus, [explode(":", $string)] retrieves the elements of [$string]—which are separated by the string ":"—in array form;
  • Line 14: The function [implode($separator, $array)] performs the inverse operation of the function [explode]. It returns a string consisting of the elements of [$array] separated by [$separator];
  • line 17: The operator [.=] appends one string to the end of another. The results show that an empty field at the end of a string results in an empty element in the array returned by [explode].

docs.title: 3.7.4. Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The script [basics-11.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict type for function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// regular expressions in php
// retrieving the different fields of a string
// the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// we only want to retrieve the sequence of digits
$pattern = "/(\d+)/";
// we match the string against the pattern
comparePattern2String($pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "12 34");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "abcd");

// the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// we want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that follow and precede it
$pattern = "/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/";
// we match the string against the pattern
comparePattern2String($pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "12 34");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "abcd");

// the pattern - a date in dd/mm/yy format
$pattern = "/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/";
comparePattern2String($pattern, "10/05/97");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "  04/04/01  ");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "5/1/01");

// the pattern - a decimal number
$pattern = "/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/";
comparePattern2String($pattern, "187.8");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "-0.6");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "4");
comparePattern2String($pattern, ".6");
comparePattern2String($pattern, "4.");
comparePattern2String($pattern, " + 4");

// end
exit;

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function comparePattern2String(string $pattern, string $string): void
{
    // compares the string $string with the pattern $pattern
    // we match the string against the pattern
    $fields = [];
    $matches = preg_match($pattern, $string, $fields);
    // display results
    print "\nResults($pattern,$string)\n";
    if ($matches === 1) {
        for ($i = 0; $i < count($fields); $i++) {
            print "fields[$i]=$fields[$i]\n";
        }
    } else {
        print "The string [$string] does not match the pattern [$pattern]\n";
    }
}

Results:

> php basics-11.php

Results(/(\d+)/,xyz1234abcd)
fields[0]=1234
fields[1]=1234

Results(/(\d+)/,12 34)
fields[0]=12
fields[1]=12

Results(/(\d+)/,abcd)
The string [abcd] does not match the pattern [/(\d+)/]

Results(/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/,xyz1234abcd)
fields[0]=xyz1234abcd
fields[1]=xyz
fields[2]=1234
fields[3]=abcd

Results(/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/,12 34)
fields[0]=12 34
fields[1]=
fields[2]=12
fields[3]= 34

Results(/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/,abcd)
The string [abcd] does not match the pattern [/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/]

Results(/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/,10/05/97)
fields[0]=10/05/97
fields[1]=10
fields[2]=05
fields[3]=97

Results(/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/,  04/04/01  )
fields[0]=  04/04/01
fields[1]=04
fields[2]=04
fields[3]=01

Results(/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/,5/1/01)
The string [5/1/01] does not match the pattern [/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/]

Results(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,187.8)
fields[0]=187.8
fields[1]=

Results(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,-0.6)

fields[1]=-
fields[2]=0.6

Results(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,4)

Results(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,.6)

Results(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,4.)

Results(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/, + 4)
fields[0]= + 4
fields[1]=+
fields[2]=4

Comments:

Here, we use regular expressions to extract the various fields from a string. Regular expressions allow us to overcome the limitations of the [explode] function. The principle is to compare a string to another string called a pattern using the [preg_match] function: [$matches = preg_match($pattern, $string, $fields)] (line 48). The function [preg_match] returns the integer 1 if the pattern can be found in the string, and 0 otherwise. If so, [$fields[0]] represents the substring corresponding to the pattern. Furthermore, if the pattern contains subpatterns enclosed in parentheses, [$fields[1]] is the portion of [$string] corresponding to the first subpattern, [$fields[2]] is the portion of [$string] corresponding to the second subpattern, and so on. Let’s return to the script:

  • line 10: The pattern matches a sequence of one or more (+) digits (\d) appearing anywhere in a string. Additionally, the pattern defines a subpattern enclosed in parentheses;
  • line 12: the pattern /(\d+)/ is matched against the string "xyz1234abcd." We see that the substring 1234 matches the pattern. Therefore, [$fields[0]] equals "1234." Furthermore, the pattern has a subpattern enclosed in parentheses. We will get [$fields[1]="1234"];
  • line 13: the pattern /(\d+)/ is compared to the string "12 34". We see that the substrings 12 and 34 match the pattern. The comparison stops at the first substring that matches the pattern. Therefore, we will have [$fields[0]=12] and [$fields[1]=12];
  • Line 14: The pattern /(\d+)/ is compared to the string "abcd". No match is found;
  • line 51: [preg_match] returns an integer (and [false] if there is an error in the pattern): it is strictly compared to 1.

Let’s explain the patterns used in the rest of the code:

$pattern = "/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/";

matches the start of the string (^), followed by zero or more (*) arbitrary characters (.), followed by one or more (+) digits, followed by zero or more (*) arbitrary characters (.). The pattern (.*) matches zero or more any characters. Such a pattern will match any string. Thus, in the pattern /^(.*)(\d+)(.*)$/, the first subpattern (.*) would match all digits except the last one, which is the only one left for the subpattern (\d+). The pattern (.*?)(\d+) matches 0 or more any characters up to the next subpattern (?), which in this case is \d+. Therefore, the digits are no longer captured by the (.*) pattern. The pattern above thus matches [start of the string (^), a sequence of any characters (.*?), a sequence of one or more digits (\d+), a sequence of any characters (.*?), the end of the string ($)].

$pattern = "/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/";

matches [start of the string (^), a sequence of 0 or more spaces (\s*), 2 digits (\d\d), the character / (\/), 2 digits, /, 2 digits, a sequence of 0 or more spaces (\s*), the end of the string ($)].

$pattern = "/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/";

matches [start of the string (^), 0 or more spaces (\s*), a + or - sign ([+-]) present 0 or 1 time (?), a sequence of 0 or more spaces (\s*), 1 or more digits followed by a decimal point followed by zero or more digits (\d+\.\d*) or (|) a decimal point (\.) followed by one or more digits (\d+) or (|) one or more digits (\d+), a sequence of 0 or more spaces (\s*)]. The PHP 7 course wrote it as [+|-]: within square brackets, the | character has no special meaning, and this pattern also accepted the | symbol before a number. [+-] is the correct notation.

Note: The term [space] in regular expressions refers to a set of characters: whitespace, newline \n, tab \t, carriage return \r, form feed \f…

docs.title: 3.8.1. Parameter Passing Method
docs.text:
The [basics-12.php] script is as follows:

<?php

// how parameters are passed to a function
// strict respect of the parameter types
declare(strict_types=1);

function f(int &$i, int $j): void
{
    // $i will be obtained by reference
    // $j will be obtained by value
    $i++;
    $j++;
    print "f[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

// tests
$i = 0;
$j = 0;
// $i and $j are passed to the function f
f($i, $j);
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";

Results:

> php basics-12.php
f[i,j]=[1,1]
test[i,j]=[1,0]

Comments:

The code above demonstrates the two ways to pass parameters to a function. Consider the following example:

function f(int &$a, int $b): void
{
    …
}

// main program
$i = 10;
$j = 20;
f($i, $j);
  • Line 1: Defines the formal parameters [$a] and [$b] for the function [f]. This function processes these two formal parameters;
  • Line 9: Calls the function [f] with two actual parameters, [$i] and [$j]. The relationships between the formal parameters ([$a], [$b]) and the actual parameters ([$i], [$j]) are defined by lines 1 and 9:
    • [&$a]: The & symbol indicates that the formal parameter [$a] will take on the value of the address of the actual parameter [$i]. In other words, [$a] and [$i] are two references to the same memory location. Manipulating the formal parameter [$a] is equivalent to manipulating the actual parameter [$i]. This is demonstrated by the code execution. This passing mode is suitable for output parameters. This passing mode is called “pass-by-reference”;
    • [$b]: The formal parameter [$b] will take on the value of the actual parameter [$j]. This is passing by value. The formal and actual parameters are two different variables. Manipulating the formal parameter [$b] has no effect on the actual parameter [$j]. This is demonstrated by the code execution. This passing mode is suitable for input parameters.

Consider the function [swap], which accepts two formal parameters: [$a] and [$b]. The function swaps the values of these two parameters. Thus, when [swap($i, $j)] is called, the calling code expects the values of the two actual parameters to be swapped. These are therefore output parameters (they are modified). We will therefore write:

function swap(mixed &$a, mixed &$b): void
{
    [$a, $b] = [$b, $a];
}

Note: One might think that passing by reference is also suitable for large data sets, arrays, and dictionaries, to avoid copying them. This is unnecessary: PHP actually copies an array passed by value only if the function modifies it. Therefore, passing by reference should be reserved for output parameters.

The following script, [basics-13.php], shows additional examples:

<?php

// how parameters are passed
// no declare(strict_types=1) in this script: we are in "coercive" mode

function f(&$i, $j)
{
    // $i will be obtained by reference
    // $j will be obtained by value
    $i++;
    $j++;
    print "f[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function g(int &$i, int $j): void
{
    // $i will be obtained by reference
    // $j will be obtained by value
    $i++;
    $j++;
    print "g[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

// tests
$i = 0;
$j = 0;
// $i and $j are passed to the function f
f($i, $j);
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
// $i and $j are passed to the function g
g($i, $j);
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
// we pass float parameters to f
$a = 5.0;
$b = 6.2;
f($a, $b);
print "test[a,b]=[$a,$b]\n";
// we pass float parameters to g
$a = 5.0;
$b = 6.0;
g($a, $b);
print "test[a,b]=[$a,$b]\n";

Comments:

  • line 4: Unlike all the other scripts in this course, this script does not include the [declare(strict_types=1)] statement: PHP operates in “coercive” mode;
  • Lines 6–13: The [f] function discussed in the previous paragraph, but the parameters are not typed;
  • lines 15–22: the function [g] does the same thing as the function [f], but the types of the expected parameters are specified. It expects two parameters of type [int]. We want to see what happens when the actual parameter passed to the function does not have the type expected by the function;
  • lines 25–26: [$i] and [$j] are two integers;
  • line 28: call to the function [f] with parameters of the expected type;
  • line 31: call to the function [g] with parameters of the expected type;
  • lines 34–35: the variables [$a] and [$b] are of type [float];
  • line 36: call to the function [f] with parameters of type [float];
  • Lines 39–41: Call to the function [g] with parameters of type [float], which is not the expected type.

Results:

> php basics-13.php
f[i,j]=[1,1]
test[i,j]=[1,0]
g[i,j]=[2,1]
test[i,j]=[2,0]
f[i,j]=[6,7.2]
test[a,b]=[6,6.2]
g[i,j]=[6,7]
test[a,b]=[6,6]
  • The function [f], whose parameters are untyped, accepted both parameters of type [float] and processed them as follows: [$i] is 6.0 (displayed as 6), and [$j] is 7.2;
  • the function [g] accepted both parameters of type [float] but converted them to type [int]. This can be seen in the variable [$a], passed by reference, which has become the integer 6.

The floating-point numbers 5.0 and 6.0 have no decimal part: converting them to integers does not result in any loss of information. What would happen with the floating-point number 5.3? In PHP 7, it was silently converted to the integer 5. Since PHP 8.1, this conversion—which loses information—has been marked as deprecated: it will become an error in a future version of PHP.

Now let’s do the same thing in strict mode. The script [basics-13b.php] is identical to the script [basics-13.php] except that it begins with the statement:

declare(strict_types=1);

This instruction specifies that the types of the formal parameters must be respected. If they are not, an error is reported. The results of the execution are then:

> php basics-13b.php
f[i,j]=[1,1]
test[i,j]=[1,0]
g[i,j]=[2,1]
test[i,j]=[2,0]
f[i,j]=[6,7.2]
test[a,b]=[6,6.2]
