Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: g(): Argument #1 ($i) must be of type int, float given, called in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/basics/basics-13b.php on line 42 and defined in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/basics/basics-13b.php:16
Stack trace:
#0 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/basics/basics-13b.php(42): g(5.0, 6.0)
#1 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/basics/basics-13b.php on line 16

The PHP interpreter raised a [TypeError] error to indicate that the first parameter passed to the [g] function was of the wrong type: g(): Argument #1 ($i) must be of type int; float was provided. The message indicates the line number of the faulty call (42) and that of the function definition (16). Since this error is not caught (there is no [try / catch]), the script terminates. It is recommended to be strict about parameter types whenever possible to detect function call errors: this is why all scripts in the course begin with [declare(strict_types=1)].

docs.title: 3.8.2. Function parameters in PHP 8
docs.text:
PHP 8 has greatly enhanced function declaration and calling. The script [basics-14.php] demonstrates these new features:

<?php

// function parameters in PHP 8
declare(strict_types=1);

// 1 - parameters with a default value
function greeting(string $name, string $phrase = "Hello", bool $uppercase = false): string
{
    $message = "$phrase $name";
    return $uppercase ? strtoupper($message) : $message;
}

print greeting("Pierre") . "\n";
print greeting("Pierre", "Good evening") . "\n";
// 2 - named arguments (PHP 8.0): we can skip a parameter and give them in any order
print greeting("Pierre", uppercase: true) . "\n";
print greeting(uppercase: true, phrase: "Hi", name: "Paul") . "\n";
// predefined functions also accept named arguments
print str_pad(string: "7", length: 3, pad_string: "0", pad_type: STR_PAD_LEFT) . "\n";

// 3 - union type (PHP 8.0): the parameter can be of one of the listed types
function double(int|float $number): int|float
{
    return 2 * $number;
}

var_dump(double(4));
var_dump(double(4.5));

// 4 - nullable type: ?string is equivalent to string|null
function length(?string $string): int
{
    // the ?? operator returns its right operand if the left operand is null
    return strlen($string ?? "");
}

print "length(\"abc\")=" . length("abc") . ", length(null)=" . length(null) . "\n";

// 5 - mixed type (PHP 8.0) and match expression (PHP 8.0)
function describe(mixed $value): string
{
    // match compares with === and returns a value
    return match (true) {
        is_int($value), is_float($value) => "the number $value",
        is_string($value) => "the string [$value]",
        is_bool($value) => "the boolean " . ($value ? "true" : "false"),
        is_array($value) => "an array of " . count($value) . " element(s)",
        default => "a value of type " . get_debug_type($value),
    };
}

foreach ([12, 3.5, "abc", false, [1, 2], null] as $value) {
    print describe($value) . "\n";
}

// match on a value
$children = 3;
$shares = match ($children) {
    0 => 0.0,
    1, 2 => $children * 0.5,
    default => 1 + ($children - 2) * 1.0,
};
print "$children child(ren) bring $shares share(s)\n";

// 6 - variable number of parameters (variadic) and the ... (spread) operator
function sum(int|float ...$numbers): int|float
{
    // $numbers is an array
    return array_sum($numbers);
}

print "sum()=" . sum() . "\n";
print "sum(1, 2, 3)=" . sum(1, 2, 3) . "\n";
$values = [10, 20, 30.5];
// the array is "spread" into actual parameters
print "sum(...\$values)=" . sum(...$values) . "\n";
// the ... operator also makes it possible to merge arrays
$all = [0, ...$values, 40];
print "all=[" . implode(",", $all) . "]\n";

Results:

> php basics-14.php
Hello Pierre
Good evening Pierre
HELLO PIERRE
HI PAUL
007
int(8)
float(9)
length("abc")=3, length(null)=0
the number 12
the number 3.5
the string [abc]
the boolean false
an array of 2 element(s)
a value of type null
3 child(ren) bring 2 share(s)
sum()=0
sum(1, 2, 3)=6
sum(...$values)=60.5
all=[0,10,20,30.5,40]

Comments:

  • line 7: The parameters [$phrase] and [$uppercase] have default values. They can be omitted when calling the function (line 13), in which case they take their default values;
  • line 10: the ternary operator [condition ? value1 : value2] returns [value1] if the condition is true, and [value2] otherwise;
  • line 16: named arguments (PHP 8.0). The actual parameter is preceded by the name of the formal parameter followed by a colon (:). This allows you to assign a value to the third parameter without specifying the second, which retains its default value;
  • line 17: With named arguments, the order of the parameters no longer matters. This improves code readability: [uppercase: true] is more descriptive than a standalone [true];
  • line 19: The predefined functions of PHP also accept named arguments. Their names are those listed in the php.net documentation;
  • line 22: The union type [int|float] (PHP 8.0) indicates that the parameter can be a [int] or a [float]. The same applies to the result;
  • line 31: the type [?string] is a nullable type: the parameter is a string or the value [null]. This is a shorthand notation for [string|null]. Note: In PHP 7, people often wrote [string $string = null] to achieve the same effect. This notation (“implicit nullable”) has been deprecated since PHP 8.4: you must write [?string $string = null];
  • Line 34: the [??] operator, which we’ve already encountered: if [$string] equals [null], the empty string is used. In fact, since PHP 8.1, passing [null] to a non-nullable parameter of a predefined function—such as [strlen(null)] here—is deprecated;
  • line 40: the parameter of type [mixed] accepts any value, including [null];
  • Lines 43–49: The expression [match] (PHP 8.0). It compares the value in parentheses to the values to the left of the => arrows and returns the value to the right of the first arrow for which the comparison is true. With [match (true)], conditions are written on the left: the first true condition takes precedence. Multiple values can be separated by commas (line 44). [default] covers all other cases;
  • line 48: the function [get_debug_type] (PHP 8.0) returns the type name of a value as written in the code: int, float, string, null, or the class name of an object. [gettype], on the other hand, returned historical names such as integer or double;
  • lines 58–62: [match] applied to a value. Here, the variable [$children] is compared to the values 0, then 1, and then 2; otherwise, the case for [default] applies. Unlike the [switch] instruction—which [match] effectively replaces—the comparison is performed using [===], [match] is an expression that returns a value, and there is no [break] instruction to worry about. If no branch is suitable and there is no *[default]*, *[match] throws a *[UnhandledMatchError] error;
  • line 66: [int|float ...$numbers] is a variadic parameter: the function accepts any number of actual parameters (even none), which PHP collects in the array [$numbers]. A variadic parameter is always the last one;
  • line 76: the [...] (spread) operator placed before an array in a call “spreads” the array: its elements become the actual parameters of the function. [sum(...$values)] is equivalent to [sum(10, 20, 30.5)];
  • line 78: the same operator allows the elements of one array to be inserted into another array.

docs.title: 3.8.3. Results returned by a function
docs.text:
The script [basics-15.php] is as follows:

<?php

// types in strict mode
declare(strict_types=1);

// results returned by a function
// a function can return several values in an array
[$res1, $res2, $res3] = f1(10);
print "[$res1,$res2,$res3]\n";
$res = f1(10);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($res); $i++) {
    print "f1: res[$i]=$res[$i]\n";
}
// an associative array can also be "destructured"
["min" => $min, "max" => $max] = minMax([4, -2, 17, 8]);
print "minMax: [min=$min,max=$max]\n";

// a function can return an object
$res = f2(10);
print "f2: [$res->res1,$res->res2,$res->res3]\n";
// what kind of object?
print "kind of object: ";
var_dump($res);

// we do the same thing with the function f3
$res = f3(10);
print "f3: [$res->res1,$res->res2,$res->res3]\n";
// what kind of object?
print "kind of object: ";
var_dump($res);

// a function can return an object or null
$res = f4(10);
// the nullsafe operator ?-> returns null instead of causing an error if $res is null
print "f4(10): res1=" . ($res?->res1 ?? "none") . "\n";
$res = f4(-10);
print "f4(-10): res1=" . ($res?->res1 ?? "none") . "\n";

// end
exit;

// function f1
function f1(int $value): array
{
    // returns an array ($value+1,$value+2,$value+3)
    return [$value + 1, $value + 2, $value + 3];
}

// function minMax
function minMax(array $numbers): array
{
    // returns an associative array
    return ["min" => min($numbers), "max" => max($numbers)];
}

// function f2
function f2(int $value): object
{
    // returns an object ($value+1,$value+2,$value+3)
    // obtained by transforming an associative array into an object
    return (object) ["res1" => $value + 1, "res2" => $value + 2, "res3" => $value + 3];
}

// function f3 - does the same thing as the function f2
function f3(int $value): object
{
    // returns an object ($value+1,$value+2,$value+3)
    $res = new stdClass();
    $res->res1 = $value + 1;
    $res->res2 = $value + 2;
    $res->res3 = $value + 3;
    // returns the object
    return $res;
}

// function f4 - returns an object if $value is positive, null otherwise
function f4(int $value): ?object
{
    return $value >= 0 ? f3($value) : null;
}

Results:

> php basics-15.php
[11,12,13]
f1: res[0]=11
f1: res[1]=12
f1: res[2]=13
minMax: [min=-2,max=17]
f2: [11,12,13]
kind of object: object(stdClass)#1 (3) {
  ["res1"]=>
  int(11)
  ["res2"]=>
  int(12)
  ["res3"]=>
  int(13)
}
f3: [11,12,13]
kind of object: object(stdClass)#2 (3) {
  ["res1"]=>
  int(11)
  ["res2"]=>
  int(12)
  ["res3"]=>
  int(13)
}
f4(10): res1=11
f4(-10): res1=none

Comments:

  • The previous program shows that a PHP function can return a set of results rather than a single one, in the form of an array or an object. The concept of an object is explained in a later chapter;
  • lines 43–47: The function [f1] returns multiple values in the form of an array ([array]);
  • line 8: the returned array is unpacked into three variables;
  • line 15: destructuring also works with an associative array: for each variable, the key of the value to be retrieved is specified. The function [minMax] returns a dictionary (line 53). The predefined functions [min] and [max] return the smallest and largest elements of an array;
  • lines 57–62: The function [f2] returns multiple values in the form of an object ([object]). It does this by converting an associative array into an object using the operator [(object)]: each key in the array becomes a property of the object;
  • Lines 65–74: The function [f3] does the same thing as the function [f2], but it explicitly creates an object of type [stdClass] (line 68) and then adds properties to it. The attribute A of an object O is denoted by [$O->A];
  • line 23: the function [var_dump] provides access to the object’s type and its content. In the results, we see that the object is of type [stdClass], that its property [res1] is of type integer and has the value 11, etc. The number #1 or #2 following the type is an internal object number;
  • line 77: the result type [?object] indicates that the function [f4] returns an object or [null];
  • Lines 35–37: The null-safe operator [?->] (PHP 8.0). If [$res] equals [null], the expression [$res?->res1] equals [null] instead of causing an error; the operator [??] then replaces [null] with “none.” Here, the operator [??] would suffice on its own, since it does not signal the absence of the property. The operator [?->] will prove particularly useful with objects and their methods: [$client?->getAddress()?->getCity()].

Note: The PHP 7 course featured a function that wrote [$res->res1 = ...] without having created the object [$res]. PHP 7 would then create a [stdClass] object by default with a simple warning. Starting with PHP 8.0, this is a fatal error (Attempt to assign property on null): an object must always be created before it is used.

docs.title: 3.8.4. Functions are also values
docs.text:
In PHP, a function can be stored in a variable, passed as a parameter to another function, or returned as a result. The [basics-17.php] script demonstrates the different ways to write and use these functions:

<?php

// functions are values too
declare(strict_types=1);

$numbers = [4, -2, 17, 8, -5];

// 1 - an anonymous function assigned to a variable
$square = function (int $x): int {
    return $x * $x;
};
print "square(5)=" . $square(5) . "\n";

// 2 - an anonymous function passed as a parameter to a predefined function
// array_map applies the function to each element of the array
$squares = array_map($square, $numbers);
print "squares=[" . implode(",", $squares) . "]\n";

// 3 - an anonymous function using an outside variable: the use keyword
$threshold = 5;
$large = array_filter($numbers, function (int $x) use ($threshold): bool {
    return $x > $threshold;
});
print "numbers > $threshold: [" . implode(",", $large) . "]\n";

// 4 - the arrow function (PHP 7.4): a single expression, outside variables captured automatically
$positives = array_filter($numbers, fn(int $x): bool => $x >= 0);
print "positives=[" . implode(",", $positives) . "]\n";
// sorting with a comparison function: the <=> operator returns -1, 0 or 1
$sorted = $numbers;
usort($sorted, fn(int $a, int $b): int => $b <=> $a);
print "descending sort=[" . implode(",", $sorted) . "]\n";

// 5 - searching in an array (PHP 8.4)
print "first negative: " . array_find($numbers, fn(int $x): bool => $x < 0) . "\n";
print "at least one > 10: " . var_export(array_any($numbers, fn(int $x): bool => $x > 10), true) . "\n";
print "all > -10: " . var_export(array_all($numbers, fn(int $x): bool => $x > -10), true) . "\n";

// 6 - the first-class callable syntax (PHP 8.1): functionName(...)
$uppercase = strtoupper(...);
print $uppercase("hello") . "\n";
$names = ["dupont", "durand", "martin"];
print "names=[" . implode(",", array_map(ucfirst(...), $names)) . "]\n";

// 7 - the pipe operator |> (PHP 8.5): the result on the left is passed to the function on the right
$result = "  Hello everybody out there  "
    |> trim(...)
    |> strtolower(...)
    |> (fn(string $s): string => str_replace(" ", "-", $s));
print "result=[$result]\n";
// equivalent without the pipe operator
$result = str_replace(" ", "-", strtolower(trim("  Hello everybody out there  ")));
print "result=[$result]\n";

Results:

> php basics-17.php
square(5)=25
squares=[16,4,289,64,25]
numbers > 5: [17,8]
positives=[4,17,8]
descending sort=[17,8,4,-2,-5]
first negative: -2
at least one > 10: true
all > -10: true
HELLO
names=[Dupont,Durand,Martin]
result=[hello-everybody-out-there]
result=[hello-everybody-out-there]

Comments:

  • lines 9–11: An anonymous (unnamed) function is assigned to the variable [$square]. Note the semicolon at the end: this is an assignment;
  • line 12: the function is called via the variable;
  • line 16: the predefined function [array_map] applies the function passed as the first parameter to each element of the array passed as the second parameter, and returns the array of results;
  • lines 21–23: the predefined function [array_filter] returns the array elements for which the function passed as the second parameter returns [true]. An anonymous function is not aware of the variables in the surrounding code: the keyword [use ($threshold)] gives it access to the variable [$threshold]. Note that [array_filter] retains the keys of the selected elements; this has no effect here because [implode] uses only the values;
  • Line 27: an arrow function (PHP 7.4): [fn(parameters) => expression]. It contains only one expression, whose value is the result of the function. It automatically has read access to the variables in the surrounding code: no need for [use]. This is the most concise way to write small functions passed as parameters;
  • Line 31: The function [usort] sorts an array using a comparison function that takes two elements, [$a] and [$b], and returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number, depending on whether [$a] should be placed before, at the same rank as, or after [$b]. The operator [<=>] (“spaceship”) returns exactly -1, 0, or 1. By writing [$b <=> $a] instead of [$a <=> $b], we obtain a descending sort. Note that [usort] modifies the array passed to it (pass-by-reference): we have therefore sorted a copy ([$sorted]) of the array [$numbers];
  • Line 35: The functions [array_find], [array_any], and [array_all] were introduced with PHP 8.4. [array_find] returns the first element for which the function returns [true] (or [null] if there are none), [array_any] returns [true] if at least one element satisfies the condition, and [array_all] if all of them do;
  • line 40: first-class callable syntax (PHP 8.1): [functionName(...)], with three dots between the parentheses, does not call the function but returns the function itself as a [Closure] object. It can then be used as an anonymous function;
  • Line 43: The predefined function [ucfirst] (first letter capitalized) is passed to [array_map];
  • Lines 46–49: the pipe operator [|>] (PHP 8.5). The expression [value |> function] calls the function with the value as its only parameter. The calls are chained from left to right, in the order in which they are read: leading and trailing spaces are removed with [trim], the text is converted to lowercase with [strtolower], and then spaces are replaced with hyphens. An arrow function used with [|>] must be enclosed in parentheses;
  • line 52: the same thing without the pipe operator. Functions are nested and read from the inside out, in the reverse order of execution.

docs.title: 3.9. Text files
docs.text:
The script [basics-16.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the type of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// sequential processing of a text file
// it is a set of lines of the form login:pwd:uid:gid:info:dir:shell
// each line is put into a dictionary in the form login => [uid, gid, info, dir, shell]
// we set the file name
$INFO = "info.txt";
// we open it for creation
$file = fopen($INFO, "w");
if ($file === false) {
    print "Error opening the file $INFO for writing\n";
    exit;
}
// we generate arbitrary content
for ($i = 0; $i < 100; $i++) {
    fputs($file, "login$i:pwd$i:uid$i:gid$i:info$i:dir$i:shell$i\n");
}
// we close the file
fclose($file);

// we process it - fgets keeps the end-of-line mark
// this avoids getting an empty string when reading a blank line
// we open it for reading
$file = fopen($INFO, "r");
if ($file === false) {
    print "Error opening the file $INFO for reading\n";
    exit;
}

// the dictionary of information
$dict = [];
// the lines are less than 1000 characters long
// reading the line stops at the end-of-line mark
// or at the end-of-file mark
while (($line = fgets($file, 1000)) !== false) {
    // we remove the end-of-line mark if it exists
    $line = cutNewLineChar($line);
    // we put the line into an array
    $info = explode(":", $line);
    // we retrieve the login
    $login = array_shift($info);
    // we ignore the pwd
    array_shift($info);
    // we create an entry in the dictionary
    $dict[$login] = $info;
}
// we close it
fclose($file);

// using the dictionary
displayInfo($dict, "login10");
displayInfo($dict, "X");

// another way to read a text file: the file function
$lines = file($INFO, FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES);
print "the file $INFO has " . count($lines) . " lines, the last one is [" . array_last($lines) . "]\n";

// end
exit;

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function displayInfo(array $dict, string $key): void
{
    // displays the value associated with key in the dictionary $dict if it exists
    if (isset($dict[$key])) {
        // value exists - is it an array?
        $value = $dict[$key];
        if (is_array($value)) {
            print "[$key," . implode(":", $value) . "]\n";
        } else {
            // $value is not an array
            print "[$key,$value]\n";
        }
    } else {
        // $key is not a key of the dictionary $dict
        print "the key [$key] does not exist\n";
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function cutNewLineChar(string $line): string
{
    // we remove the end-of-line mark from $line if it exists
    // (\n on Unix, \r\n on Windows)
    return rtrim($line, "\r\n");
}

The [info.txt] file created by the script:

login0:pwd0:uid0:gid0:info0:dir0:shell0
login1:pwd1:uid1:gid1:info1:dir1:shell1
login2:pwd2:uid2:gid2:info2:dir2:shell2
…
login98:pwd98:uid98:gid98:info98:dir98:shell98
login99:pwd99:uid99:gid99:info99:dir99:shell99

The results:

> php basics-16.php
[login10,uid10:gid10:info10:dir10:shell10]
the key [X] does not exist
the file info.txt has 100 lines, the last one is [login99:pwd99:uid99:gid99:info99:dir99:shell99]

Comments:

  • Line 12: [fopen(file_name, "w")] opens the file [file_name] in write mode (w=write). If the file does not exist, it is created. If it exists, it is cleared. The file is created in the current directory, the one from which the script was run. If creation fails, [fopen] issues a warning and returns the value [false];
  • line 13: the result of [fopen] is tested by strictly comparing it to [false];
  • line 19: [fputs($file, $string)] writes [$string] to the file [$file]. Here, the string ends with the end-of-line marker [\n];
  • line 22: [fclose($file)] closes the file [$file];
  • line 27: [fopen(file_name, "r")] opens the file [file_name] in read mode (r=read). If opening the file fails (for example, if the file does not exist), [fopen] returns the value [false];
  • line 34: the dictionary is initialized as empty before being populated. PHP would create the array on the first assignment of [$dict[$login] = ...], but if the file were empty, the variable would not exist and its use would trigger a warning;
  • line 38: [fgets($file, 1000)] reads the next line of the file, limited to 1,000 characters. The [while (($line = fgets($file, 1000)) !== false) {...}] operation consists of two successive operations: 1) [$line = fgets(...)] and 2) [while ($line !== false)]. After the last character of the file has been read, the function [fgets] returns the value [false], and the loop [while] stops. Here, the function [fgets] attempts to read up to 1,000 characters but stops as soon as it encounters a line-end character. Since all lines here have fewer than 1,000 characters, [fgets] reads one line of text, including the line-end character. The PHP 7 course wrote [while ($line = fgets($file, 1000))]: the loop would have stopped prematurely on a final line reduced to "0," without a line-end character, because the string "0" is converted to [false]. The strict comparison [!== false] avoids this pitfall;
  • line 40: the function [cutNewLineChar] removes any line-end characters;
  • line 44: the function [array_shift($array)] removes the first element of [$array] and returns it as the result;
  • line 46: here, we ignore the result returned by [array_shift];
  • Line 58: Another way to read a text file. The [file] function returns an array containing all the lines in the file. With the [FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES] option, line-end characters are removed. This is simpler than the [fgets] loop, but the entire file is loaded into memory: for a very large file, reading line by line is still preferable;
  • line 71: the function [is_array($variable)] returns [true] if [$variable] is an array, and [false] otherwise;
  • line 84: The end-of-line character is the string "\r\n" on Windows systems and "\n" on Unix systems. The function [rtrim($string, $characters)] removes all characters present in [$characters]—in this case, \r and \n—from the end of [$string]. Without a second parameter, [rtrim] removes all “spaces” (whitespace, tabs, line breaks, etc.); the function [trim] does the same at both ends of the string.

docs.title: 3.10. Encoding/Decoding JSON
docs.text:
The [scripts-console/json] folder contains the scripts for this section:

json
├── family.json
├── json-01.php
├── json-02.php
└── json-03.php

The JSON encoding/decoding (JavaScript Object Notation) is something we will use extensively in the exercise that serves as the central theme of this document. The [json-01.php, json-02.php, json-03.php] scripts explain what you need to know for the rest of the document.

The [json-01.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

$array1 = ["lastName" => "séléné", "firstName" => "bénédicte", "age" => 34];
// JSON encoding of the array array1 with escaped Unicode characters
print "JSON encoding of the array array1 with escaped Unicode characters\n";
$json1 = json_encode($array1);
print "json1=$json1\n";
// JSON encoding of the array array1 with unescaped Unicode characters
print "JSON encoding of the array array1 with unescaped Unicode characters\n";
$json2 = json_encode($array1, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
print "json2=$json2\n";
// JSON decoding into an associative array
print "JSON decoding of json2 into an associative array\n";
$array2 = json_decode($json2, true);
var_dump($array2);
foreach ($array2 as $key => $value) {
    print "$key:$value\n";
}
// JSON decoding into an object
print "JSON decoding of json2 into a stdClass object\n";
$object2 = json_decode($json2);
var_dump($object2);
print "firstName=$object2->firstName\n";
print "lastName=$object2->lastName\n";
print "age=$object2->age\n";

Results:

> php json-01.php
JSON encoding of the array array1 with escaped Unicode characters
json1={"lastName":"s\u00e9l\u00e9n\u00e9","firstName":"b\u00e9n\u00e9dicte","age":34}
JSON encoding of the array array1 with unescaped Unicode characters
json2={"lastName":"séléné","firstName":"bénédicte","age":34}
JSON decoding of json2 into an associative array
array(3) {
  ["lastName"]=>
  string(9) "séléné"
  ["firstName"]=>
  string(11) "bénédicte"
  ["age"]=>
  int(34)
}
lastName:séléné
firstName:bénédicte
age:34
JSON decoding of json2 into a stdClass object
object(stdClass)#1 (3) {
  ["lastName"]=>
  string(9) "séléné"
  ["firstName"]=>
  string(11) "bénédicte"
  ["age"]=>
  int(34)
}
firstName=bénédicte
lastName=séléné
age=34

Comments:

  • line 8: the [json_encode] function converts its parameter into the JSON string. In the resulting string, the accented character é has been replaced by its Unicode code, which begins with \u;
  • line 12: We repeat the same process, this time specifying that the Unicode characters should be preserved as-is. The resulting JSON string is much more readable;
  • Lines 16–20: We perform the reverse operation. We convert the JSON string into an associative array: this is the role of the second parameter, [true], of [json_decode]. The results show that we have indeed obtained an associative array;
  • Lines 23–27: Without the parameter [true], [json_decode] converts the JSON string into an object of type [stdClass]. Attribute A of an object O is denoted as [$O->A].

Multi-level arrays can be encoded as JSON, as shown in the following script [json-02.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

$array = [
    "lastName" => "séléné", "firstName" => "bénédicte", "age" => 34,
    "husband" => ["lastName" => "icariù", "firstName" => "ignacio", "age" => 35],
    "children" => [
        ["firstName" => "angèle", "age" => 8],
        ["firstName" => "andré", "age" => 2],
    ],
];
// JSON encoding of the multi-level array
print "JSON encoding of a multi-level array\n";
$json = json_encode($array, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
print "json=$json\n";
// the same encoding, presented in a readable way
print "JSON encoding with the JSON_PRETTY_PRINT option\n";
print json_encode($array["husband"], JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_PRETTY_PRINT) . "\n";

Results:

> php json-02.php
JSON encoding of a multi-level array
json={"lastName":"séléné","firstName":"bénédicte","age":34,"husband":{"lastName":"icariù","firstName":"ignacio","age":35},"children":[{"firstName":"angèle","age":8},{"firstName":"andré","age":2}]}
JSON encoding with the JSON_PRETTY_PRINT option
{
    "lastName": "icariù",
    "firstName": "ignacio",
    "age": 35
}

Comments:

In the JSON string:

  • non-associative arrays (lists) are enclosed in square brackets [] ;
  • associative arrays are enclosed in curly braces {} .

Line 19: The options for [json_encode] are combined using the | operator (binary OR). The [JSON_PRETTY_PRINT] option produces a JSON string that is indented across multiple lines, making it more readable.

The script [json-03.php] demonstrates how to process the following JSON file [family.json]:

{
    "wife": {
        "lastName": "séléné",
        "firstName": "bénédicte",
        "age": 34
    },
    "husband": {
        "lastName": "icariù",
        "firstName": "ignacio",
        "age": 35
    },
    "children": [
        {
            "firstName": "angèle",
            "age": 8
        },
        {
            "firstName": "andré",
            "age": 2
        }
    ]
}

The [json-03.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// reading the JSON file
$json = file_get_contents("family.json");
// is the content read valid JSON? (PHP 8.3)
if ($json === false || !json_validate($json)) {
    print "The file [family.json] is missing or does not contain valid JSON\n";
    exit;
}
// JSON decoding into an object
$family1 = json_decode($json);
print "----family1\n";
var_dump($family1);
// JSON decoding into an associative array
print "----family2\n";
$family2 = json_decode($json, true);
var_dump($family2);

Comments:

  • line 6: The [file_get_contents] function reads the contents of the file named [family.json] and stores them in the variable [$json]. It returns [false] if the read operation fails;
  • Line 8: The function [json_validate] (PHP 8.3) returns [true] if the string passed as a parameter is a valid JSON. Previously, it was necessary to decode the string and then call the function [json_last_error];
  • lines 13–19: the string is then decoded into an object and then into an associative array.

Results:

> php json-03.php
----family1
object(stdClass)#2 (3) {
  ["wife"]=>
  object(stdClass)#1 (3) {
    ["lastName"]=>
    string(9) "séléné"
    ["firstName"]=>
    string(11) "bénédicte"
    ["age"]=>
    int(34)
  }
  ["husband"]=>
  object(stdClass)#3 (3) {
    ["lastName"]=>
    string(7) "icariù"
    ["firstName"]=>
    string(7) "ignacio"
    ["age"]=>
    int(35)
  }
  ["children"]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    object(stdClass)#4 (2) {
      ["firstName"]=>
      string(7) "angèle"
      ["age"]=>
      int(8)
    }
    [1]=>
    object(stdClass)#5 (2) {
      ["firstName"]=>
      string(6) "andré"
      ["age"]=>
      int(2)
    }
  }
}
----family2
array(3) {
  ["wife"]=>
  array(3) {
    ["lastName"]=>
    string(9) "séléné"
    ["firstName"]=>
    string(11) "bénédicte"
    ["age"]=>
    int(34)
  }
  ["husband"]=>
  array(3) {
    ["lastName"]=>
    string(7) "icariù"
    ["firstName"]=>
    string(7) "ignacio"
    ["age"]=>
    int(35)
  }
  ["children"]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    array(2) {
      ["firstName"]=>
      string(7) "angèle"
      ["age"]=>
      int(8)
    }
    [1]=>
    array(2) {
      ["firstName"]=>
      string(6) "andré"
      ["age"]=>
      int(2)
    }
  }
}
  • The first part of the results shows the object resulting from the decoding of the JSON file [family.json]: The JSON objects have become [stdClass] objects, and the JSON list of children has become a PHP array;
  • the second part shows the associative array resulting from the same decoding: all JSON objects have become associative arrays.

docs.title: 5. The classes
docs.text:
Vocabulary: A class (keyword [class]) is a type PHP. A variable of this type is called an object. An object is an instance of a class.

It is in this chapter that the evolution of PHP between versions 7 and 8 is most evident. PHP 8 introduced a series of new features that make writing classes more concise and safer: typed attributes, constructor parameter promotion, read-only attributes ([readonly]), enumerations ([enum]), property hooks and asymmetric visibility (PHP 8.4), cloning with modification (PHP 8.5)... We introduce these concepts through the examples, following the progression of the PHP 7 course: we start with the most basic class and work our way up to a class written according to current best practices.

docs.title: 5.1. The script directory structure
docs.text:
The scripts for this chapter are located in the [scripts-console/classes] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes
├── json
│   ├── json-01.php
│   ├── json-02.php
│   ├── json-03.php
│   ├── json-04.php
│   ├── Person.php
│   ├── Person2.php
│   ├── Person3.php
│   └── Person4.php
├── classes-01.php
├── classes-02.php
├── ...
├── classes-26.php
├── Gender.php
├── Person.php
├── Student.php
└── Teacher.php

As in previous chapters, a console script is run in a [VS Code] terminal opened in the script’s folder, using the [php script-name.php] command.

docs.title: 5.2. Can any variable become an object with attributes?
docs.text:
In PHP 7, it was possible to write [$obj1->attr1 = "one";] to a nonexistent variable [$obj1]: PHP would then silently (with a simple warning) create a [stdClass]-type object with the [attr1] attribute. This is no longer possible in PHP 8. The [classes-01.php] script is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// in PHP 8, a non-existent variable no longer magically becomes an object
try {
    $obj0->attr1 = "one";
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// a generic object must be created explicitly
$obj1 = new \stdClass();
// a [stdClass] object can receive dynamically created attributes
$obj1->attr1 = "one";
$obj1->attr2 = 100;
// displays the object
print "object1=[$obj1->attr1,$obj1->attr2]\n";
// modifies the object
$obj1->attr2 += 100;
// displays the object
print "object1=[$obj1->attr1,$obj1->attr2]\n";
// copies the value of object1 (address of the pointed object) into object2
// the two variables are then different but point to the same object
$obj2 = $obj1;
// modifies obj2
$obj2->attr2 = 0;
// displays the two objects
print "object1=[$obj1->attr1,$obj1->attr2]\n";
print "object2=[$obj2->attr1,$obj2->attr2]\n";
// changes the object pointed to by obj1
$obj1 = new \stdClass();
print "obj1:\n";
print_r($obj1);
print "obj2:\n";
print_r($obj2);
// assigns the reference (the address) of object2 to object3
// $obj2 and $obj3 are then one and the same variable
$obj3 = &$obj2;
print "obj2:\n";
print_r($obj2);
print "obj3:\n";
print_r($obj3);
// modifies obj3
$obj3->attr2 = 10;
// displays the two objects
print "object2=[$obj2->attr1,$obj2->attr2]\n";
print "object3=[$obj3->attr1,$obj3->attr2]\n";
// changes the object pointed to by obj2
$obj2 = new \stdClass();
$obj2->attr3 = "two";
$obj2->attr4 = 20;
// displays the two objects $obj2 and $obj3
print "obj2:\n";
print_r($obj2);
print "obj3:\n";
print_r($obj3);

// is an object a dictionary?
try {
    print count($obj3) . "\n";
} catch (\TypeError $e) {
    print "Error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// the number of attributes is obtained with [get_object_vars]
print "number of attributes: " . count(get_object_vars($obj3)) . "\n";
// an object can be iterated over with [foreach]
foreach ($obj3 as $attribute => $value) {
    print "obj3[$attribute]=$value\n";
}
// an associative array can be turned into a [stdClass] object and vice versa
$obj4 = (object) ["name" => "Langevin", "age" => 48];
print "obj4=[$obj4->name,$obj4->age]\n";
print_r((array) $obj4);
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-01.php
Error: Attempt to assign property "attr1" on null
object1=[one,100]
object1=[one,200]
object1=[one,0]
object2=[one,0]
obj1:
stdClass Object
(
)
obj2:
stdClass Object
(
    [attr1] => one
    [attr2] => 0
)
obj2:
stdClass Object
(
    [attr1] => one
    [attr2] => 0
)
obj3:
stdClass Object
(
    [attr1] => one
    [attr2] => 0
)
object2=[one,10]
object3=[one,10]
obj2:
stdClass Object
(
    [attr3] => two
    [attr4] => 20
)
obj3:
stdClass Object
(
    [attr3] => two
    [attr4] => 20
)
Error: count(): Argument #1 ($value) must be of type Countable|array, stdClass given
number of attributes: 2
obj3[attr3]=two
obj3[attr4]=20
obj4=[Langevin,48]
Array
(
    [name] => Langevin
    [age] => 48
)

Comments

  • Lines 7–9: In PHP 8, the variable [$obj0] does not exist, and the operation [$obj0->attr1 = "one"] throws an error of type [\Error] (line 2 of the results) instead of creating an object. We will examine the [try / catch] structure in the chapter on exceptions. For now, just note that it allows you to catch the error and continue executing the script;
  • line 13: a generic object must be explicitly created using the [new] operator. The predefined class [stdClass] is an empty class;
  • Lines 15–16: The notation [$obj->attr] refers to the attribute [attr] of the object [$obj]. If it does not exist, it is created; this is called a dynamic attribute. The class [stdClass] is designed for this purpose: you can add as many attributes to it as you want;
  • Line 25: The expression [$obj2 = $obj1], when [$obj1] is an object, is a copy of references: [$obj2] and [$obj1] are references (addresses) to the same object. The object itself can be modified by either reference;
  • Lines 27–30: are intended to show that [$obj1] and [$obj2] are two different variables that point to the same object. [$obj2 = $obj1] copied the value of [$obj1] into the variable [$obj2] (operation 1 below). The value of [$obj1] is the address of an object. Thus, [$obj1] and [$obj2] point to the same object. When a variable [$obj] that points to an object is manipulated, PHP manipulates the object being pointed to. As shown in the diagram below, we can modify the referenced object either via [$obj1] or via [$obj2]. This is illustrated in lines 5 and 6 of the results;

  • line 39: the expression [$obj3 = &$obj2] causes [$obj2] and [$obj3] to be at the same address as [1 below]. One could say that the two variables are aliases for the same memory location. They both point to an object, Object A below: [2];
  • Line 50: The operation [$obj2 = new \stdClass()] creates a new object, Object B [3 below], and the address of this new object is assigned to the variable [$obj2] [4]. Since [$obj2] and [$obj3] are two aliases for the same memory location, [$obj3] also points to the new Object B. This is shown in lines 31–42 of the results;

  • Line 61: Is an object a dictionary? In PHP 7, the function [count] accepted an object (with a warning) and returned 1, which made no sense. In PHP 8, it throws an error [TypeError]: [count] accepts only arrays or objects that implement the [Countable] interface (line 43 of the results);
  • line 66: the function [get_object_vars] returns an object’s attributes as an associative array. The number of elements in the array is equal to the number of attributes of the object;
  • Lines 68–69: An object can be iterated over using [foreach], just like a dictionary. The keys are the names of the attributes, and the values are the values of those same attributes. Thus, an object shares similarities with a dictionary but is not one. In PHP 7, this iteration was performed using the [each] function, which has since been removed;
  • lines 72–74: the conversion operator [(object)] converts an associative array into a [stdClass] object, and the operator [(array)] performs the reverse operation.

docs.title: 5.3. A Person class with no declared attributes
docs.text:
In PHP 7, a class could use attributes it had not declared: it was sufficient to write [$p->firstName = "Paul";] to create the attribute [firstName] in the object [$p], just as one does with [stdClass]. These dynamic attributes on objects of an ordinary class have been deprecated since PHP 8.2: each time such an attribute is created, the message “Deprecated: Creation of dynamic property Person::$firstName is deprecated” is displayed. They will be removed in a future version of PHP. The reason is simple: a typo in an attribute name ([$p->firstNam = "Paul"]) would silently create a new attribute instead of reporting the error.

There are three exceptions to this rule:

  • the [stdClass] class, which we just used, still accepts dynamic attributes;
  • a class preceded by the attribute [#[\AllowDynamicProperties]] also accepts them. This attribute was designed to facilitate the migration of legacy code. We will not use it in this course;
  • a class that defines the magic methods [__get] and [__set] decides for itself what to do with an undeclared attribute.

It is this third solution that the script [classes-02.php] presents:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Person
{
    // the attributes are not declared one by one:
    // they are stored in a private array
    private array $attributes = [];

    // called when writing an undeclared attribute: $p->x = value
    public function __set(string $name, mixed $value): void
    {
        $this->attributes[$name] = $value;
    }

    // called when reading an undeclared attribute: $p->x
    public function __get(string $name): mixed
    {
        return $this->attributes[$name] ?? null;
    }

    // called by isset($p->x)
    public function __isset(string $name): bool
    {
        return isset($this->attributes[$name]);
    }

    // method
    public function identity(): string
    {
        // uses attributes that have not been declared
        return "[$this->firstName,$this->lastName,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// the attributes are created by the magic method [__set]
$p = new Person();
$p->firstName = "Paul";
$p->lastName = "Langevin";
$p->age = 48;
// calling a method
print "person=" . $p->identity() . "\n";
// isset
print "isset(\$p->age): " . var_export(isset($p->age), true) . "\n";
print "isset(\$p->address): " . var_export(isset($p->address), true) . "\n";
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-02.php
person=[Paul,Langevin,48]
isset($p->age): true
isset($p->address): false

Comments

  • Lines 6–38: define a class named [Person]. A class is a template used to create objects. It consists of attributes and functions called methods;
  • line 10: The only attribute declared for the class is a private array (we’ll soon see the meaning of the keyword [private]). This array will store the “undeclared” attributes;
  • lines 13–16: The magic method [__set] is automatically called by PHP when writing to an attribute that does not exist (or is not accessible). It receives the attribute’s name and the value to be assigned to it. Here, it stores this value in the array [$attributes]. Methods whose names begin with two underscores are called magic methods: they are not called explicitly; instead, PHP calls them;
  • lines 19–22: The magic method [__get] is called when reading an attribute that does not exist. It returns the stored value or [null]. The operator [??] returns its left operand if it exists and is not [null]; otherwise, it returns its right operand;
  • line 25: the magic method [__isset] is called by the function [isset];
  • Line 31: The method [identity] uses three attributes that are not declared in the class. The keyword [$this] refers to the object to which the method is applied. Each call to [$this->firstName] triggers a call to [__get];
  • Line 40: A [$p] object of type [Person] is created. The keyword [new] is used to create a new object. The operation returns a reference to the created object (i.e., an address). Various notations are possible: [new Person()], [new Person], [new person]. The class name is case-insensitive;
  • lines 41–43: The three attributes required by the [identity] method are created in the [$p] object by the [__set] method;
  • line 45: the [identity] method of the [Person] class is applied to the [$p] object. In the code for the [identity] method, [$this] references the same object as [$p].

This technique has its uses (configuration objects, encapsulation of data read from a file), but it is not the standard way to write a class. In a regular class, you declare its attributes.

docs.title: 5.4. The Person class with declared attributes
docs.text:
The script [classes-03.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Person
{
    // attributes of the class, public and typed
    public string $firstName;
    public string $lastName;
    public int $age;

    // method
    public function identity(): string
    {
        return "[$this->firstName,$this->lastName,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// the attributes are public
$p = new Person();
$p->firstName = "Paul";
$p->lastName = "Langevin";
$p->age = 48;
// calling a method
print "person=" . $p->identity() . "\n";
// a typed attribute only accepts values of its type
try {
    $p->age = "forty-eight";
} catch (\TypeError $e) {
    print "Error 1: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// an uninitialized typed attribute cannot be read
$p2 = new Person();
try {
    print "person=" . $p2->identity() . "\n";
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Error 2: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-03.php
person=[Paul,Langevin,48]
Error 1: Cannot assign string to property Person::$age of type int
Error 2: Typed property Person::$firstName must not be accessed before initialization

Comments

  • Lines 9–11: The class attributes are explicitly declared. The keyword [public] means that they are accessible from outside the class. In PHP 7, the course used the keyword [var], inherited from PHP 4, which is a synonym for [public] and is no longer used today;
  • Each attribute is preceded by its type: [string] for first name and last name, [int] for age. These are typed attributes, which were introduced with PHP 7.4. The possible types are those of function parameters: [int], [float], [string], [bool], [array], a class or interface name, a nullable type [?string], a union type [int|float]...;
  • line 30: a typed attribute accepts only values of its type. Any other value causes an error [TypeError] (line 3 of the results);
  • lines 35–37: A typed attribute without a default value is in the “uninitialized” state until a value is assigned to it. Reading it causes an error (line 4 of the results). Untyped attributes, on the other hand, have a default value of [null]. This is one reason to initialize all of an object’s attributes as soon as it is created: that is the role of the constructor.

docs.title: 5.5. The Person class with a constructor
docs.text:
The previous examples showed exotic classes such as those found in PHP 4. It is not recommended to follow these examples. We now present a [Person] [classes-04.php] class that follows standard best practices, as found in all object-oriented languages (Java, C#, etc.):

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Person
{
    // attributes of the class
    private string $firstName;
    private string $lastName;
    private int $age;

    // getters and setters
    public function getFirstName(): string
    {
        return $this->firstName;
    }

    public function getLastName(): string
    {
        return $this->lastName;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }

    public function setFirstName(string $firstName): void
    {
        $this->firstName = $firstName;
    }

    public function setLastName(string $lastName): void
    {
        $this->lastName = $lastName;
    }

    public function setAge(int $age): void
    {
        $this->age = $age;
    }

    // constructor
    public function __construct(string $firstName, string $lastName, int $age)
    {
        // we go through the setters
        $this->setFirstName($firstName);
        $this->setLastName($lastName);
        $this->setAge($age);
    }

    // toString method
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[$this->firstName,$this->lastName,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// creating a Person object
$p = new Person("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
// identity of this person
print "person=$p\n";
// we change the age
$p->setAge(14);
// identity of the person
print "person=$p\n";
// a class having a [__toString] method implements the [Stringable] interface
print "Stringable: " . var_export($p instanceof \Stringable, true) . "\n";
// a private attribute is not accessible from outside the class
try {
    print $p->lastName;
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-04.php
person=[Paul,Langevin,48]
person=[Paul,Langevin,14]
Stringable: true
Error: Cannot access private property Person::$lastName

Comments

  • Line 4: We specify that the declared types of the function parameters must be strictly adhered to. Without this declaration, PHP would attempt to convert a value of the wrong type (for example, the string ["48"] to an integer [48]);
  • Lines 6–60: the class [Person];
  • Lines 9–11: the class’s private attributes ([private]). These attributes are visible only within the class. Other keywords that can be used are:
    • [public]: makes the attribute a public attribute visible from outside the class;
    • [protected]: makes the attribute a protected attribute visible from within the class and its derived classes;
  • Because the attributes are private, they cannot be accessed from outside the class. Therefore, we cannot write [$p->lastName = "Landru"]: we are outside the class [Person], and the attribute [lastName] is private. Lines 72–74 verify this: attempting to read [$p->lastName] results in an error (line 5 of the results). To initialize the private attributes of the [$p] object, there are two ways:
    • use the public methods [set] and [get] (the names of these methods can be anything) in lines 14–39. In this case, we write: [$p->setLastName("Landru")];
    • use the constructor in lines 45–50. You would then write: [$p = new Person("Michel", "Landru", 44)]. This syntax automatically calls the method of the [Person] class named [__construct];
  • line 64: This line displays the person [$p] as a string. To do this, the method of the [Person] class called [__toString] (line 54) is used;
  • line 70: Starting with PHP 8.0, any class that defines a method named [__toString] automatically implements the predefined interface [Stringable] (we will cover interfaces in the next chapter). The [instanceof] operator checks whether an object is of a given type. A function can thus declare a parameter of type [string|Stringable]: it then accepts a string or any object that can be converted to a string;
  • all methods of the class have been prefixed with the keyword [public], which indicates that the method is visible outside the class. The other keywords that can be used are, as with attributes and with the same meaning, [private] and [protected]. Without an explicit visibility keyword, the method is implicitly [public]. The PSR-12 style guidelines, which the scripts in this course follow, require that visibility always be specified explicitly.

docs.title: 5.6. Promotion of Constructor Parameters
docs.text:
The previous class is verbose: each attribute is named four times (declaration, constructor parameter, assignment in the constructor, getter). Since PHP 8.0, constructor parameter promotion allows you to declare and initialize an attribute directly in the list of constructor parameters. The script [classes-22.php] demonstrates this:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Person
{
    // constructor with parameter promotion:
    // each parameter preceded by a visibility becomes an attribute of the class
    public function __construct(
        private string $firstName,
        private string $lastName,
        private int $age = 0,
    ) {
        // nothing else to do: the attributes are already initialized
    }

    // getters
    public function getFirstName(): string
    {
        return $this->firstName;
    }

    public function getLastName(): string
    {
        return $this->lastName;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }

    // setter
    public function setAge(int $age): void
    {
        $this->age = $age;
    }

    // toString method
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[$this->firstName,$this->lastName,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// classic call: the arguments are passed in the order of the parameters
$p1 = new Person("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
print "p1=$p1\n";
// named arguments: the order no longer matters
$p2 = new Person(lastName: "Lefur", age: 70, firstName: "Sylvie");
print "p2=$p2\n";
// the [age] parameter has a default value: it can be omitted
$p3 = new Person(firstName: "Steve", lastName: "Boer");
print "p3=$p3\n";
// the promoted attributes are real attributes
var_dump($p3);
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-22.php
p1=[Paul,Langevin,48]
p2=[Sylvie,Lefur,70]
p3=[Steve,Boer,0]
object(Person)#3 (3) {
  ["firstName":"Person":private]=>
  string(5) "Steve"
  ["lastName":"Person":private]=>
  string(4) "Boer"
  ["age":"Person":private]=>
  int(0)
}

Comments

  • Lines 10–14: Each constructor parameter preceded by a visibility keyword ([private], [protected], [public]) is “promoted”: PHP declares an attribute with the same name and type and assigns it the value of the parameter. These three lines replace the attribute declarations and assignments from the previous class;
  • line 13: A promoted parameter can have a default value. The comma after the last parameter has been allowed since PHP 8.0; it makes it easier to add a parameter later;
  • line 15: The body of the constructor can contain code (such as validations). Here, there is nothing to do;
  • line 52: Named arguments (PHP 8.0) allow arguments to be passed in any order by referring to them by the parameter name. This makes the code more readable, especially when a function has many parameters;
  • line 55: the parameter [age] is omitted; it takes its default value;
  • line 58: the function [var_dump] shows that the promoted attributes are true private attributes of the class (lines 5–12 of the results).

docs.title: 5.7. The Person Class with Validity Checks in the Constructor
docs.text:
A class’s constructor is the appropriate place to verify that the object’s initialization values are correct. However, an object can also be initialized using its [set] methods or equivalents. To avoid duplicating the same checks in two different places, these checks can be placed in the [set] methods. If an object’s initialization value turns out to be incorrect, an exception will be thrown. Here is an example.

First, move the definition of the [Person] class to its own file, [Person.php]:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Examples;

// class Person
class Person
{
    // attributes of the class
    private string $firstName;
    private string $lastName;
    private int $age;

    // getters and setters
    public function getFirstName(): string
    {
        return $this->firstName;
    }

    public function getLastName(): string
    {
        return $this->lastName;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }

    public function setFirstName(string $firstName): void
    {
        // the first name must not be empty
        $firstName = trim($firstName);
        if ($firstName === "") {
            throw new \Exception("The first name must not be empty");
        }
        $this->firstName = $firstName;
    }

    public function setLastName(string $lastName): void
    {
        // the last name must not be empty
        $lastName = trim($lastName);
        if ($lastName === "") {
            throw new \Exception("The last name must not be empty");
        }
        $this->lastName = $lastName;
    }

    public function setAge(int $age): void
    {
        // the age must be valid
        if ($age < 0) {
            throw new \Exception("The age must be a positive or zero integer");
        }
        $this->age = $age;
    }

    // constructor
    public function __construct(string $firstName, string $lastName, int $age)
    {
        // we go through the setters
        $this->setFirstName($firstName);
        $this->setLastName($lastName);
        $this->setAge($age);
    }

    // method acting as a second constructor
    public function initWithPerson(Person $p): void
    {
        // initializes the current object with a person $p
        $this->__construct($p->firstName, $p->lastName, $p->age);
    }

    // static factory method (named constructor)
    public static function fromPerson(Person $p): self
    {
        // creates a new person, a copy of the person $p
        return new self($p->firstName, $p->lastName, $p->age);
    }

    // toString method
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[$this->firstName,$this->lastName,$this->age]";
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 4: Specifies that the types of function parameters must be respected as declared;
  • Line 7: Defines a namespace. The full (or qualified) name of the class [Person] is therefore [\Examples\Person]. Note the character [\] at the beginning of the qualified name: this results in an absolute qualified name. If this character is absent, the name is a relative qualified name (relative to the current namespace). Thus, if two classes, A and B, belong to the same namespace E, in the code for class A, class B can be accessed using the relative notation B. If class A is part of the namespace E1 and class B is part of the namespace E2, then in class A’s code, class B can be accessed using the absolute notation [\E2\B]. Defining a class within a namespace is not mandatory but is considered best practice: two libraries can then each define a class named [Person] without conflict;
  • namespaces often correspond to the file directory structure. Thus, class A in the namespace E1 is often located in a file named [E1/A.php]. This is the PSR-4 convention used by the [Composer] tool to automatically load classes, which we will use in later chapters. The [PHP Intelephense] extension of [VS Code] does not require this. Do not confuse the file tree with a namespace: the fully qualified name of a class uses a namespace and has nothing to do with the file tree of the PHP file containing the class. Here, the class [\Examples\Person] is in the file [scripts-console/classes/Person.php];
  • lines 13–15: the class’s three private attributes;
  • lines 33–41: initialization of the [firstName] attribute and verification of the initialization value;
  • line 36: the function [trim($string)] removes the spaces at the beginning and end of [$string]. Thus, [trim(" abcd ")] is the string ["abcd"], and [trim(" ")] is the empty string.;
  • line 37: if the first name is empty, then an exception is thrown (line 38); otherwise, the first name is stored (line 40). To throw an exception, the predefined class [Exception] is used here. Here, we are required to use its absolute name, [\Exception]. If we use its relative name, [Exception], then this class will be searched for in the current namespace, i.e., in the namespace [Examples] of the class [Person]. Thus, the PHP interpreter will search for a class with the absolute name [\Examples\Exception], which does not exist;
  • lines 63–69: the constructor uses the methods [set] to initialize the attributes: the validations are written only once;
  • The methods on lines 72 and 79 are described in the following paragraph.

The class [Person] is used by the following script, [classes-05.php]:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion of the definition of the Person class
require_once __DIR__ . "/Person.php";
// for demonstration
print __DIR__ . "/Person.php\n";

// qualified name of the Person class
use Examples\Person;

// test
// creating a Person object
$p = new Person("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
// identity of this person
print "Example1, person=$p\n";
// creating an invalid Person object
try {
    $p = new Person("xx", "yy", "zz");
} catch (\Exception $e1) {
    print "Example2, error: " . $e1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (\TypeError $e2) {
    print "Example2, error: " . $e2->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// creating an invalid Person object
try {
    $p = new Person("", "yy", 10);
} catch (\Exception $e1) {
    print "Example3, error: " . $e1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (\TypeError $e2) {
    print "Example3, error: " . $e2->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-05.php
.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/Person.php
Example1, person=[Paul,Langevin,48]
Example2, error: Examples\Person::__construct(): Argument #3 ($age) must be of type int, string given, called in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-05.php on line 21
Example3, error: The first name must not be empty

Comments

  • Line 7: The script will use the [Person] class. You must therefore tell the PHP interpreter where to find the definition of this class. This is the purpose of the [include file] and [require file] statements. The difference between the two statements is as follows: if the [include file] statement encounters errors while loading [file], a [E_WARNING]-level error is issued, but execution continues, whereas [require], in the same situation, generates a fatal error and stops the script from running. Each of these two instructions has a variant: [include_once] and [require_once]. These two variants allow for handling cases where the same file is included multiple times. Consider, for example, a project consisting of several PHP scripts, some of which reference the [Person] class. Executing these scripts would then cause the file [Person.php] to be included multiple times, resulting in an error because a class cannot be defined twice. The solution is to use the [_once] variants, which ensure that the file is included only once in the project’s global script;
  • The constant [__DIR__] is a PHP constant that refers to the full name of the folder containing the script with the constant [__DIR__]. Line 9 displays it (line 2 of the results). On the reader’s machine, the result will be something like [C:\laragon\www\php8-oct-2026\scripts-console\classes/Person.php]. In a file path, you can use either [/] or [\] interchangeably on Windows. Using [__DIR__] makes the script independent of the current folder at the time of execution;
  • Line 12: The script [classes-05.php] has no namespace. When the code uses the relative name [Person], it is searched for in the root namespace [\] and will therefore not be found. There are two solutions to this problem:
    • use the full class name [\Examples\Person];
    • use the statement [use], which specifies that, in the code that follows, the name [Person] refers to the class [\Examples\Person]. In a [use] statement, the name is always absolute: the initial [\] is unnecessary (this is the recommended notation). The statement is equivalent to [use Examples\Person as Person;], which specifies that the alias [Person] refers to the class [\Examples\Person];
  • the instruction [use] tells the interpreter that the class [Person] is actually the class [\Examples\Person]. That said, where will the interpreter find the code for this class? The instruction [require_once] tells it. The two instructions have very different roles: [use] works on names, [require_once] loads a file;
  • line 16: a [Person] object is created. The [__construct] method of the [Person] class will be implicitly executed here;
  • line 18: displays the person [$p]. To be displayed, the value of the variable [$p] must be converted to a string. Implicitly, the method [Person::__toString] is then executed. This method must therefore return a string;
  • we have seen that the constructor of the [Person] class can throw a [\Exception] exception. This exception must therefore be handled. Consequently, the creation of a person should always be enclosed within a ***[try / catch] structure, as shown in lines 20–34. Here, we intentionally trigger an error by passing an age that is not an integer. In this specific case, the error is thrown by the PHP interpreter and not by the code in the [Person] class. This is because the signature of the [Person::__construct]* method is [__construct(string $firstName, string $lastName, int $age)]. Therefore, the [age] parameter passed to the constructor must be of type integer. If this is not the case, the PHP interpreter throws an error of type [TypeError]. Furthermore, the methods [set] of the class [Person]* throw an exception of type [\Exception]. Since the constructor that calls them does not have a [try / catch] structure, the exception is propagated up one level to the code that called the constructor, i.e. the code in the [classes-05.php] script. Finally, the script [classes-05.php]* can receive two types of errors: [\Exception] or [\TypeError]. For this reason, the [try] structure has two [catch] clauses to handle the two types of errors separately. When the developer is certain that certain errors cannot occur, they will not use the corresponding [catch]** clauses. Here, they are used systematically solely for demonstration purposes;
  • Line 22: You can write either [Exception] or [\Exception]. The first version uses the relative class name, relative to the script’s namespace. Since the script has no namespace, its namespace is the root of the namespaces: [\]. Therefore, writing [Exception] here is equivalent to writing [\Exception]. It is preferable to use the absolute names of the predefined PHP classes, in a script that does not have its own namespace. Thus, if you decide to assign a namespace to this script, using the absolute class names remains valid, whereas in the other case, changing the namespace will cause errors with the relative class names;
  • Line 23: When an exception occurs, the [Exception::getMessage] method retrieves the error message for the exception. The same applies to an error of type [TypeError]. In the [Person::setFirstName] method, [throw new \Exception("The first name must not be empty")] was written. This is the message retrieved by the [getMessage] method in Example 3 (line 5 of the results);
  • line 4 of the results: the error message for [TypeError]. Starting with PHP 8.0, it identifies the problematic parameter by its number and name: “Argument #3 ($age) must be of type int, string given.” The error messages in PHP 8 are more specific than those in PHP 7.

docs.title: 5.8. Adding a method that acts as a second constructor
docs.text:
In PHP, it is not possible to have multiple constructors with different parameters that would allow an object to be constructed in various ways. Therefore, methods can be used to act as constructors. The [Person] class has two such methods:

    public function initWithPerson(Person $p): void
    {
        // initializes the current object with a person $p
        $this->__construct($p->firstName, $p->lastName, $p->age);
    }

    // static factory method (named constructor)
    public static function fromPerson(Person $p): self
    {
        // creates a new person, a copy of the person $p
        return new self($p->firstName, $p->lastName, $p->age);
    }

Comments

  • Lines 72–76: The [initWithPerson] method allows the values of the attributes of another [Person] object to be assigned to the current object. Here, it calls the constructor [__construct], but this is not required. It could initialize the attributes of the class [Person] on its own. Note that a method of the [Person] class has access to the private attributes of all [Person] objects, not just those of [$this];
  • lines 79–83: The [fromPerson] method is another way of doing this, which is more common today. It is a static method (keyword [static]): it does not apply to an object but to the class. It is called using the notation [Person::fromPerson($p)]. It creates a new object using [new self(...)]: the keyword [self] refers to the class in which the code is written, in this case [Person]. The return type [self] indicates that the method returns an object of this class. Such a method is called a named constructor or factory method. We’ll come back to static methods a little later.

The new class [Person] is used by the following script, [classes-06.php]:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion of the definition of the Person class
require_once __DIR__ . "/Person.php";
// declaration of the qualified name of the Person class
use Examples\Person;

// test
// creating a Person object
try {
    $p = new Person("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
} catch (\Exception $e) {
    print "error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    exit;
}
// identity of this person
print "person=$p\n";
// creating a second person
try {
    $p2 = new Person("Laure", "Adeline", 67);
} catch (\Exception $e) {
    print "error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    exit;
}
// initializing the first one with the values of the second one
try {
    $p->initWithPerson($p2);
} catch (\Exception $e) {
    print "error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    exit;
}
// check
print "person=$p\n";

// creating a third person with the named constructor
$p3 = Person::fromPerson($p2);
print "person=$p3\n";
// $p3 and $p2 are two different objects having the same values
print "same object: " . var_export($p3 === $p2, true) . "\n";
print "same values: " . var_export($p3 == $p2, true) . "\n";
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-06.php
person=[Paul,Langevin,48]
person=[Laure,Adeline,67]
person=[Laure,Adeline,67]
same object: false
same values: true

Comments

  • Line 17, line 26, line 33: It is common that, after an exception, you must stop the execution of a console script if the error encountered is unrecoverable. This is not the case in a web script: you do not stop the script’s execution but instead display an error page. If you are inside a function, the [exit] statement will not be used; instead, [return] will be used: the script’s execution is not halted ([exit]), but the function is exited ([return]) after an error has been set;
  • line 39: call to the named constructor;
  • line 42: the [===] operator applied to two objects evaluates to true if they are the same object (same address). [$p3] and [$p2] are two distinct objects (line 5 of the results);
  • line 43: the operator [==], when applied to two objects of the same class, evaluates to true if their attributes have the same values (line 6 of the results). The function [var_export] returns a PHP representation of its parameter, in this case [true] or [false].

docs.title: 5.9. Validity checks using property hooks (PHP 8.4)
docs.text:
The previous class, [Person], protects its attributes by making them private and requiring external code to use the [get] and [set] methods. PHP 8.4 offers another solution: property hooks. A public attribute can be accompanied by a [set] hook—the code executed each time the attribute is written—and a [get] hook—the code executed each time the attribute is read. This preserves the simplicity of writing [$p->age = 49] while maintaining control over the values. This is demonstrated by the script [classes-23.php]:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Person
{
    // public attribute with a [set] hook: validation is done on every write
    public string $firstName {
        set(string $value) {
            $value = trim($value);
            if ($value === "") {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("The first name must not be empty");
            }
            $this->firstName = $value;
        }
    }

    public string $lastName {
        set(string $value) {
            $value = trim($value);
            if ($value === "") {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("The last name must not be empty");
            }
            $this->lastName = $value;
        }
    }

    // without an explicit parameter, the received value is called [$value]
    public int $age {
        set {
            if ($value < 0) {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("The age must be a positive or zero integer");
            }
            $this->age = $value;
        }
    }

    // virtual attribute: it only has a [get] hook and takes no space in the object
    public string $identity {
        get => "[$this->firstName,$this->lastName,$this->age]";
    }

    // constructor: the assignments go through the [set] hooks
    public function __construct(string $firstName, string $lastName, int $age)
    {
        $this->firstName = $firstName;
        $this->lastName = $lastName;
        $this->age = $age;
    }
}

// test
$p = new Person(" Paul ", "Langevin", 48);
print "person=$p->identity\n";
// the attributes are public: they are read and written directly
$p->age = 49;
print "age=$p->age\n";
// but writing always goes through the [set] hook
foreach (["firstName" => "  ", "age" => -4] as $attribute => $value) {
    try {
        $p->$attribute = $value;
    } catch (\InvalidArgumentException $e) {
        print "Error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    }
}
// a virtual attribute without a [set] hook cannot be written
try {
    $p->identity = "?";
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// the object has remained valid
print "person=$p->identity\n";
var_dump($p);

Results:

> php classes-23.php
person=[Paul,Langevin,48]
age=49
Error: The first name must not be empty
Error: The age must be a positive or zero integer
Error: Property Person::$identity is read-only
person=[Paul,Langevin,49]
object(Person)#1 (3) {
  ["firstName"]=>
  string(4) "Paul"
  ["lastName"]=>
  string(8) "Langevin"
  ["age"]=>
  int(49)
}

Comments

  • lines 9–17: The public attribute [firstName] is followed by a block enclosed in curly braces that contains its hooks. Here, there is only one hook, [set];
  • line 10: The hook [set] receives the value to be assigned to the attribute. It validates it using [trim], checks it, and throws an exception if it is incorrect;
  • line 15: Inside its hooks, [$this->firstName] specifies the memory location of the attribute: the value is stored there. Everywhere else, [$this->firstName] goes through the hooks;
  • line 13: an exception of type [\InvalidArgumentException] is thrown; this is a predefined class derived from [\Exception] and more specific than it, signaling an invalid argument. We will cover the predefined PHP exceptions in the chapter on exceptions;
  • line 31: when the hook [set] does not declare a parameter, the received value is available in the implicit variable [$value], and its type is that of the attribute;
  • Lines 40–42: An attribute that has only one hook, [get], and never references its own memory location is a virtual attribute: it is calculated on each read and occupies no space in the object. The notation [get => expression] is a shorthand for a hook [get] that evaluates to the value of the expression;
  • lines 45–50: the constructor assigns the attributes; these assignments are performed via the hooks [set]. Validation is therefore performed during construction as well as during any subsequent modification, without using the methods [set];
  • line 54: the first name [" Paul "] is cleared by the hook [set];
  • line 57: the attribute [age] is modified directly, but via its hook [set];
  • Lines 60–66: An attempt is made to assign invalid values. The notation [$p->$attribute] uses the contents of the variable [$attribute] as the attribute name. The [set] hooks throw their exceptions (lines 4–5 of the results);
  • line 69: the virtual attribute [identity] does not have a hook [set]: it is read-only (line 6 of the results);
  • line 75: the object retained valid values. [var_dump] shows only three attributes: the virtual attribute [identity] does not exist in memory.

Property hooks have long existed in other languages (C#, Kotlin, Swift). They eliminate the need to write getters and setters “just in case”: you start with a simple public attribute and add a hook when validation becomes necessary, without changing the code that uses the class.

docs.title: 5.10. Asymmetric Visibility (PHP 8.4)
docs.text:
It’s often the case that a property needs to be readable by everyone but modifiable only by the class itself. In the past, we would have written a private property and a public getter. PHP 8.4 allows you to set different visibility levels for reading and writing a property: this is called asymmetric visibility. The script [classes-24.php] demonstrates this using a bank account:

<?php

// strict respect of the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class BankAccount
{
    // asymmetric visibility: public read, private write
    public private(set) float $balance = 0.0;

    // parameter promotion also accepts asymmetric visibility
    public function __construct(public private(set) string $holder)
    {
    }

    // only the methods of the class can modify the balance
    public function deposit(float $amount): void
    {
        if ($amount <= 0) {
            throw new \InvalidArgumentException("The amount must be positive");
        }
        $this->balance += $amount;
    }

    public function withdraw(float $amount): void
    {
        if ($amount <= 0 || $amount > $this->balance) {
            throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Withdrawal of $amount impossible");
        }
        $this->balance -= $amount;
    }
}

// test
$account = new BankAccount("Paul Langevin");
$account->deposit(100);
$account->withdraw(30);
// direct reading of the attributes, without a getter
print "{$account->holder}: {$account->balance} euros\n";
// writing from outside the class is forbidden
try {
    $account->balance = 1_000_000;
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// the class keeps control of the validity of the balance
try {
    $account->withdraw(500);
} catch (\InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    print "Error: " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
print "{$account->holder}: {$account->balance} euros\n";

Results:

> php classes-24.php
Paul Langevin: 70 euros
Error: Cannot modify private(set) property BankAccount::$balance from global scope
Error: Withdrawal of 500 impossible
Paul Langevin: 70 euros

Comments

  • Line 9: The attribute [balance] is public for reading ([public]) and private for writing ([private(set)]). External code can read [$account->balance], but only the class’s methods can modify it. You can also write [protected(set)]: in this case, derived classes can modify the attribute;
  • line 12: asymmetric visibility is also possible for a promoted parameter;
  • lines 17–25: The methods [deposit] and [withdraw] are the only ways to modify the balance. They verify the validity of the operations;
  • line 39: attributes are read directly, without getters. The notation [{$expression}] inside a string enclosed in quotation marks allows for the insertion of an expression more complex than a simple variable;
  • line 42: Writing to the balance from outside the class causes an error (line 3 of the results). The character [_] can be used as a thousands separator in a literal number (PHP 7.4);
